The plainest finish, and the one that shows every repair in the slab beneath it. Metallic floor A pigmented resin worked while wet so the color moves. No two are the same, which is the point and also the risk. Grind and seal The concrete itself is the finish. Ground back, then sealed. Nothing is added on top to fail. What you are actually buying Not a product. Nearly all of what decides whether a coated floor is still good in five years happens before any color goes down, and none of it is visible afterwards: how much of the slab came off, what the moisture read, and whether the cracks were repaired or painted over. So we quote the preparation in detail and in writing, rather than quoting a finish and treating the grinding as something that happens on the day. If a quote you are comparing ours against does not mention a surface profile or a moisture test, those are not two prices for the same job. One number, one quote, and it does not change after the grinder comes out. What you get in writing The moisture reading, and which published test produced it. The surface profile the finish requires, as a number on the published scale. What happens to each crack, priced as its own line rather than absorbed. If we think your slab should not be coated, you hear that before you have paid for anything. You keep all of it whether or not you hire us. Plain Terms covers who does the work, the license and insurance behind it, and the one number you call when something is wrong. Outside the house Driveway and apron coating The slab that takes the sun, the tires and the blown sand. Exterior work is scheduled around weather, not around us. Patio and porch coating Resurfacing the slab you have, rather than breaking it out. Pool deck coating Textured on purpose. A deck has to stay walkable wet and bearable barefoot. Walkways and steps The awkward work: edges, risers, nosings and curves, most of it done by hand. What is different about doing this in Washington County The heat is a working condition, not a talking point St. George recorded 98 days at or above 100°F in 2024, the most on record, and the all-time high is 117°F. July has now set the record two years running. That is what the finished floor lives with. It is also a constraint on the work: resin systems have a published application temperature window and their working time shortens as the slab warms. A July install in an uncooled garage is a scheduling problem before it is anything else. The sand is why the date moves The Utah Geological Survey maps wind-blown sand as one of nine adverse construction conditions for the St. George and Hurricane area, and Washington County publishes it as its own hazard layer. Most counties do not map blowing sand at all. Utah’s Department of Environmental Quality notes that from spring through fall, high winds and dry ground combine into dust storms that “can lead to extremely high levels of particulate matter.” Wet resin holds whatever lands in it, permanently. April is the windiest month here. So an exterior date is a forecast-dependent date, and anybody who books you one three weeks out without saying so is promising something they do not control. The monsoon, and the calendar Flooding is, in Special Study 127’s words, “the most widespread and damaging geologic hazard in southwestern Utah.” It arrives as short heavy cells after long dry spells — St. George has recorded a 78-day dry spell ending with monsoon onset. An exterior coating cannot go onto a wet slab and cannot cure through a storm. At the other end of the year, the reliably non-freezing window here runs March 1 to November 21, and resin has a published minimum cure temperature. An exterior slab in January can sit under it. The ground, and what it does to concrete Gypsiferous soil and rock is another of those nine mapped conditions, and where sulfate is present in the ground it attacks concrete itself. Under the American Concrete Institute exposure classes, a soil sulfate test determines the mix a slab needs — class S1 at 0.10 to 0.20 per cent water-soluble sulfate, S2 at 0.20 to 2.00 per cent where sulfate-resistant cement is required, S3 above that. St. George culinary water itself runs to 451 parts per million sulfate, inside class S1 for water contact. We do not test soil and we are not going to tell you your slab is failing. We will tell you whether your address sits in a mapped zone, show you the county’s own map, and say plainly that the condition of the concrete is a question that comes before the question of what to put on it. Inside the house Basement floor coating A finished floor rather than a subfloor waiting for one. Moisture gets tested first, and that is not optional below grade. Interior concrete floor Laundry rooms, utility rooms, workshops and casitas. Anywhere the slab is the floor. Before, indoors. A crack is repaired as its own step; a coating laid over a moving crack telegraphs it back through. The other failure: water you cannot see Most houses here are built on a slab, and a slab on grade is in permanent contact with the ground. Water vapor moves from the ground up through the concrete toward the room. A coating is a comparatively airtight film laid across the top of that. Where the vapor drive is strong enough, pressure builds underneath and the film blisters or releases. Whether a vapor retarder was laid under your slab was decided the day the house was poured and cannot be changed now. An older house here may have none. That does not rule out a coated floor. It rules out guessing. There are three published tests and they do not measure the same thing: ASTM F2170 reads the internal relative humidity from probes set in holes drilled to 40 per cent of the slab depth. It tells you what the slab will do over time, and it has been displacing the older method since 2002. ASTM F1869 calculates a moisture vapor emission rate from the weight a dish of calcium chloride gains under a sealed dome over three days. It reflects the surface, not the interior, and since 2010 the standard has disallowed it on lightweight concrete. ASTM D4263 , the plastic sheet method, is the quick one — used, in the standard’s own words, “to indicate the presence of capillary moisture in concrete.” It shows surface conditions only. You do not have to know any of that. You have to know it exists, that it produces a number, and that you can ask for the number in writing. We will run it and hand you the reading whether or not you hire us. Commercial and industrial Commercial floor coating Retail, showroom and service floors, sequenced so the business stays open where it can. Warehouse and shop floor Large slabs, forklift traffic and a schedule that belongs to somebody else. The slab underneath Concrete slab assessment Moisture tested to the published methods, the surface profile agreed, and you get the readings whether or not you hire us. Concrete grinding and preparation Diamond grinding to take the slab back past its surface film. It is most of the labor and all of the difference. Failed coating removal and recoat Taking off what is peeling, finding out why it did, and telling you before we quote putting anything back. Concrete cleaning and sealing Washing and sealing bare or stained concrete. Recurring work, not once. Almost every failure is a preparation failure Concrete finishes with a weak, fines-rich film on its surface called laitance. It is a normal product of how a slab is poured and floated, not a defect. It is also not something a coating can bond through. A finish rolled over laitance is bonded to the laitance, and the day the laitance lets go, the floor looks like the coating failed. The requirement is published, and not by us. Sika’s surface preparation guide puts it this way: concrete substrates “must be mechanically prepared to remove cement laitance, existing coatings, curing compounds, and achieve a profile that is clean, dry, and free from dirt, grease, oil.” Diamond grinders, in the same guide’s words, “are used to create a surface profile, remove high spots on a concrete surface and remove coatings.” Shot blasting it calls “the industry standard for surface preparation of concrete.” What grinding leaves behind has a number. The International Concrete Repair Institute publishes the scale in Guideline 310.2R-2013, running from CSP 1 — essentially unchanged concrete with the loose debris removed — through CSP 9 and beyond at exposed aggregate. Physical replica chips exist so a prepared slab can be held against the number and accepted or rejected. Most coating manufacturers now state the profile their product needs on its own data sheet. That is why the useful question is not do you grind . It is what profile did you grind to, and how did you check it. Ask us. Ask whoever else is quoting you. A slab part-way through grinding. The swirls are the passes; the extractor beside it is what keeps the dust out of the air. This work What it looks like on the job. Finished work, before-and-after pairs and the preparation in between. No caption names a town: these were not all shot in Washington County and we are not going to imply otherwise. The control joints are still readable through the finish. They are part of the slab, not a defect in the floor. From above, where the coverage is easiest to judge. Close enough to see the individual chips under the clear coat. Flake is sold as a blend, and the blend is chosen. This one is blue. The blends, as samples. Pick from the chip in daylight, not from a photograph on a phone. The chips before they are thrown. They are vinyl, and they go on by hand. 12 more photographs The base coat, still wet. The flake goes into this, not onto it, which is why there is no second chance at the timing. The coating carried up the wall as a base, so there is no open joint at the floor line for water to sit in. An entry porch. The finish here is a fine broadcast rather than large flake. A quartz broadcast, close up. Coarser than flake, and meant to be. Before, elsewhere. The pale lines are earlier repairs, not cracks in a coating. A finished patio, resurfaced over the slab that was already there. A solid color with no flake. It is the plainest finish and it shows every repair in the slab beneath. The same floor from floor level. Washed down. The mirror is water, not a finish. A walkway and step ground back before anything is applied. The hand grinder is for the edges the big machine cannot reach. The edge at the threshold, which is where a floor is finished well or is not. A basement corridor. Finished concrete is a floor here, not a subfloor waiting for one. 51 photographs in the library, across the pages under this one. Questions we get asked Four of these do not have an answer yet, and they are the four everybody else answers with a number. Where that is the case it says so and says why. What does a garage floor cost? There is no price on this page, and there will not be one until it is a number that holds on the fiftieth job rather than the easiest one. A published price that gets broken is a deceptive practice, not a bad review. What decides it is the slab, not the square footage: how much grinding it needs, what is already on it, what the cracks are doing and what the moisture reads. That is why we look before we quote, and why a price quoted over the phone from a room size is a guess. How long will it last? Most pages selling this in Washington County say fifteen to twenty years. We have not been able to trace that figure to a manufacturer, a standard or a study, so we are not going to repeat it. What we can tell you is what decides it, and it is not the brochure. It is whether the laitance came off, whether the slab was tested for moisture, whether the cracks were repaired or covered, and whether the product going down is rated for the sun it will get. Those are all checkable before the work starts. Is polyaspartic better than epoxy? The honest answer is that “better” is the wrong frame, and that most of what is written about it online is written by people selling one of them. Ultraviolet stability is a property of a specific product, and the manufacturer publishes it. Sherwin-Williams describes polyaspartic floor coating as part of the urethane family and offering “UV-resistant, color-stable protection”; its aliphatic polyaspartic products state UV stability by name on the data sheet. That is checkable, which means its absence is checkable too. So the question to ask is not which chemistry. It is which product is going on my floor, and what does its data sheet say. Ask us, and ask anyone else quoting you. How long before I can park on it? That is set by the product and by the temperature of the slab, and it is printed on the data sheet for the specific system going down. You will be told it before the work starts, in writing, alongside the date. We are not going to print a number here. “One day” is the industry’s favorite claim and it is true of some systems, in some conditions, at some temperatures. A slab at 105°F and a slab at 45°F are not the same job. Can you go over my existing coating? Only if we can establish what it is and that it is sound, and usually we cannot. The safe answer is that it comes off. More to the point, if a coating has already failed once, the first job is finding out why — because a new one over the same unaddressed cause fails the same way. That is its own job and we price it as one. Do I have to empty the garage? Yes, completely, and it is the part people underestimate every time. The floor is ground wall to wall, so nothing can stay in it — including the things on shelves, because grinding dust reaches them. We will tell you exactly what has to be out and by when, and we would rather have that conversation a week early than on the morning. Will the cracks come back? A crack that is not moving is repaired and stays repaired. A crack that is moving — because the slab is settling, heaving or built over something that is — will telegraph back through any coating, usually within a season. We look at what the cracks are doing before quoting anything over them, and if the answer is that the slab is moving, we will tell you that a coating is money spent twice rather than take the job. Does my HOA have to approve it? Your documents are the only authority and we are not going to guess at them. As a general shape: the inside of a garage is almost never an association’s business, and an exterior surface visible from the street sometimes is. We will read yours before you commit. Our HOA pages cover what the recorded documents in the larger communities here actually say. Is it slippery? It depends entirely on the finish, and that is a decision rather than an accident. A full flake broadcast has real texture and grips well wet. A smooth solid color or a metallic does not, which is why we will not put a metallic on a pool deck even if you ask for one. Outside, texture comes before color in the conversation, every time. Do you do commercial work? Yes — retail and showroom floors, warehouses, shops and service bays. The technical job is the same; what changes is that the schedule belongs to you. Work gets sequenced in sections, overnight or across a closure you choose, and which of those applies changes the price openly rather than quietly. It is printed on Sherwin-Williams’ own product data sheet: most coating failures are due to inadequate surface preparation or application . The same sheet adds the part nobody likes to quote — that any preparation short of removing the old coating entirely may shorten how long the new system lasts. The federal wood research laboratory found the same thing from the other direction, and put numbers on it. Bare redcedar left in the sun before painting held its paint for shorter and shorter periods the longer it waited: painted immediately, no peeling after twenty years; weathered one week first, peeling at thirteen years; weathered sixteen weeks first, peeling within three. Their note on it is the unsettling part. After two or three weeks outside, the wood appears unchanged . Which is the whole problem with judging a paint job. Everything that decides how long it lasts is invisible on the day it looks finished, and it stays invisible for about two years. One test you can run before anyone quotes Rub a black cloth, or just your hand, firmly across the sunny side of your house. If it comes away with a chalky film, that is the coating failing, not dirt: ultraviolet light has broken down the resin that binds the pigment, and the loose pigment is what is on your hand. It matters because painting over chalk is the standard way to get intercoat peeling, where the new paint separates from the old, usually within a year. Anyone quoting your house should have an answer for the chalk. Ask what it is. Color that has faded without chalking is a different thing and not a failure of the film. The cloth tells you which one you have. Outside the house Exterior repaint The whole envelope, prepared and coated in the order and the weather the manufacturer publishes. Stucco painting and coating The most common exterior in Washington County, and the one with the most ways to go wrong. Trim, fascia and garage doors The parts the sun destroys first, repainted without doing the whole house. Why an exterior here is a scheduling problem before it is a painting problem The normal daily high in St. George is 101.9°F in July and 99.9°F in August. That is NOAA’s 1991 to 2020 average for this city’s own station, not a record and not a hot year. Now read what the people who make the paint publish. Benjamin Moore caps application of its exterior line at a surface temperature of 100°F. PPG gives 100°F for ambient and substrate. Sherwin-Williams publishes no ceiling but warns that above 80°F its exterior product sets up quickly, and that over 100°F a film can dry before it has had a chance to adhere. Dunn-Edwards, a Southwest company, allows up to 120°F with stated precautions. An average July afternoon in this city is therefore at or past what most of those manufacturers publish — and that is the air temperature. A wall in direct sun is hotter than the air around it. So the work follows the shade around the house rather than the order that would be convenient. South-facing walls get done in the morning. Midday, when the sun is highest, is the wrong time to coat anything. That is not our house rule; it is what Dunn-Edwards publishes in its own hot-weather bulletin, and it is the difference between a coating that bonds and one that dries before it can. And then August August averages 1.07 inches of rain on the same NOAA normals — more than June and July put together, which come to 0.66 between them. The National Weather Service runs the monsoon from June 15 to September 30. Every manufacturer we read says not to apply if rain is expected within two to three hours. A county whose hottest weeks are also its wettest of the summer is one where the calendar matters, and where “we can start Monday” is sometimes the wrong answer. We will tell you when the weather is wrong for the work. It is a cheaper conversation than the one about why it failed. Walls and ceilings Drywall repair and patching Holes, cracks, water damage and the patch somebody else left proud of the wall. Texture matching Knockdown, orange peel or hand texture matched so the repair disappears instead of announcing itself. Popcorn ceiling removal Scraped, retextured and repainted. On a house of a certain age it is tested first, and that is not optional. If your house is old enough, the rules change. Most here are not. Of Washington County’s 88,415 housing units, 7,613 were built before 1980 — about one in eleven, on the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey. In most of this county the federal lead rule does not apply at all, and you should not be sold containment you do not need. Where it does apply — homes built before 1978 — it is specific. Disturbing more than six square feet of painted surface in a room inside, or twenty square feet outside, brings the work under the EPA’s renovation rule, and sanding or scraping counts as disturbing it. Window replacement counts at any size. The rule requires two separate things: the company must be an EPA-certified firm, and a trained, certified renovator must be assigned to the job. Both are checkable, and you should check. EPA publishes a public search for certified firms. Anyone who tells you the rule does not matter on a pre-1978 house is telling you something useful about themselves. Ceilings, before anyone scrapes EPA lists textured paint and patching compounds used on walls and ceilings among the products that have contained asbestos. On a house old enough for that to be a question, the order is test first, scrape second. EPA is equally clear about who takes the sample: a trained and accredited professional, because there is risk in releasing fibers. Its guidance says taking samples yourself is not recommended. If a test comes back positive the work goes to a licensed abatement contractor, and we will say so rather than quietly working around it. How to check anyone’s license applies here too, including ours. Color, approval and the paperwork Before you choose a color, find out who has to approve it In most of Washington County the constraint on an exterior color is not the city. It is the CC&Rs of the community you live in, and the design review committee that reads them. Those documents are recorded, and you are entitled to your own copy. We have read them for ten communities here and published what they say, including how each one’s approval process actually runs and how long its committee takes. HOA rules, community by community What the recorded documents say about approvals, and what Utah statute adds on top of them. If your request was denied What a denial has to contain under Utah law, and what happens next. What we will not tell you We will not tell you a color needs a city permit, or that it does not. Nobody here has read the relevant sections of the St. George or Washington City code, and the honest answer to a question we have not checked is that we have not checked it. One thing worth clearing up, because people conflate them: a house being listed on the National Register carries no restrictions on what the owner does with it. The city says so itself. The zoning overlay downtown is a separate thing with its own review. If your approval is the thing standing between you and a start date, tell us and we will work to it. The quote is the number. There is no second number. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day.

handyman_st_george_ut.text: id="main"> St. George and Washington County Handyman work, and the part of it that needs a license. Most of what people call handyman work, we do — 20 kinds of it, listed below. Utah lets anyone do a lot of it without a contractor license. It does not let anyone do your heating, your gas, or your plumbing system. Here is where that line sits, in the state’s own words, and how to check anyone you call. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. One flat fee to find out what is wrong, credited to the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the state actually says Utah has a handyman exemption. It stops before your furnace. Under Utah Code § 58-55-305(1)(h)(i) , a person can do alteration, repair, remodeling or improvement work on a building without a contractor license as long as the job is worth less than $7,000, including both labor and materials , and including every change and addition to it. That is a real, lawful exemption, and plenty of good people work under it. Then subsection (1)(h)(ii) carves pieces back out, and these are the pieces most likely to be in your house: Plumbing and electrical. Work on a system has to be done by a licensed plumbing or electrical contractor. Work on a component — the statute names “a faucet, toilet, fixture, device, outlet, or electrical switch” — may be done by a licensed journeyman. Those are two different answers, and which one applies depends on the job, not on the price. Heating, ventilation and air conditioning. Installation, repair or replacement “must be performed by an HVAC contractor licensed by the division.” There is no dollar figure attached to that one. It applies to a $200 repair. Gas appliances and combustion systems. Must be done by someone certified under § 58-55-308(2). Alarm systems, fire sprinklers and radon mitigation. Each has its own licensed trade, named in the same subsection. Over $3,000 , whoever is working under the exemption has to file a one-time affirmation with the state that they carry public liability insurance, and workers’ compensation if they have employees. So the useful question is not “are you licensed.” It is “which license, and does it cover this job.” Ask that of anybody you call. Ask it of us. Utah Code § 58-55-305, Exemptions from licensure, as effective May 7, 2025 (PDF) (opens in a new tab) . Read on September 29, 2026. The ceiling was $3,000 until recently and a good deal of what is written about this online still says so; the figure above is the current text. Our working notes are in how to check a Utah contractor . Ours, so you can check it One license, named for the trade it covers. We hold one Utah license , and this site prints it beside the trade it actually covers rather than on its own, because a bare number under a page about faucets would read as covering the faucets: Heating and air conditioning — Utah DOPL 14276430-5501 . Check it on the state’s public lookup (opens in a new tab) , before you call us back. Anything needing an electrician is done by our licensed electrical partner, under their license, and we tell you who before they arrive. Ask for the insurance certificate at the same time. It comes the same day you ask. The work 20 small jobs, grouped by the trade that covers them. Every one of these has its own page, with what it involves and what decides the price here. Around the plumbing A fixture, a valve, a spigot. The statute treats these as components rather than systems, and says so by name. Drywall repair and patching Trim, doors and baseboards Interior painting Cabinet painting and refinishing Trim, fascia and garage doors All painting and drywall Heating and air This is the one place where the exemption stops outright. It has to be a licensed HVAC contractor, at any price. permanent_lighting_st_george_ut.text: id="main"> St. George and Washington County Permanent lighting. Put it up once. Orange and purple, for October. Red and green on a single-story stucco house with a tile roof. Royal blue and white, or whichever colors your team wears. Red, white and blue on a stucco and stone ranch. Cool white and icy blue on a two-story with a terracotta roof. Warm white, the setting it runs on most nights. October December Game day July Winter Warm white Permanent lighting runs in a small track tucked under the eaves, and it stays up all year. Warm white on an ordinary night. Orange and purple in October. Whatever you like in December. You change it with a remote, not a ladder. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Want it up for the holidays? Ask now. You get the install date and the whole price before you agree to anything. Read our Plain Terms Three houses, filmed the same night. No sound on any of them. Each one is described underneath, so you know what it shows before you press play. Warm white, from the driveway to the back porch The everyday setting. One house, walked from the front gable past the garage to the covered back porch. Each light throws a soft scallop down the siding, and the porch ceiling and posts are lit without a fixture on them. 26 seconds. Front door and down the side of the house A second house. From the front door, around the corner and along the side wall to the back. The lights sit tight under the eave; what you see is the wall they light, not the lights. 20 seconds. What goes up, in daylight A third house, during the install. A thin white track is fed along and pressed up into place under the eave, one length at a time. Once it is up, it follows the line of the roof. 27 seconds. All three are customers’ houses in Washington County, Utah, filmed October 17, 2026 . What the remote changes Everything on it is adjustable. That is how it follows the rules. Three towns here have rules about lights on a house, and all three are about things this system lets you change. So it is set to your town before we leave, and you are shown how to change it. Color Any color you like, one color or several along the run, or warm white. How warm the white is Set in Kelvin, so it can sit at or under your town’s limit: 3,000K in Ivins, 2,700K on new construction in Toquerville. Brightness Turned down for an ordinary night, up for a party. Steady or moving Patterns that chase or twinkle are there for a holiday. Ivins, Toquerville and La Verkin prohibit moving light outside holiday lighting, so the everyday setting there is steady. When it is on On and off at the times you set. Toquerville turns holiday lights off from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., and a schedule does that without anyone remembering. The section for each town’s rule is in Before it goes up: your town , further down this page. One install, twelve months A year on the same roofline Nothing comes down between any of these. Each one is a setting you choose from the remote, and you can save the ones you like. Most nights Warm white, steady January Cool white and icy blue February Red and pink Spring Soft pastels July Red, white and blue Football season Your team's colors October Orange and purple December Red and green, or all white How it goes Call, or send a message Tell us the town and whether there is an HOA. Those two answers decide what the everyday setting can be. We measure and quote Which rooflines, how many feet, where it plugs in. You get one number for the whole job, and that is the number you pay. It goes up The track under the eaves, then the lights, the power supply and the controller. It is set to your town Before we leave, the everyday setting meets your town’s rule, and you are shown the remote and how to save your own settings. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. Why people leave it up It looks like part of the house Most nights it is warm white, and what you notice is the roofline, not a string of lights. The track sits tight under the eave and follows it. When you want color, it is there: a holiday, October, a birthday, a team’s game. Then it goes back to white, and nothing has to come down. The house is lit The driveway, the porch and the walk to the door are lit when you get home after dark. You can see the step. So can whoever is coming to the door. And nobody goes up a ladder every November to hang strings and every January to take them down again. On a flat-roofed desert-modern house the track runs under each overhang instead of a gable. The porch on the same house. Washington County, Utah, October 17, 2026 . What the job is Included Measuring the rooflines you want lit, and quoting the whole run as one number The track, mounted under the eaves along those runs The lights, the power supply and the controller Setting up the remote with you before we leave Not included A new outdoor outlet or circuit. If there is no power where the run needs it, that is our licensed electrical partner’s work, quoted separately before anything starts. Repairs to fascia or soffit. If the wood we would mount to is damaged, you hear about it before anything is fastened to it. Path and garden lighting, too The same page covers the ground: low-voltage path, step and uplighting on a transformer and a timer. Good landscape lighting is aiming and restraint: fewer fittings, aimed carefully, at a lower level than most people expect. The failure is glare, fittings you look at instead of the thing they light. It is aimed after dark, because that is the only time aiming can be done properly. Before it goes up: your town Most towns here do not regulate lights on a house. Three do, and the rules are about color, movement and late hours, which is exactly what this system can change. So here is what each one says, with the section, before you choose a setting. Ivins The lighting chapter applies to every single-family home (§ 16.23.108(1)). Outdoor lamps on a house must be 3,000 Kelvin or warmer (§ 16.23.105(3)(b)). Lights that flash, blink or seem to move are prohibited, but “Holiday lighting is permitted” (§ 16.23.105(22)(b)); the code gives no dates. It also requires outdoor lighting to be fully shielded (§ 16.23.105(5)). Whether eave lights meet that is the city’s call, so ask the city before you buy. Toquerville 2,700 Kelvin is mandatory on new construction (§ 10-24-4(A)(5)). Holiday lights are turned off from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. (§ 10-24-4(B)(3)). Moving or blinking light is prohibited, holiday lighting excepted (§ 10-24-4(D)(7)(b)). La Verkin Flashing, blinking or moving light is prohibited (§ 4-7-4(F)(3)), and holiday lighting is exempt from the chapter (§ 4-7-4(G)(1)). No color limit. St. George The outdoor lighting chapter excludes detached single-family homes (§ 10-14-1(A)). A townhome or a commercial building is a different question. Washington, Santa Clara, Cedar City We read each city’s code and found no lighting rule that reaches a house. Codes as published on October 17, 2026. In Hurricane, ask the city: its lighting section’s reach to a single-family home is not clear from its own text. And your HOA A house in an HOA Utah law says an association rule may not stop you displaying a holiday decoration on your lot or the outside of your house. It also lets the association set a “reasonable time, place, and manner restriction” on anything visible from outside: which months, which hours, which colors. That protection does not reach a house whose outside the association maintains, which is common in townhome communities. And the law does not say whether lights left on warm white in July count as a holiday decoration at all. Read your association’s rules before you choose colors or a schedule. Utah Code § 57-8a-218(3). A condominium For condos the state’s protection stops at the inside of the unit. The eaves of a condo building are usually common area, so the association decides, not the owner. Ask them first. Utah Code § 57-8-8.1(6). The night sky DarkSky International suggests mounting roofline lights under the eaves, choosing warm tones and turning them off at a reasonable hour. Under the eaves is where these go, and warm white is the everyday setting. What people ask before they buy Can you see it during the day? Yes. You see a thin track along the underside of the eave, which is what the daylight clip above shows. Anyone who tells you it is invisible is selling, not describing. What it is not is a string of bulbs and clips on your gutter. Does it go through the roof? No. It mounts under the eave, not on the roof covering, so nothing goes through shingles or tile. That is also why a tile roof is not a problem: the track never touches the tile. What about stucco? The second clip above is a stucco house. The track goes on the eave; the stucco below it is the wall it lights. Is this what people call permanent Christmas lights? Same product. The difference is what it does the other ten months: most nights it runs warm white, and it never comes down. Do I need an electrician? Usually not for the lights. Utah’s definition of electrical work excludes “work involving class two or class three power-limited circuits as defined in the National Electrical Code,” and that is what a listed Class 2 power supply is (Utah Code § 58-55-102(18)(b)(v); the same words move to § 58-55-301(2)(b)(v) on January 1, 2027). If there is no outdoor outlet where the run needs one, adding it is electrical work, and our licensed electrical partner does it. How long do the lights last? Every brand prints an hour figure, and they are not comparable: one local seller prints two different ones on the same page. The figure is about the LEDs, not the power supply or the controller, which are what usually stop a system. Compare the warranty instead: how many years, on which parts, and who comes out to honor it. What does it cost to run? Arithmetic, not a promise. Ask for the system’s wattage. Watts, divided by 1,000, times the hours it is on each night, times 365, times the rate on your power bill, is the year. Turning the brightness down and setting a schedule both lower it. How is it priced? By the house: how many feet of roofline you want lit, how many stories, how many corners and gables, how many separately controlled zones, and whether an outlet has to be added. You get one number for all of it, and that is the number you pay. Will it make the house safer? It makes the walk to the door, the step and the driveway easier to see at night, and that is all we will claim. The studies that print a crime figure are about street lighting, not a house’s eaves, and the Justice Department’s own guide on home burglary calls lighting’s effect “highly context-specific.” What we can show you in writing Every line traces to a document we read in full. The number after a sentence points to the research below. Rodents are the quiet failure mode for outdoor wiring. University of Arizona Extension records roof rats gnawing electrical wiring as a fire hazard, and they travel along wires, rafters and rooftops at night. 1 Palms are part of that problem. Roof rats nest in the crowns of palm trees, especially where old fronds have not been removed, which puts them directly above the fixtures and the wire runs most people light a palm with. 1 Sun does not usually destroy the plastic body of a fitting. It hardens and cracks the gaskets, seals and flexible parts, and that is where outdoor equipment actually fails. On PVC the surface discoloration reaches only about 0.002 inches deep. 1 Where this comes from Every line above traces to a document we read in full. The number after a sentence points to the research below; hover it for the section. If you find a line wrong, tell us and we will fix it and say so. Environment, water and ground research, August 2026 Compiled from the cities' own water quality reports, Utah Geological Survey Special Study 127, the Utah State Hazard Mitigation Plan, Washington County GIS hazard layers, NOAA climate records, EPA radon zones and Census QuickFacts. 2 sections cited. Hover a number above for the section. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included What is the track made of, and what is it fastened to? If one light fails, is it replaced on its own, or the whole run? What warranty comes with the lights and the controller, and who honors it? If it stops working in year four, who comes out: you, or a dealer who may not be here? Does the warm white setting meet my town’s color limit? Where does it plug in, and is that outlet GFCI-protected? Is the power supply listed Class 2, or just low voltage? They are not the same thing. Up once. Changed from the remote. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays.

There are 1,057 published facts across these pages — about the water, the ground, the weather, the city’s rules, the associations and the rebates — and 71 documents behind them. Every one of those documents was opened and read before anything was written, and every link below has been followed. You should not have to take our word for any of it. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Start here Your town Almost nothing true of St. George is true of Cedar City, and the four communities out past the city line have no city water department at all. So the research is kept per town rather than pooled, and this is the way in. St. George , Washington County 121 facts, from 48 documents. What is missing, and why The figures we took out The research holds more numbers than the site publishes. Where a figure could not be traced to a document somebody can read, it is flagged in the data and it does not appear on any page. There is a build check whose only job is to catch a number that is held back in the data and asserted in prose somewhere else, because that contradiction is how a site ends up believing its own estimate. Some specific things you will not find here. There is no hardiness zone or winter temperature for the high communities, because the only figure available came from a third-party zip-code lookup rather than the USDA’s own tool. There are no paver base depths or compaction percentages, because the engineering bodies that publish them refused automated retrieval and nobody has opened the paper copy. There is no thermostat savings percentage, because the widely-quoted federal one could not be found on a federal page. Thirteen documents were dropped while this page was being built. Two had gone dead. Ten sat behind a filter that refuses anything that is not a browser, so a human has to open them and nobody had. One looked like a county government address and was not: the registrable domain belonged to a private records vendor. It had been backing fourteen facts. The documents All 71 , grouped by what they answer Primary documents, which means the issuing body’s own: a city’s water report rather than a summary of it, the statute rather than an article about the statute, the manufacturer’s warranty rather than a sales page. A document covering two subjects is listed under both, so there are 89 entries below and 71 documents. Every link was followed on 2026-10-15 , and each opens in a new tab. If one has gone dead since, tell us at info@stgeorgehomeservices.com and we will fix it and say so. Water What comes out of the tap, from each city's own annual report. Limited gas tankless water heater warranty — A. O. Smith (PDF) Excludes damage from hard water above 7 grains per gallon in a single-family home, and above 4 for other applications. St. George water runs 18 to 22. Tank water heater warranty 238-45005-00 — Bradford White (PDF) Excludes failure from sediment or lime precipitate in the tank, and voids on removal of the anode. Anode replacement is maintenance; anode deletion is a void. 2024 Water Quality Report — City of St. George (PDF) , for St. George Water Distribution Division, including the published softener setting — City of St. George , for St. George The source of the 18 grains per gallon figure, with a stated maximum of 22. It comes from the utility rather than from anyone selling a softener. 2024 Consumer Confidence Report — Ivins City (PDF) , for Ivins NPE-A series warranty — Navien NPN-U series warranty — Navien Limited warranty, tankless water heaters — Noritz (PDF) Voids outright above 12 grains per gallon. RTGH gas tankless warranty guide — Rheem (PDF) Caps total hardness at 200 mg per litre, about 11.7 grains per gallon. 2025 Consumer Confidence Report (2024 data) — Santa Clara City (PDF) , for Santa Clara Drinking water arsenic rule history — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency The federal maximum contaminant level for arsenic is 10 parts per billion. A water softener does nothing to arsenic; cation exchange does not remove it. Lead regulations — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Public water system records — Utah Division of Water Rights The state's own system-by-system record: who runs a water system, what it draws from and how many people it serves. The main valve is usually at the garage wall, outside near the front hose bib, or in the water heater closet. If it will not turn, do not force it — use the curb stop at the meter box instead. Notice which water it is. Clear and under pressure at a fixture inside the house is the culinary side. Water surfacing in the yard, at a valve box or along an irrigation run — especially if it is cloudy, and especially in July or August — may be the city’s pressurized irrigation instead. Tell us which one you are looking at; it changes the answer. Call us either way. If you cannot tell which system it is, that is the normal answer and it is the first thing we will work out with you on the phone. A person picks up at any hour. Hurricane , specifically The pressurized irrigation system, and why it matters at 9 p.m. Hurricane City’s irrigation water comes out of the Virgin River through the Quail Lake pipeline, sits in a settling pond, and passes a filter station that takes it down to 200 microns. Two hundred microns is about the thickness of two sheets of paper. It is filtered enough to run through a sprinkler and nowhere near clean enough to drink, and the city does not pretend otherwise. It also runs muddy for a few weeks in most Julys and Augusts . That is normal, it is documented, and it is the single most common reason somebody in this town thinks they have an emergency when they have a season. Two practical consequences. First, a break on that line is the city’s to fix rather than ours, and we will tell you that on the phone rather than bill you for a visit to say it. Second, if anyone has ever cross-connected irrigation to the house supply, that is not a repair, it is a contamination problem, and the backflow assembly needs checking before anything else happens. That is one of the few things in this trade that is genuinely urgent at any hour, and it is ours. Which subdivisions are on it? The city’s own page does not list them, so nobody can tell you from a map — including us. Ring us with your address and we will work it out with you. The other thing worth knowing here is what actually fails in a Hurricane winter. Lows sit right at freezing rather than well below it, so the pipes that burst are the exposed ones — hose bibs, backflow assemblies, pool equipment, attic runs — and not the pipes inside your walls. If you are going away in January, the thing to protect is outside. Checkable What is written down about Hurricane . It is a camera down the cleanout , which tells you how far the blockage is and therefore whose pipe it is in. The reading is the obvious one: individual septic, house by house , rather than a municipal main at the street. That matters because the same symptom means something different. In town, several fixtures slow at once usually means a blockage in the lateral between the house and the city main. Out here the same symptom is just as likely to mean the tank is full, or the drainfield has stopped accepting water. Those are not plumbing repairs. They are a pump-out, or in the bad case a drainfield problem, and no amount of work inside the house fixes either. So here is the thing to refuse. If somebody turns up and wants to hydro jet your line before anyone has looked at the tank, say no. Jetting a line that drains into a failed field pushes the problem thirty feet further away and buys you a few weeks. It is the most expensive way to not fix something. Camera first, tank level second, and then a decision. The rest of it is ordinary. accessibility.text: id="main"> Accessibility This site is built to be read by anyone, on any device, in any light. A company that helps people stay in their homes should have a website older eyes and hands can use. So this one is built to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, version 2.2, level AA, and past it where it matters for our readers: Body text is 18 pixels. Nothing on the site is smaller than 16. Text contrast is at least 7 to 1 against the background. Every button and link is at least 48 pixels tall, so it can be tapped without precision. The phone number is in the same place on every page. Nothing opens on hover. Nothing moves. Nothing has a time limit. Every form field has a visible label. Errors are explained in words, not just a red border. The whole site works with a keyboard alone, and with screen readers. You can zoom the page to 200 percent and it still works. If something doesn’t work for you Tell us. Email info@stgeorgehomeservices.com , call, or use the contact form. Say which page, what device you were using, and what went wrong. We read that inbox, and we’ll fix real problems within 30 days. If you can’t use part of this site, you can do anything the site does by phone: ask a question, get an estimate, book a visit. Call (435) 850-0053 A person answers.

privacy.text: id="main"> Privacy What this website collects, and what happens to it. Last updated October 8, 2026 . If we change anything here, the date changes with it. This is a short page because there is not much to say. We are a plumbing, accessible living, landscape and heating and air company. The website exists so you can read about the work and get hold of us. It does not sell anything, it does not run advertising, and it does not sell or rent anything you tell us to anyone. What you send us on purpose The contact form asks for your name, your phone number and a few words about what is going on. An email address is optional. When you press send, the form emails what you wrote to our own mailboxes, and if you gave an email address it sends you a copy so you have a record too. The email is delivered through Resend, a mail delivery service, and lands in mailboxes run on Microsoft 365. Nothing about it is automated beyond that: a person reads it and a person calls you. We keep what you sent for as long as we need it to do the work and to keep our own job records. If you want it deleted, email info@stgeorgehomeservices.com and say so, and we will, unless we are required to keep a record of a job we did for you. Anything you tell us on the phone or at the house goes into the same job records, for the same reasons: to do the work, to honor the guarantee on it, and to answer the phone knowledgeably when you call back. Giveaway entries If you enter our giveaway at /win , we collect your name and phone number, and an email address if you choose to give one. We use them to run the giveaway: to count your entry, to remove duplicates, and to call you if you win. If you give an email address, we send you a copy of your entry and nothing else. There is a box on the form that signs you up for our email newsletter and says we may call or text you about home services. It is optional and it starts unchecked. We record whether you checked it, the exact wording you saw, and when. If you did not check it, you will not get the newsletter and we will not call or text you to sell you anything. If you did, you can stop either at any time: unsubscribe from the newsletter, reply STOP to a text, or email info@stgeorgehomeservices.com . Entries arrive by email, through the same Resend and Microsoft 365 route as the contact form. If you did not check the box, we delete your entry 90 days after the drawing. We never sell entries to anyone. What the site collects on its own Google Analytics. This site uses Google Analytics 4 to count which pages are read and roughly where readers are. It sets first-party cookies in your browser (the ones that begin with _ga ), and it sends Google the page you are on, the kind of device and browser you are using, and your approximate location worked out from your connection. We use it to see which guides people actually read. We do not use it for advertising, and we do not connect it to your name. Google describes what it does with this data at policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites . You can block it by refusing cookies in your browser or with Google’s own opt-out add-on , and the site works exactly the same either way. Server logs. The site is hosted on Vercel. Like every web host, it keeps ordinary server logs: the address your connection comes from, the page requested and the time. Those exist to keep the site running and to spot abuse, and we do not use them to identify anyone. That is the whole list. There is no advertising pixel, no chat widget and no session recording. The only mailing list is the newsletter, and you are on it only if you asked to be, on the giveaway form. If that ever changes, this page changes first. Other sites we link to Our footer links to our Facebook page, and some guides link to city, county and state documents. Once you leave this site, the site you land on has its own rules, and they are not ours. Children This site is written for homeowners and is not directed at children. We do not knowingly collect anything from anyone under 18. Questions Ask a person. Email info@stgeorgehomeservices.com , call, or use the contact form . That inbox is read every day, weekends included. Call (435) 850-0053 A person answers.

A heat pump water heater in a 110 degree garage The usual objection to a heat pump water heater is that it chills the room it sits in. Here that is the feature, and the real questions are different. They are different jobs, and on some pipe a jetter is the wrong tool entirely. Look up your property's hazards in the county's own maps Washington County publishes 24 free hazard map layers built on Utah Geological Survey Special Study 127. How to read them, and what each means for your pipes. Gray pipe, 1978 to the mid-90s: how to tell, and what to do Polybutylene is gray, flexible, and stamped PB2110. Washington County's housing stock is not old enough for clay sewers and is exactly the right age for this. Radon in a slab-on-grade house Washington County sits in the EPA's middle radon band. That predicts nothing about your house. A test does, and it costs almost nothing. Closing up a St. George second home for the summer Everyone writes about winterizing. Here the house sits empty through 100 degree heat and monsoon season, with the irrigation running for nobody. That is the risk worth planning for. Slab leaks in a slab-on-grade house, and where your shutoff is A warm spot on the floor, a bill that jumped, water you can hear with everything off. How the leak gets found, and what to settle before anyone cuts. Why your relief valve drips, and then stops A relief valve that weeps for a few minutes and then quits is almost never a bad valve. It is thermal expansion in a closed system, and it has a fix. Why a sewer replacement costs more here The national trenchless market runs on old pipe. St. George mostly has young pipe in bad ground. That changes which method applies, and it is the reason the number is higher. Why your water heater has to be strapped here Utah requires your water heater to be anchored, everywhere in the state. St. George's own design criteria show why it matters more here. It is two in the morning and something is wrong What is an emergency, what can wait until the daytime rate, and the three things to do before you call anybody at all. How to check a contractor before you let them in the house The license number is two numbers, not one. Utah law says they have to give it to you on request — and a written contract with a licensed contractor is what stops a subcontractor you never met from putting a lien on your house. The gray pipe: how to tell if your house has polybutylene Installed from about 1978 to the mid-1990s, it degrades from the inside where nobody can see it, and about one home in three in Washington County was built in the two decades it was on the market. The class-action money closed in 2009. Here is how to identify it yourself in ten minutes. Accessible living Curbless walk-in showers: the complete guide A standard 60-inch tub occupies the same footprint as a 60 by 30 roll-in shower. The numbers, the slab, the hard water, and what the research honestly says. Does changing the house actually help? The best evidence gives two answers, and they point in different directions. One of them helps us sell work. The other does not. Both are printed below. Grab bars: where they go, and what holds them The standard is 250 pounds of force. The wall behind the bar matters more than the bar. And the objection is almost never that they do not work. Does my HOA have to approve a bathroom remodel? Since May 6, 2026, a Utah HOA declaration may not restrict the interior of your home except for the safety of neighbors. What that means for a bathroom. Your HOA cannot make you use their contractor Four separate provisions of Utah law say an association may not restrict you to its preferred vendor list. Two bind declarations, two bind rules. Here is where each one sits. The Utah HOA Ombudsman, and how to escalate Utah has had a state office for association disputes since 2025. It is narrower than most people expect, and knowing the boundary before you pay the $150 is the whole trick. Walk-in tub or walk-in shower? We install both, so we have no reason to steer you. Here is the comparison on the points that actually differ: the fill and the drain, the door seal, the threshold, and what each one does to the house. Who pays for accessibility work in Utah Six real funding routes, what each one actually pays, and the order to work them in. Most of them require authorization before the first tile comes off. Here is where turf still makes sense, and what planted conversion does instead. Defensible space, water savings and your wildfire fee Utah HB 48 took effect on January 1, 2026. If your property is inside the high risk boundary, a county officer now assesses an annual fee on it. The work that lowers your classification is mostly the same work that lowers your water bill. Getting a Level 2 charger installed here The federal credit expired on June 30, 2026 and half the internet has not noticed. Which utility serves you depends on which side of the Virgin River you live on. And you probably do not need the panel upgrade you were quoted. Above the flood zone and still at risk In 2005 the Santa Clara River destroyed about 30 homes at roughly half the 100 year flow. The mechanism was bank erosion, not rising water. emergency_plumbing.text: id="main"> Emergency plumbing Emergency plumbing Before you call anyone, shut the water off. Here's how. Then tell us what you're seeing. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day. We'll tell you honestly whether this can wait until morning. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day. Is this an emergency? Some of these need us right now. Most don't. We'll tell you which you've got. If it can wait until 8 a.m., we'll say so, and you'll pay the daytime rate. Call now These don't wait. No water to the house. A leak you cannot stop. A burst pipe. Sewage coming up through a tub, shower, or floor drain. A water heater leaking from the tank body. Not the relief valve, not a fitting. The tank itself. Water near an electrical panel, outlets, or where the power comes into the house. A main line break. A gas smell. Leave the house. Call 911 and Dominion Energy from outside. Not a plumber. Same day, but not an emergency Call in the morning and you'll pay the daytime rate. One fixture clogged while the other drains run fine. No hot water, with cold water working. Uncomfortable, not urgent, and cheaper to fix at the day rate. A toilet that won't stop running. It's wasting water and money, not flooding. A leaking supply stop you've been able to shut off. A relief valve dripping on the water heater. Schedule it Call when you're ready. A dripping faucet. A slow drain. Low pressure at one fixture. A fixture you want replaced. A water heater near the end of its life but not leaking. Water that tastes or smells wrong. Not sure? Call and we'll ask three questions. A wet spot in the ceiling that isn't growing. A water heater making noise. A running toilet that won't stop filling. These depend. We'd rather talk you through it tonight and see you tomorrow. Shut the water off first We'd rather you stop the damage than wait for us to stop it. If you can shut it off yourself, do it, then call. Every minute is a square foot of drywall. The standard advice is "check your basement." Most St. George houses are built on a slab. There is no basement and usually no crawlspace. There are up to three shutoffs. Know all three. The house-side main. In a slab house it's most often at or near the front hose bib, where the line comes up out of the ground, sometimes inside a small access box or behind a panel. Or in the garage, on the wall shared with the front of the house, often near the water heater or the softener. Or in an interior utility closet. The curb stop at the meter box, if you are on a city system. A plastic or concrete box at the property line, usually in the park strip or near the sidewalk. It takes a long T-handled meter key. Buy one before you need it. The valve on the street side of the meter belongs to the city. For city-side work, call St. George Water Services at 435-627-4802. Out in Dammeron Valley, Diamond Valley, Central and Leeds there is no city water department and there may be no curb stop at all, so do not spend the minutes that matter looking for one. The water heater's cold inlet valve, and the small angle stops under every sink and toilet. For one fixture, these are enough. If the valve won't turn Gate valves seize in hard water, and St. George water is hard. A shutoff that hasn't been turned in fifteen years may not turn, or the stem may fail the moment it does. Don't force it. A snapped stem turns a leak into a flood. Go to the curb stop instead. Find and tag your main shutoff before you need it. Two minutes on a Saturday. Turn it once a year so it keeps working. In a condominium or townhome, the shutoff may not be yours. Utah Code § 57-8-7.2 sets where the association's pipe ends and yours begins. If the valve is on common ground, call the association or the manager as well as us. If you smell gas A gas smell is not our call. Leave the building. Call 911 and Dominion Energy from outside. Call a plumber after, if there's still something for a plumber to do. Freezing, and what actually breaks here St. George does freeze. The average January low is 28.4°F. Roughly 60 mornings a year drop to freezing, and the freeze window runs from mid-November to mid-March. People who moved here from milder climates don't expect it. But the lows sit right at freezing, not well below it. Pipes inside the house stay above freezing. What breaks is exposed brass and plastic outside: hose bibs, especially with a hose still attached; the backflow assembly on your irrigation system, which the city requires and which sits above ground; pool and spa equipment; attic runs where insulation got pushed aside; exposed lines in an unheated garage; RV hookups and outdoor kitchens. Dripping faucets and opening cabinet doors is advice for another climate. Here, disconnecting your hoses and winterizing the backflow is nearly everything. Disconnect and drain hoses by November 1. Put insulated covers on hose bibs. Winterize the backflow assembly and blow out the irrigation zones. Winterize pool equipment. Check that attic insulation still covers the pipe runs. Know where the shutoff is. Water damage: the first hour In order. The first step matters more than all the others together. Shut the water off at the main. Everything else is secondary. If water is near outlets or the panel, kill power to those circuits from a dry spot. If the panel itself is wet, don't approach it. Call the utility. Stop the source. For a water heater, close the cold inlet and turn the gas control to OFF. Photograph and video everything before you move anything. Wide shots and close-ups, the source and every damaged item. This is the step most people skip, and it's the one that decides how the claim goes. Get the standing water out and get air moving. Mold starts in wet material in roughly 24 to 48 hours. Our dry air is a real advantage, but only if the fans start now. Call your insurer and open the claim. Don't throw away the failed part. The adjuster will want it. Save every receipt. What it costs at night An emergency is the worst possible time to find out what something costs. So we published it. We charge more at night. You'll be told exactly how much more on the call, before anyone is dispatched, so you can decide whether to call us now or wait for the morning. It doesn't change based on how bad it looks. If it can wait until morning, we'll say so, and you'll pay the daytime rate. The diagnostic fee is credited to the repair if you go ahead. Nobody should have to negotiate a price standing in water. Same promise as every other job: the quote is the number. Emergencies included. What happens when you call Here's what happens next, in order. A person answers. Any hour. Tell us what you’re seeing. We tell you if it can wait. If it can wait until morning, we say so, and you pay the daytime rate. You know who is coming. Name, photo and the time window, before the knock. If the window slips, we call you We'll give you a real window when you call. If it slips, we call you. You shouldn't have to wonder. If we can't get to you tonight, we'll say so on the phone, not at 11 p.m. after you've waited. A stranger at the door after dark is the last thing you want. You'll have the technician's name and photo before he leaves our shop. If someone shows up who isn't the person we told you about, don't let him in. Call us. Two towns with something else going on The plumbing code is the same across Utah. What is not the same is the water, the second water system some towns run, and who the utility is. Emergency plumbing in Hurricane — the city runs a pressurized irrigation line that is not your drinking water and not your plumber’s to fix. Work out which one is leaking first. Emergency plumbing in Washington City — the city publishes total dissolved solids of 210 to 656 ppm, and the top of that range is above what Rinnai and Rheem warrant a tankless heater to run on. Out past the city line Four communities where there is no city water department at all. The water comes from a private company or an association, the sewer is mostly septic, and the first question when something fails is whose pipe it is. Dammeron Valley — a private water company on three wells, and a sewer main the district owns while the lateral to it is yours. Diamond Valley — the closest of the four, and on septic, which changes what a slow drain means. Central — the highest ground we cover, and the honest version of what does and does not justify a night drive. Leeds — its own town, its own water users association, and the only one east of I-15. Shut the water off. Then tell us what you're seeing. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day. The quote is the number. There is no second number. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. plain_terms.text: id="main"> Plain Terms Plain Terms You shouldn't have to take anyone's word for it. That's why ours is in writing. Five things you can hold us to on every job, what everything costs, and the parts most companies keep in a drawer. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day. 1. The quote is the number. There is no second number. Most people have been handed a second number. The job opens up, something is "worse than we thought," and the price moves. We write the price after we've looked at the work, not before, and then we hold it. If we missed something, that's our miss to eat, not your bill to absorb. No change-order ambush. No hidden contingencies. No post-completion adjustments. If the price changes, it's because you asked for something different, and you'll approve it first. Same promise on an emergency call. The quote is the number. Emergencies included. The diagnostic fee comes off the job We charge one flat fee to find the problem. $150 during standard hours, $50 more in the evening, at weekends and on holidays. If you hire us, that fee comes off the job. It doesn't change based on what we find. No “free” estimate that turns into a sales visit. A real diagnosis, at a published price, credited back. You're told which rate applies on the phone, before anyone is dispatched. Never after. 2. Not everything needs doing today. We'll tell you what does. A technician who finds five problems and calls all five urgent is either careless or selling. When we look at your system, you'll get a plain list: what has to be fixed now, what should be watched, and what can wait. We'll put a rough timeline on each one. You decide what happens and when. The honest answer is sometimes "leave it alone." You'll hear that from us when it's true. We would rather come back in two years than sell you two years early. Needs doing Should be watched Can wait 3. Nobody knocks on your door that you haven't already met. Before your appointment you'll get a message with the name and photo of the technician coming, and the time window. He'll be in a marked truck and a company shirt. You should never have to guess who is standing on your porch, and you should never have to take someone's word for who they work for. If someone shows up who isn't the person we told you about, don't let him in. Call us. 4. We don't start work you didn't approve. Not one part, not one hour. You will not be asked to decide on the spot. We'll walk the work with you, write the number, and leave. If you want to think about it for a week or send it to whoever helps you decide, that's the normal way to do this, not an inconvenience. You can say no, and the visit still ends politely. Take the estimate, sit with it, get another bid. We'll still be here. 5. Floor coverings down before the tools come out. You shouldn't be able to tell we were here. Except that it works. Boot covers, drop cloths, and a broom. Every visit, not just the big jobs. We haul our own debris. Nothing sits in your driveway overnight. The last thing we do is walk it with you. The guarantee: one year Our labor, the materials we buy for your job, and the craftsmanship are guaranteed for one year from the day the work is signed off. If something we installed or something we did fails inside that year, we come back and put it right, and you are not billed for the visit. Materials you supply yourself aren't covered by our guarantee. We'll still fit them, and we'll tell you before we start if we think they're wrong for the job. Manufacturer warranties are ours to chase, not yours. If a unit fails under its own warranty, we handle the claim, the paperwork and the return. You shouldn't have to argue with a manufacturer about a machine we chose and installed. What you pay, and when Work is paid in stages, and the stages are written on your quote before you sign anything. You are never asked for money we haven’t already told you about. On a small job there is one payment at the end, and you are told which kind yours is before we start. 30 percent when you accept the quote. That buys the materials for your job. You get a dated receipt saying what it's for and what happens to it if the job doesn't go ahead. 50 percent at the halfway point, which is a point we agree and write down at the start, not one we decide when we get there. The balance when the work is finished and you've walked it with us. If a payment is missed Work stops until it is made. We will tell you before we stand down rather than simply not turning up, and we will leave the site safe and weathertight. We are not responsible for what happens to an unfinished job while it is stopped for a payment we did not receive. That is the honest consequence of a stoppage, and you should know it before the first invoice rather than after the third. Paying by card The number on your quote is the price if you pay by card. Pay by cash, check or bank transfer and we take three percent off it. You will never pay more than the number on the quote. That's the whole point of the first promise on this page, and a card fee added at the end would break it. Quotes, extra work and permits A quote is good for 30 days from the date printed on it. After that, material prices have usually moved, and we'd rather requote than hold you to a number we can no longer buy at. We only do the work that's on your estimate or invoice. If we find something else that needs doing, we stop, put it in writing with a price, and wait for you to say yes. We don't do it and bill you afterwards. Permit fees are yours unless your quote says otherwise. We pull the permit and deal with the inspector. The fee is passed through at what it cost, and you get the receipt. Changing your appointment A booked slot is a van, a technician and a day we turned other work down for. So there are limits, and you get them here rather than on an invoice. Cancel with 24 hours’ notice: no charge. Reschedule with 6 hours’ notice: no charge, twice. A third reschedule of the same job: $150. Who does the work Most of it is our own crew. Some of it isn’t: electrical is done by a licensed electrical partner, and occasionally another trade is too. They carry their own license and their own insurance, and we’ll send you both the same day you ask. They work to our schedule and our standard, and the guarantee above covers their work exactly as it covers ours. You have one number to call, and it’s ours. Being handed a subcontractor’s phone number when something goes wrong is the thing this company exists not to do. What the guarantee doesn’t cover Two things. Both are worth understanding before you buy anything, from us or from anyone else here. St. George water runs 18 to 22 grains per gallon, and that is over every hardness limit the manufacturers publish. A.O. Smith stops at 7 grains. Noritz and Rheem stop at 12. Rinnai’s manual says replacement of components due to water quality damage is not covered. Those are their words, in their own warranty documents, and they mean scale damage is excluded from the manufacturer’s warranty on almost any water-carrying appliance in this valley. Ours excludes it too, and we’d rather say so here than at your kitchen table. What we will do is tell you what maintenance a unit needs to survive this water, put it in writing, and tell you honestly when something already at the end of its life is not worth the repair. The other one is digging. If your job needs a trench, we’ll show you the route before we start and we put the ground back. We don’t guarantee that plants, sod or decorative rock along that line survive it. We have public utilities located before we dig, and that locate does not cover your sprinkler lines or your landscape lighting, so tell us where they are if you know. What we won't do Negative promises cost something, which is why they're worth more. We won't give you a second number. We won't call everything urgent. We won't send someone to your door you haven't been told about. We won't start work you didn't say yes to. We won't publish a price on this site and charge a different one at your door. We won't tell you a repair makes sense on a unit too old for it. Why we put these in writing Every contractor says he's honest. There's no way to check that, and the people who say it loudest are often the reason you're asking. So instead of asking you to believe us, we wrote down five things you can hold us to, and we hand you a page at the end of every job that says the same thing. If we break one of these, you'll know. You'll have it in writing. The quote is the number. There is no second number. Call (435) 850-0053 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. , weekdays. Emergency calls answered any hour, every day. Read our Plain Terms
