The City of St. George's Water Distribution Division instructs residents to set water softeners to 18 grains per gallon, with a maximum of 22 grains. 1 18 grains per gallon is about 308 mg/L as calcium carbonate and 22 gpg about 376 mg/L, both classed as very hard on the USGS scale. 1 The city asks residents to keep softener settings low because softener salt raises the dissolved-solids level of the reclaimed water the city reuses for irrigation. 1 St. George's 2024 water quality report shows total dissolved solids ranging from 118 to 936 ppm, and the 2025 report gives a 580 ppm average. 1 Sulfate in St. George water ranges from 1.38 to 451 ppm, with a reported average of 185 ppm. 2 Calcium in St. George water ranges from 18 to 95 ppm and sodium from 5 to 153 ppm. 1 12 more facts , with sources Arsenic in St. George water has been measured at 1 to 13 ppb with a running annual average of 8.68 to 9 ppb, against a federal limit of 10 ppb. 1 St. George disinfects with chlorine (residual 0.10 to 1.19 ppm), not chloramine. 1 Total trihalomethanes in St. George water ranged from 0.58 to 56.6 ppb and HAA5 from not detected to 16.5 ppb; the federal TTHM limit is 80 ppb. 1 Hexavalent chromium has been measured in St. George water at 0.279 ppb; there is no federal limit for chromium-6. 1 St. George water is in compliance with federal drinking-water law; arsenic at 9.58 ppb is under the 10 ppb limit and TTHM at 35.4 ppb is under the 80 ppb limit. 1 No St. George water quality report publishes hardness, because hardness is not a federally required reporting parameter. 1 Every major tankless water heater manufacturer publishes a hardness limit of 7 to 12 grains per gallon, and St. George's city-recommended 18 gpg setting exceeds all of them. 3 Noritz's tankless warranty excludes damage from hardness above 12 grains per gallon (200 mg/L), and Rinnai, Rheem and Navien all cap total hardness at 200 mg/L. A.O. Smith's current gas tankless warranty publishes no hardness figure at all. 4 Rinnai and Rheem tankless units cap total dissolved solids at 500 mg/L, and the high end of St. George's 118 to 936 ppm range exceeds that limit. 3 Softened water leaving a properly set softener is functionally 0 to 1 grain per gallon; the city's 18 gpg figure is the incoming hardness the softener is set to, not the output. 5 The city asks residents to avoid irrigating between 4 and 6 a.m. because simultaneous demand in that window causes a noticeable pressure drop across the distribution system. 2 A water softener does not remove arsenic. 3 The city's rules Lawn, irrigation, lighting and permits, from the municipal code. St. George City Code § 10-7-7 caps residential lawn at 8 percent of lot size, to a maximum of 1,500 square feet, on lots up to 20,000 square feet. 6 Lots over 20,000 square feet may have up to 2,000 square feet of lawn, and lots under 7,500 square feet may have up to 600 square feet even if that exceeds 8 percent. 6 St. George City Code § 10-7-7 prohibits lawn in park strips, in any landscape area less than eight feet wide, and on slopes over 15 percent. 6 Each single-family home in St. George must have two water-conserving trees of at least 1½-inch caliper, and § 10-23-3 separately requires at least one water-conserving tree of that caliper in the front yard. 6 St. George limits decorative water features to one per residence, no larger than 50 gallons, with a recirculating pump. 6 St. George City Code § 10-23-1 sets the outdoor watering window at 8 p.m. to 10 a.m. from June 1 to September 1, and the city asks all residents to follow it. As codified, that section applies to development in all zones except agriculture, gravel and grazing, open space and single-family residential. 7 16 more facts , with sources St. George requires an approved backflow assembly on all outside watering systems, tested annually, plus hose bib vacuum breakers on every exterior hose connection. 3 St. George City Code §8-2-4(A) makes property owners responsible to purchase, install, test, inspect and maintain backflow devices wherever polluted water could enter their potable system. 3 Because St. George requires backflow assemblies on outside watering systems, many local homes are closed plumbing systems and need thermal expansion control on the water heater. 5 St. George City Code §8-4-14 requires grease traps to be cleaned no less than weekly and interceptors to be serviced at 25 percent of design hydraulic depth. 8 The St. George pretreatment program, codified at City Code Title 8 Chapter 4, was EPA-approved on June 6, 1991; illegal discharges are reported to 435-627-4266. 3 St. George building permits run through the CityInspect portal; CitizenServe handles business licensing only, and a contractor registered in another city's CityInspect must re-register for St. George. 8 St. George's front-yard fence limit is 4 feet. 8 St. George's outdoor lighting chapter, Title 10 Chapter 14, excludes detached single-family dwellings entirely, and there is no color temperature or Kelvin limit anywhere in it. 8 St. George publishes its structural design criteria as Seismic Design Category D, 105 mph wind, 21 psf ground snow, 20 psf roof snow, a 12-inch frost line and moderate-to-heavy termite exposure. 3 Utah replaces the model water heater anchoring section with its own under Utah Code 15A-3-205, and Utah's version has no seismic design category trigger: anchoring or strapping is required statewide, at points within the upper third and the lower third of the appliance. 9 Utah adopts construction code statewide under Title 15A; St. George City Code §9-1-1 adopts whatever the state adopts, so the plumbing code does not vary city to city. 8 Under WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards, where a city ordinance and the District standard conflict, the rule giving the greater water-conservation benefit applies, so St. George's 1,500 square foot lawn cap and 15 percent slope limit govern over the District's 2,500 square foot and 25 percent figures. 2 WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards (October 2023) require every drip zone to have a pressure regulator, filter, flush-end assembly and emitters rated 20 gallons per hour or less, and prohibit drip and spray on the same valve. 2 WCWCD standards require a WaterSense-labeled smart controller on automated irrigation systems, cap ornamental water features at 25 square feet per parcel, and require hot-water recirculation in homes over 1,400 square feet unless hot water arrives within 0.6 gallons. 2 Under Utah Code §57-8a-231, an HOA may not require lawn in any area less than eight feet wide, which matches the city's own park-strip prohibition, so an HOA in St. George cannot lawfully require more lawn than the city permits. 8 St. George's residential landscape standards apply to new construction and to a remodel that increases the dwelling's footprint, while the completion and maintenance obligations apply to all residential properties. 10 Who serves the house Water and power providers, which changes what a rebate is worth. the housing stock is predominantly 1980s to 1990s ranch homes on quarter- to half-acre lots with mature trees. 12 6 more facts , with sources Bloomington Ranches is managed by Advanced Realty, and Bloomington Knolls is a 55-plus townhome association built in 1988 with a full-service HOA. 12 The Ledges is governed by two different documents: White Rocks caps irrigated landscape at 5,000 square feet and trees at 20 feet, while Cinder Bluffs caps trees at 25 feet and has no irrigated-area cap but requires compliance with WCWCD conservation provisions. 8 The Ledges (White Rocks) requires contractors to carry $1 million per occurrence / $2 million aggregate general liability, allows work 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday with none on Sunday, permits tile roofs only, and limits retaining walls to 4 feet. 8 The Ledges (Cinder Bluffs) design review is deemed approved if the committee fails to act within 30 days; Utah Geological Survey Special Study 127 maps geologic hazards and adverse construction conditions across 366 square miles including St. George, with 14 hazard maps at 1:24,000 scale. 1 The Utah Geological Survey calls flooding 'the most widespread and damaging geologic hazard in southwestern Utah' and expansive soil and rock 'the most troublesome construction condition.' 1 The nine adverse construction conditions mapped for the St. George area are expansive soil and rock, collapsible soil, gypsiferous soil and rock, shallow bedrock, caliche, wind-blown sand, breccia pipes and paleokarst, soil piping and erosion, and shallow groundwater. 1 St. George's blue clay is the Petrified Forest Member of the Chinle Formation, an expandable illite/smectite clay that occurs in an arc across the St. George area and dips deeper below the surface toward the north. 1 Documented blue-clay damage in St. George includes tilted and cracked walls and foundations and the complete destruction, requiring demolition, of condominium units on Bluff Street and the Knights Inn Motel. 1 Caliche, a calcareous hardpan the Utah Geological Survey says 'can be very difficult to excavate,' is mapped as an adverse construction condition in the St. George area. 1 12 more facts , with sources Collapsible soil, which has strength when dry but settles by hydrocompaction when wetted, is mapped in the St. George area in five susceptibility classes from Very High to Low. 1 Gypsiferous soil and rock are separately mapped for the St. George area; gypsum dissolves in water, creating voids, and sulfate-rich soil is corrosive to buried ferrous metal. 1 Whether sulfate-resistant cement is required for a St. George footing or slab depends on a site soil-sulfate test under ACI 318 exposure classes; it is not a blanket local requirement. 1 At about 3:00 a.m. on January 19, 2013, a 12-by-9-foot boulder dislodged from sandstone on Foremaster Ridge and crashed into a house, seriously injuring a woman; the state hazard plan attributes it to a 40,000-gallon water leak from a house atop the ridge. 1 The September 2, 1992 St. George earthquake was magnitude 5.8 according to UGS Special Study 127 (the state hazard plan lists 5.5); it caused liquefaction and property damage and triggered the Springdale landslide. 1 The Hurricane fault is capable of earthquakes as large as magnitude 6.5 to 7, and liquefaction susceptibility is mapped for the St. George area. 1 Rockfall conditions are widespread in the St. George area and UGS expects rockfall damage to increase with hillside development. 1 The Washington County Hazards MapServer publishes 24 free public layers, including FEMA flood hazard, erosion hazard boundary, flood hazard based on geologic deposits, dam-break inundation, fault special study zones, liquefaction, rockfall, collapsible soils, expansive rock and soil, gypsiferous soil, wind-blown sand, piping and erosion, and wildfire history. 1 The EPA maps Washington County as Radon Zone 2, the middle of its three categories, meaning a predicted average indoor screening level between 2 and 4 picocuries per liter. The action level is 4, and a zone map is a geological prediction that does not describe any individual house. 13 The Utah Geological Survey publishes a dedicated report, Public Information 35, on radon-hazard potential in the St. George area. 1 USU Extension states termites 'are most common in the southern counties' of Utah and that prevention includes repairing water leaks and sealing foundation cracks. 1 The Utah State Hazard Mitigation Plan attributes 5,630 Utah deaths (1973 to 2015) to radon-induced lung cancer, 92.7 percent of all Utah geologic-hazard fatalities. 1 The seasons Heat, monsoon, wind and freeze, and how they set the calendar. St. George's all-time high is 117°F, set in July 1985 and matched on July 11, 2021; its all-time low is −11°F, set January 26, 1937. 1 St. George recorded 98 days at or above 100°F in 2024, the most on record, and had back-to-back hottest Julys on record in 2023 and 2024. 1 St. George's wettest year on record was 16.2 inches in 2019, and its greatest single-day rainfall was 2.4 inches on August 31, 1909; annual precipitation is roughly 8 to 9.3 inches. 1 St. George's precipitation is bimodal: February is the wettest month at 1.38 inches, August third at 1.07 inches from monsoon, and June the driest at 0.16 inches. 8 Southwest Utah has a defined monsoon season that produces flash flooding; St. George once recorded a 78-day dry spell that ended with monsoon onset. 1 WCWCD warns that low-lying neighborhoods near rivers and drainages, such as Bloomington and the Virgin River bottoms, are colder than the zone map implies because cold air settles there, so marginally hardy plants are more likely to freeze. 2 5 more facts , with sources Most of Washington County's populated area sits in Sunset climate zone 10, with up to 300 growing days a year and elevations of 3,300 to 5,000 feet. 2 Penn State measured synthetic turf at 200°F on a 98°F day in Provo, Utah; watering dropped it from 174°F to 85°F but it rebounded to 120°F within five minutes. 1 Hail is a low-frequency hazard in Washington County; the county recorded two tornadoes and four severe-weather injuries from 1950 to 2018, and lightning and flash flooding are the more relevant threats. 1 WCWCD's published watering schedule steps down on September 1 (sprinklers from 4 to 3 days a week, drip from 3 to 2) and says irrigation is typically not needed in December or January. 2 WCWCD says to avoid watering from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. in summer and recommends cycle-and-soak (three 5- to 10-minute cycles an hour apart) because local clay absorbs only about half an inch of water per hour. 2 The houses How homes here were built, and what that means for the pipes. Santa Clara adopted its own water ordinance in February 2022 that limits lawn sizes and the types of plants that may be installed. 1 Snow Canyon State Park's December 2025 dark-sky designation directly affects Santa Clara, one of the two submarkets where lighting rules bite hardest. 3 Utah adopts construction code statewide under Title 15A, so the plumbing code in Santa Clara is the same as in neighboring cities; what varies is permit triggers, fees, process, irrigation rules, and lighting. 3 Utah H.B. 215 (2026) amended Utah Code 10-20-619 so that a municipality may not require a property owner to install or keep lawn or turf in an area less than eight feet wide, and may not block vegetation removal required for defensible space under the Wildland Urban Interface Code. 4 Utah H.B. 48 took effect January 1, 2026 and requires each municipality to adopt and enforce the Utah Wildland Urban Interface Code for its incorporated area. 5 WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards (October 2023) require that all non-lawn plant material be irrigated by drip with a pressure regulator, filter, flush-end assembly, and emitters rated 20 gallons per hour or less, and that drip and spray never share a valve. 5 3 more facts , with sources WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards apply to landscape installation, not just new construction, and where they conflict with a city ordinance or HOA requirement the regulation providing the greatest water conservation benefit applies. 5 WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards cap single-family lawn at 8 percent of the lot or 2,500 square feet, whichever is less, allow up to 600 square feet on lots under 7,500 square feet, bar lawn narrower than 8 feet in any dimension, and bar lawn on slopes over 25 percent. 5 WCWCD's Water Efficiency Standards limit ornamental water features to 25 square feet per parcel. 5 Who serves the house Water and power providers, which changes what a rebate is worth. In January 2005 a flood on the Santa Clara River washed away about 20 homes and damaged another 10 beyond repair, roughly 30 structures lost, according to a university teaching case study on the flood. 1 The 2005 flood was driven by a weak El Niño that steered a southerly Pacific storm track over existing snowpack. 1 During the 2005 flood the Santa Clara River widened to a hundred yards in places. 1 The 2005 flood's discharge was less than the expected 100-year flood; the destruction happened at below 100-year flow. 1 Most homes destroyed in 2005 sat above the 100-year floodplain, leaving their owners without flood insurance, according to a university teaching case study on the flood. 1 The 2005 damage mechanism was stream bank erosion from meander migration, not inundation. 1 13 more facts , with sources The documented lesson of the 2005 flood is that analyzing risk along streams requires knowledge of both flood and stream-bank erosion hazards. 1 Washington County publishes three separate flood-related GIS layers, FEMA Flood Hazard (layer 0), Erosion Hazard Boundary (layer 3), and Flood Hazard Based on Geologic Deposits (layer 4), because FEMA's map alone is insufficient here. 1 Washington County also maps dam-break inundation areas (GIS layers 5 to 7) downstream of Quail Creek and Sand Hollow reservoirs. 1 The Utah Geological Survey calls flooding the most widespread and damaging geologic hazard in southwestern Utah. 1 Expansive blue clay of the Chinle Formation's Petrified Forest Member has caused documented damage to homes in the Santa Clara area. 1 The Utah Geological Survey illustrates expansive soil damage with a photograph of cracks in a Santa Clara house foundation. 1 The Utah Geological Survey calls expansive soil and rock the most troublesome construction condition in the St. George area. 1 The blue clay's mineralogy is illite/smectite, an expandable clay that absorbs water and swells; it occurs in an arc across the St. George area and dips deeper below the surface toward the north. 1 Utah Geological Survey Special Study 127 maps geologic hazards and adverse construction conditions across 366 square miles including Santa Clara, at 1:24,000 scale. 1 The Utah Geological Survey defines collapsible soil as soil with considerable strength when dry that settles significantly by hydrocompaction when wetted, typically in young alluvial fans and debris flows. 1 Washington County publishes 24 free public hazard map layers, and the Utah Geologic Hazards Portal offers a second free lookup. 1 The EPA maps Washington County as Radon Zone 2, the middle of its three categories, meaning a predicted average indoor screening level between 2 and 4 picocuries per liter. new trees need water every two to four days in their first summer and take a year or two to establish. 3 USU Extension names conifers, including junipers, as flammable plants that ignite more quickly, and says nothing flammable should be within 5 feet of a house in the wildland-urban interface. 3 The houses How homes here were built, and what that means for the pipes. Washington County had 91,460 housing units as of July 2025, 69,786 households, 71.6% owner-occupancy, a median home value of $510,700, a population of 213,670 and 2,857 building permits in 2025. 1 Washington County's population is 22.4% aged 65 or older per Census QuickFacts. 5 The EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule applies to homes built before 1978 with no small-residential exemption, so contractors renovating those homes must be trained and certified in lead-safe work practices. 1 Utah Admin. Code R307-801-9 exempts residential structures of four units or fewer from the asbestos inspection requirement and contains no 1992 date trigger. 1 Polybutylene supply pipe was manufactured from 1978 to mid-1995, is usually gray and marked PB2110, and fails because chlorine-based disinfectants react with it; the systems in this county that report a disinfectant use chlorine, not chloramine. 1 Seasonal residents who occupy a home about half the year use only about 10% less water annually than full-time residents, according to the water district, because the landscape is irrigated year-round for an empty house. 4 Rebates and easements The conversion program as it applies here. The WCWCD Water Efficient Landscape rebate pays $3 per square foot on the first 1,000 square feet of lawn removed and $2 per square foot after that for projects completed before June 1, 2027; the standard rate is $2. 3 Washington County residents do not apply to the state Utah Water Savers landscape program; the state's eligibility page routes them to the WCWCD rebate, and the district rate already includes the state money plus a local enhancement. 3 Never remove or kill the lawn before receiving the district's written approval email and a pre-conversion site visit; doing so permanently voids rebate eligibility, and living grass must still be visible at inspection. 3 The district issues landscape rebates in less than 60 days after the project is completed and all paperwork is submitted. 3 The Washington County Water Conservancy District caps the landscape rebate at $100,000 per property per calendar year. There is no five-year waiting rule on the district side; that limit belongs to the separate state program, which Washington County applicants are routed away from. 7 Every rebated conversion attaches a conservation easement recorded with the Washington County Recorder that continues in perpetuity, restricts only the converted area, and prohibits irrigated grass, spray irrigation, swimming pools, ponds, other bodies of water and water features there forever. 3 11 more facts , with sources If an easement violation is found, the owner gets written notice and 45 days to cure, after which the full rebate plus administrative costs plus 5% annual interest is repayable; the district checks compliance by aerial imagery. 3 The easement must be granted before the incentive is issued; transferring the property to a new owner before the easement is granted makes the applicant ineligible. 3 The converted area must reach 50% living plant and tree cover at maturity; the district credits each tree at 350 square feet and each shrub or perennial at 35 square feet, so one tree equals ten plants, and existing trees kept inside the area count. 3 The rebate program does not dictate plant species and publishes no approved plant list; it requires only 50% mature coverage. 3 Ungrouted pavers and dry-set flagstone count as mulch inside a rebated conversion, permeable artificial turf is accepted in lieu of mulch, and poured concrete or mortared work is subtracted from the rebated area. 3 A rebated conversion must have either no irrigation or low-volume drip with a filter, pressure regulator and emitters rated 20 gallons per hour or less, must be covered by permeable mulch, and must be free of bare soil and impermeable barriers. 3 WCWCD also offers a smart-controller rebate of up to $100 for WaterSense-labeled controllers and a toilet-replacement rebate of up to $150 per WaterSense toilet for toilets made before 1994, up to two toilets per property; these are separate applications from the landscape rebate. 3 For an owner-occupied primary residence the district does not collect a W-9 or issue a 1099 for the landscape rebate; owners of secondary residences, rentals and commercial properties do receive a 1099. 3 The district's own guidance says a contractor-installed conversion costs about $4 to $6 per square foot, rebates commonly cover 30 to 50 percent of the cost, and a typical residential conversion can save up to $300 a year in water costs. 3 Utah Water Savers says most HOA residents can qualify for a landscape rebate if the landscaping is the applicant's property, and that an HOA may still require plan approval before changes. 3 If an HOA compels a homeowner to keep grass, the district asks to be emailed at conservation@wcwcd.org and will take reasonable steps to inform the HOA of applicable state and local law. 3 Something on this page describe your house? the Utah State Hazard Mitigation Plan lists it as magnitude 5.5. 1 The Washington County Hazards MapServer publishes 24 free public layers including FEMA flood hazard, erosion hazard boundary, fault special study zone, liquefaction, rockfall, collapsible soils, expansive rock and soil, gypsiferous rock and soil, wind-blown sand, piping and erosion, and wildfire history. 1 The EPA maps Washington County as Radon Zone 2, the middle of its three categories, meaning a predicted average indoor screening level between 2 and 4 picocuries per liter. The action level is 4, and a zone map is a geological prediction that does not describe any individual house. 6 The Utah Geological Survey calls radon Utah's leading geologic hazard in terms of fatalities; the state hazard plan attributes 5,630 Utah deaths (1973–2015) to radon-induced lung cancer, 92.7% of all Utah geologic-hazard fatalities. 1 Utah State University Extension reports that termites can be found throughout Utah but are most common in the southern counties, and that they require moisture and wood-to-soil contact; repairing water leaks is on the Extension's prevention list. 1 The seasons Heat, monsoon, wind and freeze, and how they set the calendar. The Washington County Water Conservancy District states that the county's more densely populated areas are in USDA hardiness zone 8, that a warm winter can be closer to zone 9 and extremely rare years as cold as zone 7, and that homeowners planting zone 9 plants are taking a risk. 3 Per the water district, neighborhoods at low elevations near rivers and drainages are cooler because cold air settles at the lowest points, so marginally hardy plants are more likely to freeze there. 3 Most of Washington County falls in Sunset climate zone 10, a high desert with hot summers, cold winters and up to 300 growing days a year, at elevations of 3,300 to 5,000 feet. 3 Southwest Utah has a defined monsoon season that produces flash flooding after long dry spells; St. George recorded a 78-day dry spell that ended with monsoon onset in one recent year. 1 At the St. George station, February is the wettest month (1.38 in.), August third (1.07 in.) from monsoon rain, and June the driest (0.16 in.). 4 The Utah Geological Survey maps wind-blown sand as one of the nine adverse construction conditions for the St. George–Hurricane area, which is unusual and signals that blowing sand is materially significant here. 1 4 more facts , with sources Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research measured synthetic turf at 200°F on a 98°F day in Provo, Utah, and found that 30 minutes of watering dropped turf from 174°F to 85°F but it rebounded to 120°F within 5 minutes. 1 The water district states that shade keeps areas up to 25°F cooler, shade trees can lower surface temperatures by up to 50°F, and grass uses four times more water than trees and shrubs. 3 Water-wise plants, as USU Extension defines them, need watering only about once every two weeks after establishment; new trees need water every two to four days in their first summer and take a year or two to establish. 3 USU Extension names conifers, including junipers, as flammable plants that ignite more quickly, and says nothing flammable should be within 5 feet of a house in the wildland-urban interface. 3 The houses How homes here were built, and what that means for the pipes. Washington County had 91,460 housing units as of July 2025, 69,786 households, 71.6% owner-occupancy, a median home value of $510,700, a population of 213,670 and 2,857 building permits in 2025. 1 Washington County's population is 22.4% aged 65 or older per Census QuickFacts. 5 The EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule applies to homes built before 1978 with no small-residential exemption, so contractors renovating those homes must be trained and certified in lead-safe work practices. 1 Utah Admin. Code R307-801-9 exempts residential structures of four units or fewer from the asbestos inspection requirement and contains no 1992 date trigger. 1 Polybutylene supply pipe was manufactured from 1978 to mid-1995, is usually gray and marked PB2110, and fails because chlorine-based disinfectants react with it; the systems in this county that report a disinfectant use chlorine, not chloramine. 1 Seasonal residents who occupy a home about half the year use only about 10% less water annually than full-time residents, according to the water district, because the landscape is irrigated year-round for an empty house. 4 Rebates and easements The conversion program as it applies here. The WCWCD Water Efficient Landscape rebate pays $3 per square foot on the first 1,000 square feet of lawn removed and $2 per square foot after that for projects completed before June 1, 2027; the standard rate is $2. 3 Washington County residents do not apply to the state Utah Water Savers landscape program; the state's eligibility page routes them to the WCWCD rebate, and the district rate already includes the state money plus a local enhancement. 3 Never remove or kill the lawn before receiving the district's written approval email and a pre-conversion site visit; doing so permanently voids rebate eligibility, and living grass must still be visible at inspection. 3 The district issues landscape rebates in less than 60 days after the project is completed and all paperwork is submitted. 3 The Washington County Water Conservancy District caps the landscape rebate at $100,000 per property per calendar year. There is no five-year waiting rule on the district side; that limit belongs to the separate state program, which Washington County applicants are routed away from. 7 Every rebated conversion attaches a conservation easement recorded with the Washington County Recorder that continues in perpetuity, restricts only the converted area, and prohibits irrigated grass, spray irrigation, swimming pools, ponds, other bodies of water and water features there forever. 3 11 more facts , with sources If an easement violation is found, the owner gets written notice and 45 days to cure, after which the full rebate plus administrative costs plus 5% annual interest is repayable; the district checks compliance by aerial imagery. 3 The easement must be granted before the incentive is issued; transferring the property to a new owner before the easement is granted makes the applicant ineligible. 3 The converted area must reach 50% living plant and tree cover at maturity; the district credits each tree at 350 square feet and each shrub or perennial at 35 square feet, so one tree equals ten plants, and existing trees kept inside the area count. 3 The rebate program does not dictate plant species and publishes no approved plant list; it requires only 50% mature coverage. 3 Ungrouted pavers and dry-set flagstone count as mulch inside a rebated conversion, permeable artificial turf is accepted in lieu of mulch, and poured concrete or mortared work is subtracted from the rebated area. 3 A rebated conversion must have either no irrigation or low-volume drip with a filter, pressure regulator and emitters rated 20 gallons per hour or less, must be covered by permeable mulch, and must be free of bare soil and impermeable barriers. 3 WCWCD also offers a smart-controller rebate of up to $100 for WaterSense-labeled controllers and a toilet-replacement rebate of up to $150 per WaterSense toilet for toilets made before 1994, up to two toilets per property; these are separate applications from the landscape rebate. 3 For an owner-occupied primary residence the district does not collect a W-9 or issue a 1099 for the landscape rebate; owners of secondary residences, rentals and commercial properties do receive a 1099. 3 The district's own guidance says a contractor-installed conversion costs about $4 to $6 per square foot, rebates commonly cover 30 to 50 percent of the cost, and a typical residential conversion can save up to $300 a year in water costs. 3 Utah Water Savers says most HOA residents can qualify for a landscape rebate if the landscaping is the applicant's property, and that an HOA may still require plan approval before changes. 3 If an HOA compels a homeowner to keep grass, the district asks to be emailed at conservation@wcwcd.org and will take reasonable steps to inform the HOA of applicable state and local law. 3 Something on this page describe your house? Cedar City supplies its own drinking water from groundwater: 8 wells and 4 springs. 1 The utility is Cedar City Waterworks, state water system ID 11002. 1 Cedar City's water system served 10,414 connections in 2021. 1 The system has 10 storage tanks, 3 pump stations, 5 pressure zones and about 250 miles of pipe from 4 to 20 inches in diameter. 1 The city's wells are in two well fields: two wells near Enoch, north of city limits, and six west of Quichapa Lake, connected to town by transmission pipelines. 1 Cedar City's 2025 water quality report gives total dissolved solids of 180 to 804 ppm across its sources, against a limit of 2,000. 1 12 more facts , with sources Sulfate ranged from 2.762 to 347.495 ppm across sources in 2025, against a limit of 1,000. 1 Sodium ranged from 3.573 to 27.517 ppm in 2025; EPA sets no limit for sodium. 1 Nitrate (as nitrogen) ranged from 0 to 3.08 ppm in 2025, against a limit of 10. 1 Arsenic ranged from 0 to 4.4 ppb in 2025, against a limit of 10. 1 In the city's most recent lead sampling (2024), the 90th-percentile lead result was 0 ppb and no site exceeded the action level. 1 Cedar City has completed an initial inventory of lead service lines. 1 The State Engineer has declared Cedar City Valley a critical management area because groundwater withdrawals exceed safe yield. 1 The state estimates the basin's safe yield at 21,000 acre-feet a year against current depletion of 28,000 acre-feet a year. 1 If every approved or perfected groundwater right were used, depletion would be about 50,000 acre-feet a year. 1 Under the 2021 groundwater management plan, water rights will be cut by priority date in five phases from January 1, 2035 to January 1, 2080. 1 Cedar City owns about 13,000 acre-feet of groundwater rights, of which about 2,800 have enough priority to survive the state's cuts. 1 The city's own master plan says groundwater in the valley is being withdrawn at an unsustainable rate. 1 The city's rules Lawn, irrigation, lighting and permits, from the municipal code. From April 1 through October 31, Cedar City prohibits outdoor irrigation with culinary water between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. (City Code 37-7-1). 1 The watering-hours rule exempts new lawns for their first 30 days and short system tests with a person present. 1 A second watering-hours violation in a calendar year gets the property's water shut off. 1 Anyone planting new sod or seed in Cedar City should call the Water Division at (435) 586-2968. 1 In new Cedar City developments, lawn is not allowed on park strips or in areas less than 8 feet wide. 1 In new residential development, lawn may not exceed 50% of front and side yard landscaping, except on lots with less than 250 square feet of landscaped area. 1 13 more facts , with sources Cedar City adopted its water-efficient landscape standards on May 24, 2023, by Ordinance 0524-23. 1 Cedar City allows no physical connection between the city's culinary water and any other water system. 1 In Cedar City the property owner buys, installs, tests and maintains any required backflow prevention device. 1 Backflow devices must be inspected and tested at least once a year when the city requests it. 1 Cedar City requires a building permit for plumbing or mechanical changes, including mechanical equipment upgrades and replacements. 1 A new furnace or water heater on a gas line needs a gas meter or mechanical permit in Cedar City if no other permit covers the work. 1 Cedar City has adopted the 2024 International Plumbing Code and the 2024 International Mechanical Code. 1 Cedar City has adopted the 2021 IECC residential provisions with Utah amendments. 1 Cedar City's design frost depth is 30 inches. 1 Cedar City's building design standards use Seismic Zone D1 and a 90 mph wind speed with 115 mph gusts. 1 When Cedar City requires a subdivision soils report, it must address subsidence, hydro-compaction, settling and sinking of soil. 1 Cedar City's building inspector keeps approved subdivision soils reports open to public review. 1 Cedar City and Iron County both have ordinances protecting drinking-water source zones, and the city publishes a protection-zone map. 1 Who serves the house Water and power providers, which changes what a rebate is worth. Rocky Mountain Power supplies electricity in Cedar City. 1 Builders in Cedar City get work order numbers for electric service from Rocky Mountain Power at 888-221-7070. 1 Enbridge Gas serves Cedar City with natural gas. 1 About 72% of Cedar City's occupied homes (9,009 of 12,480) heat with utility gas, per ACS 2020–2024 Table B25040. 1 2,983 of Cedar City's 12,480 occupied homes heat with electricity, per ACS 2020–2024 Table B25040. 1 The associations What the documents say, by community. Confirm with your own. Cedar Highlands Homeowners Association is an active master HOA registration with the state, number 14258617-MHOA. 1 The Central Iron County Water Conservancy District runs the Cedar Highlands water system and chose a different tank site after its geotechnical consultant advised against the old one, which sits at the toe of a landslide. 1 Utah law bars an HOA from prohibiting water-wise landscaping on a detached home's lot (Utah Code 57-8a-231). 1 Except for erosion control, an HOA may not require lawn in an area less than 8 feet wide. 1 The ground Soils, faults, flood and rockfall, from the state's hazard mapping. The Utah Geological Survey documented land subsidence and earth fissures in Cedar Valley in Special Study 150 (2014). 1 Groundwater pumping in excess of recharge has lowered water levels in Cedar Valley by as much as 114 feet since 1939, according to the UGS. 1 Cedar Valley's aquifer contains a high share of fine-grained sediment that compacts when it is drained. 1 The largest subsidence the UGS measured at a benchmark was 0.9 foot, near Enoch; vertical offset across the Enoch fissure zone is about 3 feet in places. 1 At least 8.3 miles of earth fissures have formed in the southwestern and northeastern parts of Cedar Valley. 1 The UGS concluded that long-term groundwater pumping in excess of recharge is the cause of the subsidence and fissures. 1 13 more facts , with sources If water levels keep falling about 2 feet a year, the UGS expects basin-wide subsidence of 0.02 to 1.2 inches a year to continue, and new fissures to form. 1 Satellite radar (InSAR) identified about 100 square miles of Cedar Valley subsiding from groundwater mining. 1 The UGS says the fissure inventory is likely incomplete, because many fissures are hairline cracks hard to see. 1 Documented fissure damage is limited to the Parkview subdivision in Enoch and a stock pond west of Quichapa Lake. 1 In Enoch's Parkview subdivision, fissure movement reversed the flow of a sewer line so it could no longer drain by gravity; the UGS calls it the first extensive fissure damage to the built environment in Utah. 1 Several large-capacity Cedar City municipal wells sit near the fissure zones around Quichapa Lake. 1 Subsidence can continue long after groundwater decline stops, because clay layers take years to decades to finish compacting. 1 The UGS's 2025 hazard study (Special Study 177) says collapsible soil and flooding have been the costliest geologic hazards in Cedar Valley. 1 The UGS identifies radon gas as a hazard in the Cedar Valley study area. 1 The UGS also maps expansive, corrosive and soluble soil and rock, shallow groundwater, landslide and rockfall hazards in Cedar Valley. 1 The UGS hazard maps are public on the Utah Geologic Hazards Portal and are not a substitute for a site-specific investigation. 1 Collapsible soil in Cedar City itself was studied as far back as 1978. 1 The Hurricane fault runs along the Hurricane Cliffs at the east edge of Cedar Valley, and the cliffs are up to 2,000 feet high. 1 The seasons Heat, monsoon, wind and freeze, and how they set the calendar. Cedar City's NOAA 1991–2020 normals come from station USW00093129, Cedar City Municipal Airport, at 1,702.6 meters. 1 Cedar City's normal daily high in July is 91.0°F. 1 Cedar City's normal daily low in January is 18.0°F, and 16.3°F in December. 1 The normal daily low in Cedar City is below freezing every month from October through April. 1 Cedar City averages about 168 nights a year at or below 32°F, against about 62 in St. George. 1 Cedar City averages 5.4 nights a year at or below 0°F; St. George averages none. 1 6 more facts , with sources Cedar City averages 1.4 days a year at or above 100°F, against 63.1 in St. George. 1 Cedar City's normal is 6,002 heating degree days a year, nearly twice St. George's 3,205, and 678 cooling degree days against St. George's 2,416. 1 The median last spring freeze in Cedar City is May 21 and the median first fall freeze is September 29. 1 Cedar City's median growing season is 130 days, against 239 in St. George. 1 Both Cedar City ZIP codes, 84720 and 84721, are USDA hardiness zone 6b on the 2023 map; St. George's 84770 is 8b. 1 Iron County is Building America climate "Cold" and IECC 2021 Climate Zone 5B; Washington County is the only Utah county in Zone 3B. 2 The houses How homes here were built, and what that means for the pipes. Cedar City has 13,572 housing units (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25001). 1 About 57% of Cedar City's occupied homes are owner-occupied (7,077 of 12,480), against 68% in Iron County (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25003). 1 The median Cedar City housing unit was built in 1999 (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25035). 1 About 23% of Cedar City housing units (3,064 of 13,572) were built before 1980 (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25034). 1 3,414 Cedar City units were built in 2010 or later: 2,667 in 2010–2019 and 747 since 2020 (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25034). 1 6,900 of Cedar City's housing units are single-family detached homes and 368 are mobile homes (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25024). 1 1 more fact , with sources The median value of an owner-occupied home in Cedar City is $377,000 (ACS 2020–2024, Table B25077). 1 Rebates and easements The conversion program as it applies here. Cedar City is in the Central Iron County Water Conservancy District, not the Washington County Water Conservancy District. 1 The district estimates the Cedar Valley aquifer is being overdrawn by 7,000 acre-feet a year and that homes use about 60% of their water outdoors. 1 Cedar City residents qualify for the State of Utah's landscape incentive, run by the Utah Division of Water Resources through Utah Water Savers. 1 The state incentive pays $2.00 per square foot of lawn replaced with water-efficient landscaping, up to $50,000 per application. 1 Lawn must not be removed before the application is approved and the participation agreement is signed. 1 The project area must be at least 200 square feet. 1 7 more facts , with sources Plants must cover at least 50% of the converted area at maturity, and the area must be watered by drip. 1 Artificial turf, pools, water features and concrete do not count as water-efficient landscaping for the incentive. 1 Projects must be finished within 365 days of approval, and homes on private wells are not eligible. 1 The state inspects the finished project and mails the incentive check to the property owner. 1 Utah Water Savers pays up to $100 for a WaterSense-labeled smart irrigation controller, open to all Utah homes. 1 The state's toilet replacement rebate closes November 1, 2026. 1 Utah Water Savers, the state program that pays Cedar City's landscape rebate, limits its rebates to one rebate per property every five years. 1 Something on this page describe your house? guides_artificial_turf_heat.text: id="main"> Guides · Water-wise landscape Artificial turf, measured: 200 degrees on a 98 degree day The highest published synthetic turf surface temperature was recorded in Utah. Watering cools it for about five minutes. Here is where turf still makes sense, and what planted conversion does instead. Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research keeps the best published temperature data on synthetic turf, and the highest figure in it was taken in Utah. On a 98 degree day in Provo, synthetic turf reached 200 degrees Fahrenheit. Their central Pennsylvania maximum, measured six years later, was 175. Across their work, synthetic turf generally runs 35 to 55 degrees hotter than natural grass, which on a hot day sits between 75 and 95 degrees and rarely exceeds 100, because transpiration cools it. Provo is not St. George. St. George recorded 98 days at or above 100 degrees in 2024, with an all time high of 117 degrees, set in July 1985 and matched in July 2021. The 200 degree measurement was taken at 98 degrees ambient, which makes it a floor for this market rather than a ceiling. That is the honest starting point for the conversation, and it is not the end of it, because there are places where turf is still the right call. The watering rebound The obvious answer to a hot surface is to wet it, and that has been tested. In work run at Brigham Young University and reported inside the Penn State research, thirty minutes of irrigation brought a synthetic turf surface down to the temperature of the natural grass beside it, about 85 degrees. Within five minutes it had rebounded to 120. Penn State's own published figure for how long watering helps is a reduction of as much as 20 degrees an hour and a half later. Read those two results together and the water argument gets thinner. If the surface needs irrigating to be usable on a July afternoon, then a product bought to eliminate irrigation is being irrigated. It is still using far less water than a lawn. But it is not the zero it was sold as, and the cooling it buys is measured in minutes, not afternoons. The practical version for a homeowner: plan for a surface you will not walk on barefoot in the middle of a summer day, and do not plan on hosing your way out of that. Where turf is the right answer There are four situations where we will recommend it without hedging. Small areas in real shade. The Water Conservancy District's own urban heat material makes the point that shade trees can lower surface temperatures by up to 50 degrees, and that shading keeps areas up to 25 degrees cooler. Shade beats material choice by a wide margin. Turf under an established canopy is a different product than turf in open sun. Strips where lawn is not legal anyway. St. George City Code § 10-7-7 caps residential lawn at 8 percent of lot size with a maximum of 1,500 square feet, and prohibits lawn outright in park strips, in any landscape area less than eight feet wide, and on slopes over 15 percent. A four foot side yard is never going to be grass. The choice there is between turf, mulch, gravel and pavers, not between turf and a lawn. Dog runs and small use areas where the alternative is bare dirt. And places where the surface has to take traffic that would kill a planting in the first season. In each of those cases the deciding factor is the same: the area is small, it is shaded or it is not walked on barefoot at two in the afternoon. How the rebate treats it, which is not how most people assume This is the part that surprises people. Under the Washington County Water Conservancy District's program, artificial turf is accepted in lieu of mulch if it is permeable to air and water. The District's own answer to whether there is a rebate for replacing lawn with artificial turf is, verbatim, not exactly, but you may use artificial turf as a component of your project. In lieu of mulch is the whole sentence. Turf is treated as a ground covering, not as a landscape. It does not count toward the living plant coverage the program requires, and the plants still have to be there. The District's agreement sets the depth for the ground covering generally: at least 2 inches of mulch, with permeable artificial turf named as one of the acceptable materials. Permeability is also doing real work in that rule, and not only for the rebate. The District's urban heat material identifies impermeable surfaces, streets, sidewalks and buildings, as the main contributors to urban heat because they absorb and release it, raising nighttime temperatures. What goes down on the ground affects the air over it. One municipal caveat the District's rule does not reach. Toquerville City Code § 10-21A-5 says "Synthetic turf is not permitted as a substitute for planting materials." The water district accepts permeable artificial turf in lieu of mulch; Toquerville city code does not accept it as a substitute for planting. At a Toquerville address the District rule is not the whole story, and the city code has to be read before anyone specifies turf. How surfaces are treated in the WCWCD rebate calculation Surface Counts inside the rebated area? Note Permeable artificial turf Yes, in lieu of mulch District program only. Must pass air and water Ungrouted pavers, dry set flagstone Yes, treated as mulch Grout defeats permeability and the credit Decomposed granite, gravel, rock mulch, bark Yes, it is mulch The ordinary case Poured concrete No, subtracted The District subtracts non-permeable areas when calculating the incentive Mortared or grouted paver and flagstone No, subtracted Same reason as concrete Pool, pond, water feature No Also prohibited in the conversion area by the recorded easement Bare soil Only for native desert restoration The program agreement and Standards §5.D allow it where native plants restore an area to native desert; the easement's Exhibit B does not carry the exception The state program takes the opposite position Worth knowing if you have been reading around. Utah's statewide landscape incentive program excludes artificial turf outright: its definition of water efficient landscaping does not include artificial turf, a swimming pool, water feature or concrete. Utah Water Savers explains why in its own FAQ, saying research has shown that artificial turf can cause much more environmental harm than it can offset by its water saving potential. In Washington County the district program is the one that applies, because the state's own eligibility page routes every Washington County jurisdiction to the district, which is why these are best understood as one program administered locally rather than two you could stack. Confirm that with the district before you plan around it. So the District's permeable in lieu of mulch rule governs a conversion here. But the disagreement between two state level water agencies is a fair thing for a homeowner to weigh, and pretending it does not exist would be the wrong way to sell anything. What fails on turf in this climate The fiber is usually not what goes. The backing and the infill degrade under ultraviolet and thermal cycling, and the backing typically fails before the surface looks worn out. That is the same failure pattern that takes out exposed plastics generally here: irrigation boxes, exposed poly tubing, plastic edging, sealants and caulks all embrittle or crack under this ultraviolet load faster than manufacturer literature written for other climates implies. Two consequences for a specification. Ask what the backing is warranted for in a high ultraviolet, high temperature installation, and read the temperature exclusions rather than the headline year figure. And treat the drainage under it as real construction rather than as a mat on dirt, because a permeable surface over compacted subgrade is not permeable in any way that matters when the first August cell arrives. What planted conversion does instead The rebate program requires 50 percent living plant cover at maturity across the converted area, and the way the District measures it is more generous than most people expect. Mature size is what counts, not the size at installation. Trees are credited at 350 square feet of cover each and shrubs, groundcovers and other perennials at 35 square feet each, which makes one tree equal to ten plants. Existing trees and plants in the lawn area that survive the conversion are applied to the calculation, and the District specifically lists you must remove your trees as a myth it is debunking. Do the arithmetic on a 1,000 square foot conversion. You need 500 square feet of mature cover. Two trees is 700. One tree plus five shrubs is 525. Fifteen shrubs and perennials is 525. That is a real planting, not a token one, and it is achievable without covering the ground in vegetation. The trees are doing the heavy lifting on heat, which is the point of this whole page. The District's own material says shade trees are far more effective at cooling temperatures than grass, with the potential to lower surface temperatures by up to 50 degrees, and that grass uses four times more water than trees and shrubs. St. George City Code § 10-7-7 separately requires two water conserving trees at each single family dwelling, at a minimum one and one half inch caliper, and § 10-23-3 requires at least one of them in the front yard. The District publishes its own top ten list to choose from, including Chinese Pistache, Desert Willow, Texas Red Oak, which its notes describe as well adapted to our alkaline soils, and Mondell Pine. One thing we tell every customer before they sign anything. Low water is not no maintenance, and the District says so in its own materials. A planted conversion needs pruning, emitter checks and weed control, and the first three years are the ones that decide whether it looks like the rendering. Anyone who tells you a xeriscape is finished on install day has not maintained one. The way we would decide it Look at the area in question at two in the afternoon in July and ask three questions. Is it shaded. Will anybody stand on it barefoot. Is it small. Three yeses and turf is a sensible product used the way the District treats it, as a ground covering that does not need irrigation. A no on shade and a yes on foot traffic, and you are buying a surface you cannot use during the months you are most likely to want it. In that case the money goes further in trees, and the trees keep working on the house behind them. What we’d do at your house We walk the area with you in the sun and tell you honestly which parts of it are shaded enough for turf and which are not. Where lawn is prohibited by the eight foot rule or the slope rule, we lay out the real options rather than defaulting to plastic. At a Toquerville address we read the city code before specifying turf at all, because § 10-21A-5 does not permit synthetic turf as a substitute for planting materials even though the water district accepts it in lieu of mulch. If turf is going in, it goes in permeable and over drainage we actually built, because that is what the rebate rule and the ground both require. We do the plant cover arithmetic in front of you, with mature sizes and the tree credit, so you can see how the 50 percent is met. We will tell you where the state program and the district program disagree about turf rather than quoting whichever one suits the sale. We explain the recorded conservation easement before you commit to the conversion, not after. guides_backflow_testing.text: id="main"> Guides · Plumbing Your backflow test notice, explained St. George requires an approved assembly on every outside watering system, protected from freezing, and tested every year. Here is what that device does. A notice arrives telling you your backflow assembly is due for its annual test. Most people have never looked at the thing. It is the brass device standing above ground near where your irrigation system leaves the house, and it is the only part of your sprinkler system that protects your drinking water. This page covers what the city requires, why irrigation systems in particular get this treatment, what the test actually measures, how these assemblies fail here, and what happens when one does not pass. What St. George requires The city's backflow page lists four things asked of homeowners. Install approved backflow assemblies on all outside watering systems. Protect the assemblies from freezing. Have it tested annually. And maintain hose bib vacuum breakers on exterior garden hose connections. The ordinance behind it is St. George City Code Title 8, Chapter 2, Backflow and Cross Connections. Section 8-2-4 covers when a device or assembly is required, section 8-2-5 covers testing and inspection, and section 8-2-16 is the penalty section. Section 8-2-4(A) puts the duty on the property owner in plain words. The owner must "purchase, install, test, inspect and maintain backflow prevention devices or assemblies wherever it will be possible for used, unclean, polluted or contaminated water ... to enter any portion of his potable water system." That is the whole legal structure in one sentence. The device is yours, the maintenance is yours, and the test is yours to have done. Water Services is at 620 East Waterworks Drive, 435-627-4802. They are the right call for how the city wants the test result handled for your address, and for anything on the street side of your meter. Why irrigation systems specifically An irrigation system is a permanent, pressurized connection between your drinking water and an environment that is contaminated by definition. Emitters and spray heads sit in soil that holds fertilizer, herbicide, pesticide and animal waste, and after a cycle they often sit in standing water. Normally pressure pushes outward, from the main to the house to the sprinkler head, and nothing travels backward. Then something drops the pressure in the street: a hydrant flush, a water main break, a fire flow, a pump station event. The gradient reverses, and the plumbing does the obvious thing. It draws water backward, out of the soil, through the heads, into your house and into the street main. That is the part worth sitting with. Backsiphonage does not require anything to go wrong at your house. It only requires something to go wrong at the street. The city frames it the same way: backflow occurs when water pressure drops, potentially allowing contaminated water from irrigation systems to flow back into the municipal supply, and the program exists to prevent contamination of the culinary water system. The assemblies, and where each one belongs Not every device on this list is testable, and not every device is acceptable for every hazard. The type you have should match the hazard your system presents. Backflow devices and assemblies, what they protect against, and where each is used Device Protects against Testable Typical use Hose bib vacuum breaker Backsiphonage at a hose connection No Required by St. George on exterior garden hose connections Atmospheric vacuum breaker (AVB) Backsiphonage only No Must sit at least 6 inches above the flood level rim of the fixture or device it serves, measured to the device's critical level, with no valve downstream, and never under continuous pressure for more than 12 consecutive hours Pressure vacuum breaker (PVB) Backsiphonage only, not backpressure Yes The standard residential irrigation assembly in Utah. Must sit at least 12 inches above all downstream piping and the highest point of use, installed vertically, never below grade or in a pit. Above grade, so freeze vulnerable Spill resistant vacuum breaker (SVB) Same as a PVB, without spilling on test Yes Indoor locations where a PVB's spill would cause damage Double check valve assembly (DCVA) Backsiphonage and backpressure, non health hazard only Yes Fire sprinkler systems without chemical additives, some commercial premise isolation Reduced pressure principle assembly (RPZ) Backsiphonage and backpressure, including health hazards Yes Irrigation with fertilizer or chemical injection, boilers with treatment chemicals, commercial process water Air gap Everything. The only non mechanical protection Not applicable Two pipe diameters, minimum 1 inch. St. George requires a permanently affixed air gap on every chemical vehicle that takes water from the city supply The fertigation trap Here is the change that catches homeowners, and it is worth knowing before you buy anything at a garden center. An irrigation system on its own is generally treated as a pollutant hazard, not a health hazard, and a pressure vacuum breaker is adequate protection for it. Add a fertilizer or chemical injector to that system and it becomes a contaminant hazard under backpressure. The required protection goes up with it, from a PVB to a reduced pressure principle assembly. People install fertigation kits on a Saturday without any idea they have changed what the code requires at their meter. If you have one, or you are thinking about one, that is the conversation to have first. One siting rule that goes with an RPZ: it discharges out of a relief port when it does its job, so it has to be above grade with an air gapped relief drain. An RPZ in a pit that can flood is worse than no assembly at all, because a discharging relief valve sitting under water creates exactly the cross connection the assembly was installed to prevent. What happens during the test The tester closes the isolation valves, attaches a differential pressure gauge to the test cocks on the assembly, and measures whether each check valve holds the required pressure difference in the correct direction. On an RPZ the relief valve is also checked, to confirm it opens and closes at the right differential. Your irrigation is shut down for the few minutes this takes. The whole test is a measurement of numbers a device either makes or does not make. There is no judgment call in it, which is why it is worth two questions before anyone touches yours. Ask what backflow certification the tester holds. Ask when the gauge was last calibrated. A test report is only as good as the gauge that produced it, and a gauge that has drifted will pass an assembly that should fail and fail one that should pass. Call Water Services at 435-627-4802 to confirm how the city wants your result submitted, and keep a copy. It is a one page document and it is the only proof you have that the device on the side of your house works. Freezing, which is how most of these die here A PVB or an RPZ holds standing water in its body, its bonnet, and its check chambers, above ground, out in the open. Water expands about 9 percent when it freezes. With nowhere to go, it splits the brass body, cracks the bonnet, or ruptures the check assembly. A cracked body is not repairable. The local pattern is distinctive, and it is worth understanding rather than just being told to winterize. St. George averages a January low of 28.4°F, sees roughly 60 mornings a year at or below freezing, has a historical freeze window running November 12 to March 14, and holds a record low of minus 11°F. Most of those freezes are short overnight dips right at 32°F, not sustained hard freezes. That means the assembly that cracks here is usually not one that was left running all winter. It is one that was nominally winterized but had water trapped inside it: blown out but never drained, drained but with the test cocks left closed, or ball valves left fully open or fully closed so a slug of water sat inside the ball. The order that avoids that: shut the isolation valve upstream, open both test cocks and any bleed, then set both ball valves to roughly 45 degrees so nothing is trapped inside the ball body. Blow out the irrigation zones with compressed air at 50 psi or less, never at high pressure through the assembly's internals. Then insulate or cover it, secured well enough to survive the wind. The 45 degree step is the one that gets skipped, and it is the most common cause of a cracked valve. What a failed test means A failure means the assembly did not hold the required differential pressure. A check valve leaked backward, or on an RPZ the relief valve did not open or close at the correct differential. It is a specific mechanical finding, not an opinion. The usual causes are ordinary. Debris on a check seat, which is sand, scale flakes or pipe chips. A worn poppet or disc rubber. A weak or broken spring. A fouled relief valve. A leaking isolation valve that looks like a check failure until someone rules it out. Or a freeze cracked body, which is the one cause with no repair. Most failures are rebuilt with the manufacturer's kit of springs, discs, seats and O rings, and rebuilding is normally the right answer. Replacement is correct in three cases: the body is cracked, the assembly is obsolete and parts are no longer available, or the assembly is the wrong type for the hazard. That last one is the fertigation case, and a failed test is the right moment to correct it rather than rebuild the wrong device. After any repair or relocation, the assembly is tested again. A rebuild that has not been retested is a rebuild nobody has verified. What we’d do at your house We test with a gauge, we show you the numbers it produced, and you get the report. If it fails, we tell you whether it is a rebuild or a replacement and why, before we quote either one. If you have added a fertilizer injector, we will tell you the assembly type has to change, even though that is the more expensive answer. We winterize with the ball valves set part open, because that is the step that keeps the body from cracking in February. We look at your hose bib vacuum breakers while we are there, since the city asks for those too and they cost almost nothing. We are not going to sell you an RPZ for a system that only needs a pressure vacuum breaker. guides_condo_pipe_who_pays.title: A pipe broke in the wall of your condo. Who pays?
guides_condo_pipe_who_pays.meta: Utah Code § 57-8-7.2 draws the line at the finished surface. Everything behind it is common area, and a pipe gets sorted by how many units it serves.
heads: A pipe broke in the wall of your condo. Who pays?
First, make sure you are actually a condominium
Insurance, in the order it actually runs
Access, notice, and what to do in the first ten minutes
What we’d do at your house
The work this guide is about
guides_condo_pipe_who_pays.text: id="main"> Guides · Plumbing A pipe broke in the wall of your condo. Who pays? Utah Code § 57-8-7.2 draws the line at the finished surface. Everything behind it is common area, and a pipe gets sorted by how many units it serves. Water is coming through a ceiling or down a wall and someone is going to be told to write a check. In a Utah condominium the answer is not a matter of who is nicer about it. There is a statute that draws the boundary, and it draws it in an unintuitive place: at the back of the paint. This page walks through where the unit ends, how a pipe gets classified, who repairs what, whose insurance goes first, and what a published 2026 advisory opinion decided when exactly this happened. Two cautions before the detail. The statutory rules below apply unless your declaration says otherwise, and Washington County declarations differ from each other on precisely this point, so the declaration is the first document to read, not the last. And this is a description of what the statutes and one advisory opinion say. It is not legal advice. Confirm your own situation with the association and, where the money justifies it, an attorney. First, make sure you are actually a condominium People use the word loosely and the two Utah acts are different. Since 2026 there is a bright-line test. Under § 57-8-2 the Condominium Ownership Act applies if the association's declaration says the chapter applies, or, if the declaration is silent on the question, if the plats of the association are designated as condominium plats. That section applies regardless of when the association was created. Section 57-8a-103 does the mirror image for the Community Association Act: it applies if the declaration says so, or, if silent, if the plats are not designated as condominium plats. This matters because the boundary rules described below live in Chapter 8. If you are a townhome on a lot in a planned community, your maintenance architecture is § 57-8a-224, which uses the same structure: except as otherwise provided in the declaration or the insurance part, the association maintains, repairs and replaces common areas, and the lot owner does the same for the lot. Section 57-8a-224 also does not apply during the period of administrative control, which is worth knowing in a community still under the developer. Washington County has a lot of attached product where owners genuinely do not know which act governs them. Pull the plat and the first pages of the declaration. Five minutes there saves an argument later. Where your unit ends Section 57-8-7.2 applies unless the declaration provides otherwise, and only where the declaration designates a wall, floor, or ceiling as a unit boundary. Where it does, subsection (2)(a) lists what belongs to the unit: lath, furring, wallboard, plasterboard, plaster, paneling, tiles, wallpaper, paint, finished flooring, "and any other material constituting part of the finished surface of a wall, floor, or ceiling." Then subsection (2)(b) does the rest of the work in one sentence: "Any portion of a wall, floor, or ceiling not listed in Subsection (2)(a) is part of the common areas and facilities." Everything behind the finished surface is common area. Studs, sheathing, the cavity, the framing. Not yours. Subsection (4) keeps the inside of the unit yours: subject to the pipe rule below, spaces, interior partitions, and other fixtures and improvements within the boundaries are part of the unit. And subsection (5) reaches the other direction, making shutters, awnings, window boxes, doorsteps, stoops, porches, balconies, patios, exterior doors, exterior windows and any other fixture designated to serve a single unit but located outside the boundaries into limited common areas allocated to that unit. The pipe rule Subsection (3) is the one you came for. If a chute, flue, duct, pipe, wire, conduit, bearing wall, bearing column, or any other fixture lies partially within and partially outside the unit boundary, then the portion serving only that unit is limited common area, and the portion is common area if it serves more than one unit or serves any portion of the common areas. So a pipe is not sorted by where it runs. It is sorted by how many units it serves. A supply line that crosses the boundary and feeds nothing but your kitchen is limited common area. A vertical stack that carries three units' waste is common area, even where it passes through your wall. The step most people miss is what limited common area means for repairs. Section 57-8-3 defines limited common areas as the common areas designated in the declaration as reserved for the use of a certain unit or units to the exclusion of the others. Limited common area is a kind of common area. And § 57-8-7(7) says that except as otherwise provided in the declaration or in § 57-8-43, the association is responsible for the maintenance, repair and replacement of common areas and facilities, and the unit owner is responsible for the unit. Put those together and the repair of a line serving only your unit but sitting outside your boundary is presumptively the association's, unless your declaration reassigns it. Many declarations do reassign it. That is why the declaration comes first. The practical line, in a condominium whose declaration sets wall, floor and ceiling boundaries What failed Classification Repair obligation absent a declaration that says otherwise Faucet, valve, trap, fixture, finished tile and paint Unit Owner Branch line inside the unit boundary Unit Owner Line crossing the boundary that serves only your unit Limited common area Association, under § 57-8-7(7)(a) Vertical stack or main serving two or more units Common area Association Any line serving a portion of the common areas Common area Association Balcony, patio, exterior door or window serving one unit Limited common area Association, under § 57-8-7(7)(a) The case that confirms it Advisory Opinion No. 2026-19, issued by the Office of the Homeowners' Association Ombudsman and published on the Utah Department of Commerce site, dealt with exactly this. A pipe broke in a common-area utility stack and damaged a unit. Four holdings are worth carrying around. The association had to repair the broken common-area line, under § 57-8-7(7). The association's property policy was primary, under § 57-8-43(3)(a) and (9)(f). The association had to reimburse the owner for payments he made under his personal policy that should have been covered by the association's policy. And the owner still owed his proportional share of the association's deductible, under § 57-8-43(9)(g)(ii). Then the holding nobody expects: the diagnostic costs remained the homeowner's responsibility. Finding the leak and proving where it sits is the owner's expense. The repair of the common line is the association's. That is a strange-sounding split until you see the logic of it, and it is exactly why the locate matters. A leak documented to the inch, in writing, with the line identified and the units it serves counted, is the difference between a claim the association pays and a months-long argument about whose pipe it was. Insurance, in the order it actually runs Section 57-8-43 applies to policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2011, and it is more owner-friendly than most people assume. Subsection (3)(a) requires the association to maintain, to the extent reasonably available, blanket property or guaranteed replacement cost insurance on the physical structures including common areas, limited common areas and units. Subsection (9)(b) sets coverage at not less than 100 percent of full replacement cost at purchase and at each renewal. Subsection (9)(c) is the one to read out loud if anyone tells you your remodel is not covered. Coverage must include any fixture, improvement or betterment installed at any time to a unit or to a limited common area associated with a unit, whether installed in the original construction or in any remodel or later alteration, including floor covering, cabinets, light fixtures, electrical fixtures, heating or plumbing fixtures, paint, wall covering and windows. Where both policies cover a loss, subsection (9)(f) makes the association's policy primary and puts the association's deductible on the owner. The owner's share is the unit damage percentage multiplied by the association's deductible, under (9)(g)(ii), and if it goes unpaid for 30 days after substantial completion of repairs the association may levy an assessment for it, under (9)(g)(iii). The association must give notice of its deductible and of any change to it; under (9)(i), if it fails to give that notice it absorbs the portion it could otherwise have assessed. One flip to know about. Under (9)(j), if the board, exercising business judgment, determines the loss is not likely to exceed the association's deductible, then the owner's own policy is primary for damage to the unit and its appurtenant limited common area, the association stays responsible for common-area loss, and the association need not tender the claim. Two more provisions worth knowing: under (7) the association's insurer waives subrogation against a unit owner and anyone residing with a resident owner, and under (8)(b) any provision of a declaration, bylaw or rule contrary to this section has no effect. Access, notice, and what to do in the first ten minutes The association does not get to walk in. Under § 57-8-7(1) and (8), access to a unit for common-area repair requires reasonable notice, which the statute defines as written notice hand delivered at least 24 hours ahead. For emergency repairs, meaning repairs that if delayed will likely result in immediate and substantial damage, notice is whatever is reasonable under the circumstances. Under § 57-8-7(9) the association is liable to repair damage it causes to common areas, or to a unit it used to access common areas, within a time that is reasonable under the circumstances. In the first ten minutes, none of that matters. Stop the water. In a condominium the shutoff may not be yours, and that is a genuinely confusing thing to work out at midnight, which is why it is worth finding out on a calm afternoon instead. Know where your unit's shutoff is, know whether there is one, and know who to call if the valve is on common ground. If a valve will not turn, do not force it. At 18 to 22 grains, old gate valve stems seize, and a snapped stem turns a leak into a flood. Then document. Photographs before anything is cut, the time the water started, and where it is coming from. If the line turns out to serve more than your unit, that record is the file the association's carrier will ask for. What we’d do at your house We find the leak and write down what we found, where, and how many units the line serves, because that sentence is what decides who pays. The report is written so it can be handed to a manager or a board without translation. We read the declaration before we tell you whose pipe it is, since the statute yields to the declaration on this exact question.
