guides_curbless_shower_guide.text: id="main"> Guides · Accessible living Curbless walk-in showers: the complete guide A standard 60-inch tub occupies the same footprint as a 60 by 30 roll-in shower. The numbers, the slab, the hard water, and what the research honestly says. A curbless shower has no step. You walk in, or roll in, on the same floor you crossed to get there. The reason it fits so many houses here is a matter of dimensions: a standard 60-inch alcove tub has exactly the footprint of a 60 by 30 inch roll-in shower. The fixture most people fall getting out of occupies the same space as the one with nothing to step over. This guide covers the numbers that matter, the two St. George problems that make the job different from the version on a national website, and the honest answer to whether the work prevents falls. It is written about staying in a house, not leaving it. A private home is not an ADA facility The Americans with Disabilities Act governs public accommodations: stores, clinics, hotels. It does not govern your bathroom. What people want when they ask for "ADA" is the set of dimensions and clearances in the ADA standards and in ANSI A117.1, the accessible-design standard those numbers come from. Those are a design benchmark, and a good one, worked out for wheelchairs, walkers and a person steadying herself on a wall. One number gets published wrong more than any other. Grab bars are designed and tested to 250 pounds of force. There is no 500-pound requirement in any code or standard; that figure traces to product marketing and to people informally doubling the real number. We say 250 because that is what the standard says. The numbers that matter Exact mounting heights, bar diameters and clearances come from ANSI A117.1, and from your occupational therapist if you have one. Send the recommendations; we build to them. Grab bars: rated at 250 pounds-force. Into solid blocking when the wall is open, or rated retrofit anchors when it isn't. Placed at the toilet, the shower entry and the shower seat. Floor tile: a wet dynamic coefficient of friction of 0.50 or higher. The 2022 revision of ANSI A326.3 moved barefoot wet areas into their own, higher category; the 0.42 on some tile boxes is for a different category of floor. A hand-held shower on a slide bar, so the spray comes to the person. A fold-down or built-in seat, with a bar within reach of it. Lever handles, rocker light switches, a comfort-height toilet. Lighting and contrast planned for older eyes; the Illuminating Engineering Society publishes a recommended practice for older adults and we work from it. Large-format wall tile with as little grout as the layout allows, for a reason explained below. Grab bars that don't look like grab bars The objection to bars is almost never that they don't work. It is that they look like a hospital. The answer is a bar that is also a towel bar or a shelf, rated to the same 250 pounds and anchored the same way. Built so it doesn't look built. During a remodel the wall is open, and solid blocking goes in behind every place a bar might ever go, including places you don't want a bar today. That costs a few pieces of lumber now and nothing later. On a finished wall, rated retrofit anchors do the job, installed to the rating, into the material that is actually there. A suction-cup bar is a decoration. The St. George problem: the floor is a slab A curbless shower has to drain, so the shower floor sits lower than the bathroom floor, or the bathroom floor comes up to meet it. On a joisted wood floor that is carpentry. On a slab-on-grade house, which is most of St. George, it is concrete: the pan is recessed into the slab, or the surrounding floor is built up over it. The second option adds a small step at the bathroom door, which is often the trade-off worth making. It is a different job from the one on a national website, and it is priced as one. Then the warning that belongs on any page about cutting a slab. Some slabs are post-tensioned: steel tendons run through the concrete under tens of thousands of pounds of force each. Cutting one blind can kill someone; the strand releases its energy instantly and whips out of the concrete, and the slab loses the reinforcement that tendon provided. Post-tensioned slabs are the standard engineering response to expansive soil, and St. George's blue clay is exactly that soil, so the odds a local home sits on one are real. How common they are here has not been confirmed, and we say "may be" until it is. How to tell: round, grouted stressing pockets two to three inches across around the slab edge; a placard in the garage reading "POST-TENSIONED SLAB, DO NOT CUT OR CORE"; tendon layout drawings in the builder's or county's plan file. No visible pockets is not proof; stucco and patios cover them. What a careful contractor does: establish whether the slab is post-tensioned before anything else, and if in doubt, treat it as if it is. Get the tendon drawing. Scan the cut area with ground-penetrating radar and mark every tendon on the floor. Keep the cut between tendons. If a tendon can't be avoided, stop; that is a job for a structural engineer and a post-tensioning specialist, not a plumber. On some slabs the right answer is to build the floor up rather than cut down. The other St. George problem: the water The City of St. George tells residents to set water softeners to 18 grains per gallon, maximum 22. At that hardness a glass shower door etches and grout stains, and no amount of squeegeeing keeps up. On a curbless shower that is a cleanability point, and cleanability is what keeps a shower usable for someone who no longer wants to scrub on her knees. So the design changes. Large-format wall tile, to minimize grout lines. A curbless layout that does not need a glass door at all, because the floor slope and the spray placement keep the water where it belongs. And a softener, which takes hardness at the tap to functionally zero to one grain and is the only thing that fixes the problem rather than managing it. The softener is a plumbing job; we do both. Does this actually prevent falls? The honest answer The best evidence is a 2023 Cochrane review of environmental interventions for preventing falls in older people at home. Two results, reported together. In adults at higher risk of falling, home modification reduced the rate of falls by 38 percent, high-certainty evidence. In the general older population, unselected for risk, it showed no effect, a rate ratio of 1.05, also high certainty. That means two different conversations. If someone in the house has a history of falls or a mobility limitation, the shower is a safety measure with strong evidence behind it. If you are 68, healthy, and playing pickleball at the Senior Games, it is not a safety device and we won't sell it as one. It is a better bathroom: easier to clean, easier to use, and already right for whatever comes later. Both are good reasons. They are not the same reason. Age matters more than the headline number suggests. The CDC's fall-injury rate roughly doubles at each step from 65 to 74, to 75 to 84, to 85 and over, on the order of 112, then 241, then 515 per 100,000. The 75-plus household is where the safety case is strongest. Walk-in tub or walk-in shower? We install both, so take this as a comparison rather than a pitch. A walk-in tub fills and drains with the door closed and you inside it, so you sit in an empty tub while it fills and a cooling one while it drains. The door seal is a wear item, and a failed seal in a full tub is a flood. The threshold is lower than a standard tub but it is not zero. A curbless shower has none of those failure modes and fits the same 60-inch alcove. The tub wins when someone wants to bathe sitting down and soak, which a shower cannot do. We have a longer comparison on its own page. On resale, the usual worry is whether removing your only tub hurts value. In Washington County, where the Census puts 22.4 percent of the population at 65 or over, a no-step shower is a feature a large share of buyers are looking for. If the house has a second bathroom, we generally recommend keeping a tub there. Your HOA, and doing it in phases A bathroom is interior work. Since May 6, 2026, Utah Code § 57-8a-212(4)(n) bars an association's declaration from restricting the interior of a dwelling except as reasonably necessary for the safety of adjacent lots, and under the Fair Housing Act an association cannot deny a reasonable modification for a disability, including a walk-in shower or grab bars. Our HOA approval guide has the details. The work can be staged: the shower now, the toilet and lighting later, the second bath after that. Universal design, the idea that a space should work for as many people as possible without adaptation, is a different discipline from accessible design, which solves a specific limitation. A curbless shower is universal design. It looks like a nice bathroom because it is one. What we’d do at your house We measure the alcove first, because in most houses here a 60 by 30 roll-in shower fits where the tub is without moving a wall. We check the slab for post-tensioning before we quote, and if there is any doubt we quote the job as though it is. Blocking goes in behind every plausible bar location while the wall is open, whether or not you want bars today. Tile is specified to a wet DCOF of 0.50 or higher and the hardware to 250 pounds; the spec sheets go in your file. If you have an occupational therapist, we build to her recommendations, and we'll do the job in phases if that's easier. guides_defensible_space_and_water.text: id="main"> Guides · Water-wise landscape Defensible space, water savings and your wildfire fee Utah HB 48 took effect on January 1, 2026. If your property is inside the high risk boundary, a county officer now assesses an annual fee on it. The work that lowers your classification is mostly the same work that lowers your water bill. Most homeowners here heard about the wildfire fee from a neighbor and have not read the bill. The bill is nineteen pages, it is public, and what it actually does is narrower and more specific than the rumors. This page is read from the enrolled text of House Bill 48, Wildland Urban Interface Modifications, from the 2025 general session. It states what the statute says and stops there, then covers the physical work: the three zones around a house, what burns near a structure, and the overlap that lets one landscape project do three jobs. What HB 48 actually does The bill took effect on January 1, 2026. It enacts a new Part 4 of Utah Code Chapter 65A-8, along with Section 17-16-22 on county evaluation and fees and Section 31A-22-1310 on insuring wildland urban interface property. Three things follow from it. First, adoption of the building standard is no longer optional for local government. Under Section 65A-8-203(9)(a), when the state adopts an edition of the Utah Wildland Urban Interface Code, the county shall adopt and enforce it for unincorporated areas and the relevant municipality shall adopt and enforce it for incorporated areas, with two years to follow any later edition. Second, Section 17-16-22(3) requires that beginning January 1, 2026, a county officer shall annually assess a fee against the owner of high risk wildland urban interface property, in the amount set by the Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands. Under subsection (4), a county may hold a political subdivision lien on the property for a fee that is past due. Third, there is an evaluation behind the fee. Section 65A-8-401(2) defines a triage scale as a scale with three classifications, adopted by the Division, used to evaluate and classify property in the wildland urban interface as to what actions are needed to prepare it for fire. A wildland urban interface coordinator performs the evaluation. The fee, exactly as the statute writes it Section 65A-8-402(4) is short and it is the whole of what the statute says about the amount. The Division shall annually set a fee amount that is based on the square footage of a structure within the high risk wildland urban interface, to pay for the costs of implementing this part, to be assessed and collected by a county. And the Division may tier the fee amount to account for what level on the triage scale a property is assigned by a coordinator. That is it. The dollar figures are not in the bill. They are set by the Division annually and by administrative rule, and anyone quoting you a schedule should be able to tell you which rule it came from. We do not publish a number we cannot cite. One more thing in the statute matters to a homeowner and is easy to miss. Under Section 65A-8-402(2), after the evaluation the coordinator has to tell the owner three things: the triage classification, the fee owed, and the resources available from the Division or the county to bring the property to the first or second classification. The classification is meant to be something you can move. Whether you are in it The fee applies to high risk wildland urban interface property, and Section 65A-8-401(1) defines that by reference to a specific instrument: the wildfire risk assessment mapping tool required under Section 65A-8-203(8)(a). The Division develops and maintains that tool, with boundaries established by rule, using a scientific assessment focused on the risk to dwellings. So there is one authoritative answer to the question of whether your property is inside, and it is that map. Not an insurance letter, not a neighborhood rumor, and not our opinion at the kitchen table. Adoption of the code by your city is mandatory rather than discretionary, so the useful question is not whether your jurisdiction has adopted it but where the process currently stands. Your city's building department is the place to ask. What it changed for insurance This is the part of HB 48 that gets the least attention and affects the most people. From January 1, 2026, Section 31A-22-1310 restricts insurers to the Division's wildfire risk assessment mapping tool boundary when deciding whether a property is high risk wildland urban interface. A carrier canceling or not renewing for wildfire risk has to state the facts behind the decision with reasonable precision, and a premium increase of more than 20 percent over the prior term has to be explained on request. And beginning January 1, 2028, under Section 65A-8-402(3)(b), the Division maintains a database a wildland urban interface insurer may access to learn a property's triage classification. The classification will not stay private to you and the county. The three zones The physical work is organized by distance from the structure. The national convention divides it at 0 to 5 feet, 5 to 30 feet and 30 to 100 feet. Utah State University Extension's publication, Landscaping in the Utah Wildland-Urban Interface, names the first zone 0 to 30 feet with a hardened sub-zone inside the first five, and the second 30 to 100. The substance is the same. Zero to five feet is the one that decides the outcome. USU's language is blunt: there should not be anything flammable next to, on, or within five feet of the house. Exterior materials in the nonflammable category, which the publication names as stucco, concrete and asphalt shingles. In practice this strip is gravel, pavers, flagstone or bare mineral ground, and nothing else. Five to thirty feet takes sparse, low-growing plantings, watered adequately so they do not dry out. That is the sentence that reconciles fire work with irrigation work: a drip-irrigated plant is a fire-resistant plant, and a dead one is fuel. Thirty to a hundred feet is about keeping the fuel discontinuous rather than removing it. Plant in small clumps, not in large patches. Space tree canopies at least twenty feet apart. Remove lower branches so fire cannot climb into the canopy. USU calls this zone ideal for turfgrass and paved surfaces. Propane tanks want a ten foot buffer clear of flammable material. What burns near a house USU names the hazardous category directly: conifers, meaning pines, spruces, firs and junipers, which contain flammable compounds and ignite more quickly because of their needle composition. The fire-resistant choices it names are broadleaf, maples, oaks, ash and lindens, with smaller species providing less fuel. That has a specific local consequence and it is not a comfortable one. Junipers are one of the most common foundation plantings in Washington County. A mature juniper against a wall sits in the five foot zone, holds years of dead interior material, and is on the hazardous list. If there is one plant to move out of the ignition zone first, it is that one. Mulch is the other quiet problem. USU's own figure flags flammable wood mulch as a less than ideal feature near a structure. Wood chips are excellent horticulture and they are also fuel, so they belong out past the first five feet, with rock or gravel against the building. The same rule reaches ornamental grasses even though the publication does not name them. Nothing flammable belongs within five feet of the house. Grasses build standing dead thatch, so they go outside the ignition zone and get cut back annually, which the District's perennial guidance recommends anyway. One clause in the code shows how seriously the state takes this work. Under Section 15A-5-203, a single-family dwelling is exempt from a residential fire sprinkler requirement if it is outside the wildland urban interface, built in a one-lot subdivision, and has fifty feet of defensible space on all sides. Defensible space is already, in that one narrow case, a code-recognized substitute for a sprinkler system. Why one job does three things A water-wise conversion and a defensible space project are largely the same physical work. One conversion can lower the water bill, qualify for the water district's landscape rebate, and move a property toward a lower triage classification. The reason to design for all three at once is that the three sets of rules mostly agree, and where they disagree it is expensive to find out afterwards. Where a water-wise conversion already does the fire work The conversion does Defensible space wants Replaces continuous turf with spaced plantings Plant in small clumps, not in large patches Rock and gravel mulch fields Noncombustible ground cover in the first five feet Ungrouted pavers, flagstone and decomposed granite paths Paved surfaces are ideal in the outer zone Low, spaced plantings replacing foundation shrubs Sparse, low-growing plantings close to the house Drip irrigation to every plant Plants need adequate watering to prevent drying out Annual cutback of perennials and grasses Removal of dead fine fuel Trees spaced by mature canopy for the coverage credit Space tree canopies at least twenty feet apart Where the two goals disagree Every rebated conversion attaches a conservation easement to the converted area. It continues in perpetuity, runs with the land, binds heirs and assigns, is recorded with the Washington County Recorder and shows up in a title search. Inside that area, irrigated grass, spray irrigation, pools, ponds and water features are prohibited forever. Enforcement is by aerial imagery, and a violation runs written notice, 45 days to cure, then repayment of the full rebate plus administrative costs plus five percent annual interest. Now put that next to USU calling turfgrass ideal in the thirty to hundred foot zone. If a green buffer might ever be wanted out there, that ground must be left outside the conversion area, and the decision has to be made before the pre-approval site visit. Afterwards it is permanent. A well-designed conversion does most of the defensible space work for free. It only works that way if it was designed for both from the beginning. Organic mulch. Good soil practice, and flagged as flammable near a structure. Rock in the first five feet, wood chips further out; the rebate accepts either, as long as the mulch is permeable to air and water. Conifers. Present in the county plant guide and named as hazardous by USU. Keep them well away from the structure and use them as specimen trees. Density. The rebate wants 50 percent living cover at maturity; defensible space wants separation. Well-spaced trees over a sparse understory satisfy both, since the District counts a tree at 350 square feet. Fifteen tightly packed shrubs satisfy the rebate and fail the fire logic. The easement, which cannot be undone. Read it before the site visit. What we’d do at your house We check the Division's wildfire risk assessment mapping tool for your address before we design anything, because it is the same boundary your insurer is restricted to using. We clear the first five feet around the structure to noncombustible ground and keep every plant and every wood mulch bed out of it. We look hard at any juniper against a wall, and we will tell you plainly if we think it should come out. We space trees for mature canopy so the same trees satisfy the coverage credit and the separation rule. We decide with you, before the pre-approval site visit, which ground stays outside the conversion area, because the easement on that ground is permanent. We explain the easement in full before you sign anything, including the cure period and the clawback terms. We will tell you what the statute says and point you to the section, and where a number depends on a rule rather than the statute we will tell you that too. guides_does_modification_prevent_falls.text: id="main"> Guides · Accessible living Does changing the house actually help? The best evidence gives two answers, and they point in different directions. One of them helps us sell work. The other does not. Both are printed below. Every company that sells bathroom work says the work prevents falls. The best available evidence says that is true for some households and not true for others, and the gap between the two is wide enough that you should know which household you are before you spend anything. This page reports both halves of that finding. Half of it argues for the work. Half of it argues against selling the work to people who do not need it. We publish both because you can go and check them, and because a contractor who only tells you the useful half has told you something about himself. What the review found The reference is the 2023 Cochrane review of environmental interventions for preventing falls in older people living at home. A Cochrane review pools the trials on a question, weighs them by quality, and then grades how much confidence the pooled answer deserves. Low certainty means the number could move a lot with better trials. High certainty means it probably will not. This review produced two results at once. In adults selected for higher risk, meaning people who had already fallen or who had a mobility limitation, changing the home environment reduced the rate of falls by 38 percent. Cochrane graded that high certainty. In the general older population, not selected for risk, the same kind of work showed no effect. The rate ratio was 1.05, which is a wash. Cochrane graded that high certainty as well. Why the second half is not a technicality A high-certainty null is not the absence of evidence. It is evidence, and it is strong. It says that if you take a broad group of older adults who have not had a problem and modify their homes, you should not expect the falls to go anywhere. Further trials are unlikely to overturn it. Compressing the two findings into the single sentence "home modification prevents falls" throws away the more certain of the two. It is the sentence the whole industry uses. We do not use it, because it is not what the review says, and because a claim you can check is worth more than a claim you cannot. What the split does give you is a clean way to sort yourself. There are two honest reasons to change a bathroom here, and they are different reasons for different people. Track one: something has already happened If someone in the house has fallen, or uses a cane or a walker, or has a limitation that makes the bathroom the hardest room in the house, the 38 percent result is the one that applies to you. That is the strongest evidence available for anything in this trade, and it is worth acting on. The fixture at the center of it is usually the tub. A standard 60 inch alcove tub has exactly the footprint of a 60 by 30 inch roll-in shower, so in most houses here the room already has space for a no-step shower without moving a wall. What goes in it is not decoration. Floor tile specified to a wet dynamic coefficient of friction of 0.50 or higher, which is the barefoot wet category the 2022 revision of ANSI A326.3 created; the 0.42 printed on some tile boxes is a different category. Grab bars rated to 250 pounds of force, anchored into solid blocking or into rated retrofit anchors. A hand-held shower on a slide bar so the water comes to the person. A seat, with a bar within reach of it. Lever handles, rocker switches, a comfort-height toilet. If an occupational therapist has written recommendations, send them to us and we build to them. She has seen the person move. We have not. Track two: nothing has happened, and you would like to keep it that way The Huntsman World Senior Games brought 12,034 registered athletes aged 50 and over to this county in 2024. Nobody in that group needs a safety pitch, and most of them would be insulted by one. The same is true of a large share of the people who call us. The honest case for that household is not medical. It is that a curbless shower is a better room. It is easier to clean, which matters more every year. It is easier to use with a hose and a seat. It does not have a tub wall to swing a leg over when you are carrying a towel. And it is already right if the situation changes, which means the work happens on your schedule instead of during a bad month. That is a design argument and an independence argument, and we will make it plainly. We will not dress it up as a medical device. How to tell which track you are in The trials sorted people by history and by measured limitation, not by age or by how anyone felt about the stairs. You can do a rough version of the same sort at your kitchen table, and it takes about a minute. A yes to any of the following puts you in the first track, where the evidence is strong. All no puts you in the second, where the case for the work is a design case and we will make it as one. Has anyone in the house fallen in the last year, including a fall that did not cause an injury and that nobody mentioned to a doctor? Does anyone use a cane, a walker, a wheelchair or a shower chair, even occasionally? Has a doctor, a physical therapist or an occupational therapist raised the subject of the house? Is anyone avoiding the tub, washing at the sink, or waiting for someone else to be home before bathing? Is anyone holding the towel bar, the sink, the toilet or the shower valve to steady themselves? A towel bar is not rated for that and it is a common way people find out. Age is the variable that actually moves Fall death rates do not rise gently across later life. The National Center for Health Statistics put the 2020 rate per 100,000 at roughly 24 for men and 13 for women aged 65 to 74, 82 and 57 at 75 to 84, and 330 and 270 at 85 and over. Those are deaths from falls rather than injuries, and the shape is the point. The rate more than triples at each step. That curve is why the headline number for everyone over 65 is too coarse to plan from. A 67 year old and an 87 year old are not in the same conversation, and treating them as one group is how the industry ends up selling grab bars to people who do not need them and missing the houses where they matter most. What the numbers say about this county The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate puts St. George city at 108,713 people with 21.8 percent aged 65 or over. Washington County runs 22.4 percent. Those are the figures to use; other numbers circulate locally and do not match the Census file. The CDC's analysis of Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data reports that 41.7 percent of US adults 65 and over have a disability. Mobility is the most common at 26.9 percent, then hearing at 14.9 percent, independent living at 9.8 percent, cognition at 9.5 percent, vision at 6.6 percent and self-care at 5.5 percent. Across all adults the figure is 25.7 percent. Multiply the two local numbers and roughly nine percent of the adult population here is an older adult with a disability. That is not an edge case being accommodated. In a bathroom conversion business it is most of the phone calls. What we are not claiming The Cochrane review measured falls in the home. It did not measure independence, hospital admissions, how long anyone stayed in the house, or whether the bathroom was pleasant to use. None of those were the outcome, so none of them are ours to claim on the strength of it. We are also not offering medical advice, and we do not assess anyone. We build rooms. The people qualified to say what a particular person needs are that person's doctor and occupational therapist, and their recommendations outrank our opinion every time. Everything cited on this page is public. The Cochrane review is indexed and free to read the abstract of, the CDC tables are published, and the Census figures are three clicks from the QuickFacts page. You should not have to take our word for any of it. What we’d do at your house We ask first whether anyone in the house has fallen or uses a cane or a walker, because the honest answer changes what we recommend and what we say about it. If the answer is yes, we walk the whole route, bed to bathroom, in the dark, not just the bathroom in daylight. If the answer is no, we design for how you want the room to work now and build it so it is already right if that changes. We measure the tub alcove early, because in most houses here a 60 by 30 shower fits where the tub is without moving a wall. If you have an occupational therapist, send us her recommendations and we build to them. We will tell you which lines on a quote are doing real work and which ones are decoration, including ours. guides_ev_charger_installation.text: id="main"> Guides · Water-wise landscape Getting a Level 2 charger installed here The federal credit expired on June 30, 2026 and half the internet has not noticed. Which utility serves you depends on which side of the Virgin River you live on. And you probably do not need the panel upgrade you were quoted. A home charger is a 240 volt circuit, a piece of listed equipment on a wall, and a permit. What makes it complicated in St. George is not the wiring. It is that almost every page you will read about it was written for somewhere else. Rocky Mountain Power is not your utility here in most of the county. The federal tax credit that every incentive listicle still promotes has expired. And the panel upgrade that turns a modest job into an expensive one is often avoidable under a code section most quotes never mention. This page covers all three, plus what an association can and cannot do about it. Who does the electrical First, plainly, because it changes how you should read everything below. EV charger installations are performed by our licensed electrical partner, under their own electrical license. We do not do the electrical ourselves and we will not pretend to. Level 2 charging is 240 volt line-voltage work, which in Utah is electrical trade requiring an electrical contractor license, and Section 58-55-501(4) requires the permit to be pulled by the party licensed for the work. What is ours is the rest of the job: the site walk, the coordination, the permit schedule, the association paperwork, the finish work, and one point of contact. You know who the electrician is before he arrives. Which utility serves your address Washington County electricity is split across at least five utilities, and the boundary that catches people out runs through the middle of St. George. St. George is divided by the Virgin River. North of it, service is St. George City Energy Services, the municipal utility. South of it, service is Dixie Power, a member co-operative. Washington City splits in a similar way, and Hurricane is primarily Hurricane City Power, with Rocky Mountain Power in the Harrisburg development. This matters for one reason: every rebate and every rate is set by the utility, so an article about a Rocky Mountain Power EV program is describing a company that probably does not serve you. Check your bill before you believe any incentive claim. Electric service across the area, and why the river matters Community Utility St. George, north of the Virgin River St. George City Energy Services St. George, south of the Virgin River Dixie Power Washington City, north of the river Washington City Power Washington City, elsewhere in city limits Dixie Power Hurricane Hurricane City Power, with Rocky Mountain Power in Harrisburg and Dixie Escalante in other zones Santa Clara Santa Clara municipal power The federal credit is gone The Alternative Fuel Vehicle Refueling Property Credit, Section 30C of the Internal Revenue Code, applied to qualified property placed in service through June 30, 2026. It has expired. For individuals it had been worth 30 percent of cost, capped at 1,000 dollars per item at a main home, and only where the property sat in a low-income or non-urban census tract, so plenty of homeowners never qualified even while it existed. Nearly every competitor page and every stale incentive listicle still advertises it. If a quote nets out a thousand dollar federal credit, the quote is wrong, and you would find that out at tax time rather than at signing. On the local side, Dixie Power is the one utility in this county we found running a residential Level 2 charger rebate for its members. The amount and the conditions are theirs and they change, so get them from Dixie Power rather than from any contractor's website, ours included. St. George City publishes no time-of-use rate and no EV rate. Do you actually need a bigger panel? This is where most of the money is won or lost, and it is the question most quotes answer lazily. The lazy method adds up the nameplate rating of everything in the house, finds that a 100 or 125 amp service cannot carry a 48 amp charger on paper, and quotes a service upgrade. The better method is NEC 220.87, which permits sizing against the actual measured demand of the existing house. It uses the maximum demand recorded over a year, from metering or utility records, taken at 125 percent, with the charger load added on top. Where a year of data is not available, a 30 consecutive day recorded demand study can be used instead. Houses use far less than their nameplate, so a 220.87 calculation frequently finds room where the paper calculation does not. The licensed electrical contractor performs it, and we ask for it first rather than last. There are cases where an upgrade is genuinely required and we will say so. A 100 or 125 amp service already carrying an electric range, an electric dryer and air conditioning. A panel with no available breaker spaces. And an obsolete panel, specifically Federal Pacific or Zinsco, which should be replaced on its own merits whether or not a charger is going in. Energy management, the cheaper answer When the load calculation lands slightly over the line, there is a third option between doing nothing and replacing the service. An energy management system watches the whole house: current transformers clamp onto the main service conductors and sample the draw continuously, and when household demand approaches a set threshold the device modulates the charger's pilot signal to throttle its amperage, restoring full rate when the other loads drop. The car charges slower for twenty minutes while the oven and the dryer are running, and you do not notice, because it is parked until morning either way. NEC 625.42 expressly permits an energy management system that limits charger power to available capacity, Article 750 governs such systems generally, and the demand factors in 220.82 and 220.83 let the load calculation reflect the managed load rather than the full nameplate. This is a code-sanctioned answer, not a shortcut. It is the right call when the calculation lands modestly over the line on an otherwise healthy panel and the car charges overnight. It is the wrong call on a 100 amp service with electric heat, on an obsolete panel, or when you need consistent fast daytime charging. Hardwired, a receptacle, and the heat A charger can be hardwired to the circuit or plugged into a NEMA 14-50 receptacle. We default to hardwired. It goes faster, because a cord-and-plug unit is limited to 80 percent of the branch circuit rating, capping a 14-50 at 40 amps while a hardwired unit runs 48 amps and up. It has no plug and socket to wear out. And in most cases it is cheaper all in, because it does not need a ground fault breaker. That last point is worth explaining, because it is the most common callback in this trade. Two code sections force ground fault protection on a 14-50 used for EV charging: 210.8(A), covering 125 to 250 volt receptacles in garages, and 625.54, covering receptacles installed for EV charging regardless of location. The charger itself already contains a listed internal charge circuit interrupting device, and two protection devices watching one circuit produce overlapping detection and spurious trips. A hardwired unit is not a receptacle, so 625.54 does not reach it. A 14-50 still makes sense for a renter, or for someone who expects to move and take the charger. Two more code points. Charging equipment is a continuous load, so conductors and circuit are sized at 125 percent of maximum load: 32 amps on a 40 amp breaker, 40 on 50, 48 on 60. And under the 2023 NEC as adopted in Utah, a separate disconnecting means is required above 60 amperes or 150 volts to ground, which a normal 240 volt install at 48 amps does not trigger. An 80 amp unit does. One last local point. NEC Table 310.15(B)(1) corrects conductor capacity for ambient temperature, and the bands start at 105 degrees Fahrenheit. An interior garage usually stays under them. An exterior wall run, a south-facing conduit, an attic run or a sunlit run to a detached garage does not, in a county that recorded 98 days at or above 100 degrees in 2024, and the correction can force a larger conductor. A quote built on Salt Lake assumptions will be short here. Your association cannot ban it Utah Code Section 57-8a-802 says an association may not prohibit a lot owner from installing a charging system in a parking space on the owner's lot used for parking or storage of vehicles, or in a limited common area parking space designated for that owner's exclusive use. Condominiums have a parallel provision at Section 57-8-8.2. What the association may do is substantial. It may require an application before installation, require a licensed electrical contractor, require reimbursement for any increase in its insurance premium, enforce reasonable design criteria governing dimensions, placement and external appearance, require code compliance, charge reasonable review and permitting fees, and require the owner to bear installation, metering, electricity and damage costs. Two limits people miss. The protection covers your own lot or an exclusive-use limited common area space; an owner whose only parking is general common area is not covered, and that is a negotiation with the board rather than a right. And there is no Utah statutory right for a renter to install charging. The statute also settles the exit: the system stays the owner's property, and on sale the owner discloses it and removes it unless the buyer takes it on. None of that is legal advice, it is what the sections say. The application step is the most common reason a promised timeline slips, so we build it into the schedule. Permits, and which code applies A new 240 volt branch circuit, or any panel or service change, requires an electrical permit and inspection in every Utah jurisdiction. There is no version of this job that skips that step, and the permit is pulled by the licensed electrical contractor. One correction worth carrying, because a lot of contractor websites get it wrong. Utah's electrical code is the 2023 NEC, adopted effective May 7, 2025, and the residential code remains the 2021 IRC, notwithstanding the 2024 I-code suite the state adopted for other trades effective July 1, 2026. Any page citing 2026 NEC rules for a Utah install is describing a code that is not in force here. What we’d do at your house We look at the panel, the meter and the intended charger location on the first visit, and we photograph the panel label. We ask our licensed electrical partner to run the NEC 220.87 calculation against your actual measured demand before anyone quotes a service upgrade. If the calculation lands close, we price energy management alongside the upgrade so you can see both numbers next to each other. We default to a hardwired charger, and we will explain the tripping problem before you choose a receptacle instead. We route conductors to stay out of sunlit conduit and attic spaces wherever the house allows it. If you are in an association, we prepare the application and build the review window into the schedule rather than promising a date we cannot hold. We tell you who the electrician is before he arrives, and he pulls the permit for his own work. guides_flood_and_erosion.text: id="main"> Guides · Water-wise landscape Above the flood zone and still at risk In 2005 the Santa Clara River destroyed about 30 homes at roughly half the 100 year flow. The mechanism was bank erosion, not rising water. The universal homeowner assumption is that a FEMA flood map answers the question. Outside the shaded area, nothing to think about. There is a documented local event that takes that assumption apart, and it happened here. In January 2005 a weak El Nino drove a southerly Pacific storm track that dropped heavy precipitation onto existing snowpack. The Santa Clara River widened to a hundred yards in places. Roughly 20 homes washed away and another 10 were damaged beyond repair, about 30 structures lost. Two findings from the case study are the reason this page exists. The discharge was less than expected for the 100 year flood. And most destroyed homes were situated above the 100 year floodplain, leaving residents uninsured. The mechanism was stream bank erosion as the channel migrated, not water rising over the banks. Why the county publishes three flood layers instead of one The stated lesson from the 2005 case study is that analyzing risk along streams requires knowledge of both flood and stream bank erosion hazards. Washington County's hazard mapping reflects that. Alongside the FEMA Flood Hazard layer, which is layer 0, the county publishes an Erosion Hazard Boundary as layer 3 and a Flood Hazard Based on Geologic Deposits as layer 4. Three layers, because one was not enough in 2005 and is not enough now. Layer 4 is the interesting one and the least understood. It maps flood hazard from what the ground is made of, which is to say from the deposits left behind by water that has already been there. A wash that has not run in your lifetime still left its record in the dirt. Layer 3 maps where a channel can move sideways, which is the hazard that destroyed those Santa Clara homes. The county also maps dam break inundation as layers 5 through 7, which matters because Quail Creek and Sand Hollow reservoirs sit upstream of a lot of houses. All of it is free to look at. Utah Geological Survey Special Study 127, the study the county layers are built on, states flatly that flooding is the most widespread and damaging geologic hazard in southwestern Utah. Washington County Hazards MapServer, which carries all 24 layers including the three flood layers and the erosion boundary. The Utah Flood Hazards and Flood Risk Atlas at floodhazards.utah.gov. Utah's Division of Emergency Management is a FEMA Cooperating Technical Partner under Risk MAP. The FEMA Map Service Center, for the FIRM panel itself. The Utah Geologic Hazards Portal from the state survey, for the same study area in the survey's own viewer. What being outside the mapped floodplain actually bought those homeowners Nothing, and that is the part worth sitting with. Flood and surface water are handled separately from a standard homeowners policy and are covered through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood policy. A house outside the mapped floodplain is a house whose owner has usually decided not to buy that separate coverage, which is a rational decision made from a map that was answering a narrower question than the owner thought. We are plumbers and landscapers, not insurance agents, and this is not coverage advice. Read your own policy or ask the person who wrote it. The only point we are making is a factual one, and it comes from a university teaching case study on the flood rather than from a state or county report: the destroyed homes were above the 100 year floodplain and the residents were uninsured, and the water never had to rise into the house to take it. Washington County's own Santa Clara River Master Plan puts numbers on it. The 2005 peak was about 6,200 cubic feet per second at St. George, roughly a 25 year event, against a USGS estimate of about 13,000 for the 100 year flood. The plan states plainly that the primary damage was the result of large lateral erosion. Half the 100 year flow took thirty houses, because the river moved sideways instead of rising. Monsoon loading on soil that has been baking since May Precipitation here is bimodal and the second peak is the dangerous one. February is the wettest month at 1.38 inches, delivered by winter frontal systems as steady rain. June is the driest at 0.16 inches, half of May, a third of July and an eighth of February. August is the third wettest at 1.07 inches, behind February and January, delivered in convective bursts. The monsoon season runs officially from June 15 to September 30 and generally arrives in Utah after about the Fourth of July. Now put that on the ground. Utah State University Extension puts the infiltration rate of local clay at about half an inch an hour. Through June the clay has dried, developed a hydrophobic crust and opened shrinkage cracks. The first monsoon cell arrives faster than half an inch an hour, so most of it runs off rather than soaking in, and what does soak in goes down the cracks fast and unevenly, which is the worst possible wetting pattern for expansive soil under a slab or a patio. Add one more feature of this weather. A storm fifteen or twenty miles upstream can flash flood a wash with no visible rain over your house. People watch their own sky and make decisions from it. That combination makes the first monsoon storm after a long dry spell the highest risk moment of the year for a house here. Not the biggest storm. The first one. Erosion and piping, which happen without a river Special Study 127 maps soil piping and erosion as one of its nine adverse construction conditions, coded PES for susceptible soil and PER for susceptible rock, at 1:24,000 scale. The county publishes it as layer 22. Piping is subsurface erosion. Water moving through the soil carves underground channels, and the ground stays intact overhead until it does not. The visible symptom is a sinkhole or a depression appearing in a yard or under hardscape with no obvious cause, which is a disconcerting thing to walk out to. The trigger is the same one that drives most of the soil trouble in this county: concentrated water introduced in one place. Roof drainage discharging at a single point. An irrigation line leaking under a bed. A failed sewer lateral. Collapsible soil, which the survey defines as soil with considerable strength while dry that settles significantly through hydrocompaction when wetted, responds to exactly the same input by settling. Two different mechanisms, one cause, and the cause is usually plumbing or drainage rather than weather. Which is why a monsoon page belongs on a plumbing and landscape site. The storm supplies the volume. The house decides where it goes. Drainage work that actually helps Utah State University Extension's guidance is direct: poor drainage can and should be improved if possible by grading or installing drain tiles to carry water away, and where it cannot be improved, plant high, with a third of the root ball above grade or the plant fully bermed. Extension also lists reduced runoff as a benefit of proper soil preparation, alongside better rooting depth and water holding capacity. The rest is our own approach rather than published guidance, and it starts from the same idea as cycle and soak irrigation. A landscape should be built to absorb water in increments instead of shedding it in one pass. Get roof and hardscape runoff away from the foundation and into planting basins rather than into one concentrated discharge point. Shallow detention, which means basins, swales and planting beds set a couple of inches below the mulch grade, converts first flush runoff into infiltration. Rock mulch over a properly prepared bed absorbs far better than rock over compacted subgrade, which is a difference nobody can see after the job is finished and everybody feels in August. And keep moisture uniform at the foundation perimeter, because expansive clay does its damage through differential wetting rather than through wetness as such. One constraint on all of it if your yard is inside a rebated conversion. The recorded conservation easement prohibits ponds, water features and other bodies of water in the conversion area in perpetuity. Detention has to stay shallow, ephemeral and plainly a planting basin, and the design should be confirmed with the District before it is built rather than argued about afterward. What this means before you buy, build or re-landscape Three things are worth doing, and all three are free. Pull your parcel on all three flood layers, not just the FEMA one, and pay attention to the erosion hazard boundary if there is any channel or wash near you. Look at layer 22 for piping and erosion, and at layer 18 for collapsible soil, because those decide how much damage a concentrated leak can do on your particular lot. Then walk your own drainage during a storm, or right after one. Where does the roof water land. Where does the driveway send it. Is there a low spot against the foundation that holds water for an hour. A year of rainfall here is 9.31 inches on the 1991 to 2020 normal, so you do not get many chances to watch the system work, which makes the ones you get worth standing outside for. And treat a leak as a soil problem. On this ground, water that gets into the wrong place does not simply cost you on the bill. It moves the dirt that everything else is sitting on. What we’d do at your house We pull the FEMA, erosion and geologic deposit flood layers for your parcel, plus piping and collapsible soil, before we design any drainage. We walk the roof drainage and the hardscape runoff with you and show you where the water is being concentrated. Where grading can carry water away, we grade. Where it cannot, we plant high rather than pretending the drainage is fine. We build shallow detention into planting beds so first flush runoff soaks in rather than sheeting off, and we keep it inside what a rebate easement allows. We prepare the soil under rock mulch instead of laying rock on compacted subgrade, because that is the difference nobody sees and everybody feels. If a leak is wetting ground that is mapped collapsible or piping susceptible, we treat it as a foundation problem first and a water bill second. Where the question stops being drainage and becomes structural or channel engineering, we tell you to get an engineer. guides_grab_bars_where_they_go.text: id="main"> Guides · Accessible living Grab bars: where they go, and what holds them The standard is 250 pounds of force. The wall behind the bar matters more than the bar. And the objection is almost never that they do not work. A grab bar is one of the cheapest things in a bathroom and one of the few that has a published performance standard. It is also the item people refuse most often, and almost never for a reason that has anything to do with performance. This page covers the number the standard actually sets, what has to be inside the wall for a bar to reach it, where bars go and why, and how to get all of that without the room looking like a ward. A private home is not an ADA facility The Americans with Disabilities Act governs public accommodations. Stores, clinics, hotels, restaurants. It does not govern your bathroom, and no inspector is coming to measure it. What people mean when they ask for an ADA bathroom is the set of dimensions and clearances published in the ADA standards and in ANSI A117.1, the accessible design standard those numbers come from. Those are a design benchmark, and a good one. They were worked out for wheelchairs, for walkers, and for a person steadying herself with one hand while turning. So we use the numbers and we are clear about what they are. Not a legal requirement on your house. The best available answer to the question of what height and what clearance actually work. 250 pounds, and where the other number came from Grab bars are designed and tested to 250 pounds of force. That is the standard, and it is the figure we specify and the figure on the product literature we will hand you. A larger number circulates widely on remodeling websites and in showroom conversations. It does not appear in any code or standard. It traces to product marketing and to people informally doubling the real figure to sound safe. On a page that homeowners and other contractors build from, publishing it would be the worst mistake available, because someone would design to a rating that does not exist and assume everything below it is inadequate. The load rating is a property of the whole assembly, not the bar in the box. A bar rated to 250 pounds screwed into drywall is rated to nothing. What the bar is fastened to is the entire question. What holds a bar There are two honest answers, and which one applies depends on whether the wall is open. During a remodel, the wall is open, and the answer is blocking: solid lumber let into the studs behind the finish, continuous through every place a bar might ever go. We put blocking behind places you do not want a bar today, because the lumber costs a few dollars now and a wall costs real money later. Ten years from now someone can mount a bar anywhere on that wall in twenty minutes. On a finished wall, the answer is a rated retrofit anchor, installed to its rating, into the material that is actually behind the tile. That means knowing whether it is drywall, cement board, plaster, or a stud, and using the anchor listed for it at the load it is listed for. Done properly this is not a compromise; it is a different engineered solution. There is a third answer people arrive at by accident, which is the towel bar, the soap dish or the shower valve. None of those is rated to be pulled on, and finding that out is how a lot of bathroom projects begin. If something in the room is already being used as a handhold, tell us which one, because it marks exactly where a real bar belongs. What is not an answer: a suction cup bar. It is a convenience item for a hotel room, it is not rated for the job, and it fails at the moment it is being used. We do not install them and we will tell you so. Where they go Exact mounting heights, bar diameters and clearance from the wall come out of ANSI A117.1. We build to those numbers rather than to a rule of thumb, and if an occupational therapist has written recommendations for the person who will use the room, hers outrank the standard. She has watched the person move. A standard has not. One more placement worth planning even if you decline the bar: the hand-held shower on a slide bar. It brings the water to the person rather than making the person stand under it, and the slide bar itself is often what people reach for. The three placements that matter, and what has to be behind each one Location What it is for What has to be in the wall Beside the toilet Lowering down and standing back up, which is the movement people do most often and think about least Blocking, or a rated retrofit anchor into what is actually there At the shower entry The transition from a dry floor to a wet one, with one hand occupied Blocking, or a rated retrofit anchor At the seat Reaching the controls and rising from the seat without pushing off the wall Blocking, or a rated retrofit anchor Bars that do not look like bars In our experience the objection is almost never that a grab bar will not work. It is that it announces something. People say the room will look like a hospital, and they are usually picturing a specific chrome bar in a specific building they visited. The answer is a bar that is also something else. Towel bars, shelf brackets, corner shelves and shower niche rails are all made in versions rated to the same 250 pounds and anchored the same way. Finishes match the rest of the room rather than fighting it. The bar is doing two jobs and only one of them is visible. Built so it does not look built. That is the standard we work to on this whole pillar, and grab bars are where it matters most, because a bar that never gets installed protects nobody. The rest of the room None of that is expensive relative to the rest of a bathroom. Most of it is a specification decision made once, at the point where somebody is choosing hardware anyway. Lever handles instead of knobs, on doors and on faucets. A lever works with a closed fist, a wet hand, or an elbow. Rocker switches instead of toggles, for the same reason. A comfort-height toilet, which shortens the distance of the movement the toilet bar is there to support. A hand-held shower on a slide bar, adjustable in height, so one fixture works for a person standing and a person seated. A fold-down or built-in seat, positioned so the controls are reachable from it. Floor tile specified to a wet dynamic coefficient of friction of 0.50 or higher, the barefoot wet category the 2022 revision of ANSI A326.3 created. The 0.42 figure printed on many tile boxes is a different category of floor. Light, and contrast Eyes change with age in three ways that a bathroom design can answer directly. Near focus is lost, essentially universally, by the mid fifties. Contrast sensitivity drops, so the gap between technically visible and comfortably visible widens. And light scatters more inside the eye, which makes glare a bigger problem than dimness. Two more changes matter for choosing colors. The lens yellows, which degrades blue against green and blue against purple first. And dark adaptation slows, so walking from a lit hallway into a dark bathroom takes longer to resolve than it used to. What we do with that: more light than a builder would put in, layered rather than one fixture, and aimed so nothing shines off a wet floor or a mirror straight back at the person. Contrast where an edge matters, so the floor, the shower floor and the seat do not read as one continuous surface. No color scheme that depends on telling blue from green. A night light on the route from the bedroom, because the walk is where the dark adaptation problem lives. The Illuminating Engineering Society publishes a recommended practice for lighting for older adults, and we work from it rather than from a showroom's opinion. Universal design and accessible design are not the same thing Accessible design solves an identified limitation for an identified person. It is targeted, it is often prescribed, and the ADA and ANSI numbers are its vocabulary. Universal design is a broader discipline, organized around seven principles, and its goal is different: a space that works for as many people as possible without any adaptation at all, and without announcing that it was designed for anyone in particular. A lever handle is universal design. So is a curbless shower, a hand-held on a slide bar, and good light. The distinction is worth knowing because it decides how a room reads. A bathroom built to accessible design solves a problem and looks like it. A bathroom built to universal design solves the same problem and looks like a nice bathroom, which is what most people actually want, and what makes the work easy to do early instead of urgently. What we’d do at your house We put blocking behind every plausible bar location while the wall is open, whether or not you want bars today. On a finished wall we identify what is actually behind the tile before we choose an anchor, and we install to the anchor's rating. Every bar we install is rated to 250 pounds and the product literature goes in your file. If you do not want anything that looks like a grab bar, we will show you the towel bars and shelves that are rated the same and mount the same. We plan the lighting with the tile, not after it, and we will point out where the light will be in your eyes. If you have an occupational therapist, send us her recommendations and we build to them. guides_hard_water_and_water_heaters.text: id="main"> Guides · Plumbing What St. George water does to a water heater The city says set your softener to 18 grains. The tankless makers stop at 200 mg/L. The warranty documents, quoted, and what to do about it. The City of St. George's Water Distribution Division tells residents to set their water softeners to 18 grains per gallon, with a maximum of 22. That is the hardness number to use, because it comes from the utility and not from someone selling a softener. At 17.1 milligrams per liter per grain, 18 grains is about 308 mg/L as calcium carbonate; the U.S. Geological Survey calls anything over 180 mg/L "very hard." Every major tankless water heater manufacturer publishes a hardness limit in its warranty or installation manual. Four of them stop at 200 milligrams per liter, which is about 12 grains per gallon. St. George runs 18 to 22. This page quotes the documents, explains what the exclusions do and do not mean, and covers why your neighbor's heater may outlast yours. What the manufacturers wrote The figures below were taken from the manufacturers' own warranty PDFs and installation manuals. Noritz limited warranty, excluded: "Damage as a result of use with non-potable water, untreated or poorly treated well water, or water with high PH levels or hardness levels in excess of 12 grains per gallon (200 mg/L)." Rinnai installation manual: "Replacement of components due to water quality damage is not covered by the warranty." And: "If you install this water heater in an area that is known to have hard water or that causes scale build-up, the water must be treated and may require a more frequent flushing schedule." Bradford White (tank) warranty, excluded: failure from "sediment or lime precipitate in the glass lined tank," and "maintenance contrary to the written instructions furnished with the unit." Anode removal is listed under misuse, with an express carve-out for "removal of the anode rod (except for inspection and/or replacement)." Published limits, from each manufacturer's own current warranty document or installation manual. One grain per gallon is 17.1 mg/L. A.O. Smith is not in this table: its current gas tankless warranties list water quality exclusions for pH and iron and publish no hardness figure. Manufacturer Published limit In gpg At 18 gpg At 22 gpg Noritz 12 gpg / 200 mg/L, explicit void language 12 1.5x over 1.8x over Rinnai Hardness up to 200 mg/L; TDS up to 500 mg/L; chlorides up to 250 11.7 1.5x over 1.9x over Rheem (RTGH) Total hardness up to 200 mg/L 11.7 1.5x over 1.9x over Navien Maximum allowable total hardness 200 mg/L, which Navien states as 12 grains 12 1.5x over 1.8x over How to read those exclusions honestly Read what kind of clause it is, because they are not all the same. Rheem's is an exclusion on the damage, so a scaled heat exchanger claim is denied while an unrelated control board failure normally is not. Noritz is stronger: its heading says the warranty "becomes null and void." Either way the accurate summary is this: in St. George, an untreated tankless installation is effectively an uninsured heat exchanger. The maker has already written the denial letter. One maker goes the other way, and it is worth knowing before you choose a unit. A.O. Smith's current limited gas tankless warranty publishes no hardness figure at all. Its water quality exclusions name pH outside 6.5 to 8.5 and iron above 0.3 mg/L, and it says that failure of a heat exchanger due to excessive scale accumulation on units equipped with X3 technology is eligible for warranty coverage for 15 years. That is the opposite of an exclusion. We read the document rather than repeating what circulates about it. Two more traps sit in the same documents. Rinnai and Rheem both cap total dissolved solids at 500 mg/L. St. George's 2024 water quality report shows TDS from 118 to 936 ppm depending on which source blend feeds your street, so the high end is 1.9 times the limit, a second and independent ground for exclusion. And Rinnai and Rheem both end warranty coverage at 12,000 operating hours regardless of calendar years. A scaled unit runs longer to deliver the same gallon at the same setpoint, so scale runs the hours clock faster too. Now the part that gets written wrong more than any other. The city's 18 grains is what you tell the softener the incoming water is. It is not the output. Softened water leaving a properly sized and set softener is functionally 0 to 1 grain, which clears every limit in the table. Anyone who says softened water here still measures in the high teens has confused the two numbers. Salt-free "conditioners" using template-assisted crystallization do not remove calcium or magnesium; total hardness at the tap is unchanged. The manufacturers' limits are written as total hardness, so on our reading a conditioner does not bring an 18 grain house under the 200 mg/L limit. That is our reading, not a manufacturer's ruling; confirm with the maker of your unit. What a conditioner does do is add zero chloride to the sewer, which matters here for a reason below. What hardness does to any water heater: the Battelle numbers The Water Quality Research Foundation commissioned Battelle Memorial Institute to measure it. A gas storage heater loses 4 percent efficiency for every 5 grains of hardness; softened water held factory efficiency over a 15-year test life. An electric heater accumulates about 0.4 pounds of scale a year per 5 grains. Showerheads lost 75 percent of their flow in under 18 months, and faucet strainers were nearly plugged after 19 equivalent days. A tankless heater on 26 grain water failed completely after 1.6 years of equivalent use. Applied to the city's own figure, 18 grains works out to roughly a 14 to 15 percent efficiency loss on a gas tank; at 22 grains, about 17 to 18 percent. The study's tankless failure case was 26 grains, above St. George's stated range. We are not telling you a tankless fails here in 1.6 years. We are telling you the failure case was 26, the city's number is 18 to 22, and the manufacturers wrote their exclusions because the failure is real. Why your neighbor's heater lasts longer St. George draws from three kinds of source: springs on Pine Valley Mountain, wells in the Gunlock and Snow Canyon areas, and Virgin River surface water stored in Quail Creek and Sand Hollow and treated at the Quail Creek plant. Within one city the 2024 report shows TDS from 118 to 936 ppm and sulfate from 1.38 to 451 ppm. That is not measurement noise. It is the difference between Navajo Sandstone groundwater and river water that drains gypsum-bearing formations upstream. Your scaling rate depends on which pressure zone serves your street, and it shifts through the year as the city blends sources. No water quality report in the county publishes hardness; it is not a federally required parameter. A city-wide number is not your number, and a treatment recommendation should come from a test at your tap. Sulfate has its own effect inside a tank. A standard magnesium anode rod reacts with sulfate-reducing bacteria to make hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell, and homes on the higher-sulfate blends are more likely to get it. The usual fix is an aluminum-zinc rod. A powered anode, which protects the tank with an external current instead of sacrificing metal, works better as TDS rises. Note the Bradford White line above. Replacing an anode is maintenance and is expressly carved out. Pulling one and leaving it out is listed under misuse. The advantage St. George has for tankless, and the one objection left A tankless unit's output depends on how far it has to raise the incoming temperature, and St. George's incoming water is far warmer than northern Utah's. Using a winter inlet near 60°F, a 199,000 BTU condensing unit delivers roughly 6.3 gallons per minute at 120°F; the same unit in a 45°F-inlet market delivers about 5.0. That leaves hard water as the only serious objection, and hard water is solvable: the softener is part of the water heater installation here, not an accessory to it. What else is in the water Arsenic is the real local story. St. George's running annual average is 8.68 to 9 parts per billion against a federal limit of 10, with individual samples as high as 13. Ivins and Santa Clara both run dedicated arsenic-removal treatment on their well sources. The water is legally compliant, with little headroom. A softener removes no arsenic. A point-of-use reverse osmosis unit at the kitchen sink does. Hexavalent chromium is measured at 0.279 ppb in St. George and 1.22 ppb in Hurricane; there is no federal limit for it. The disinfectant is chlorine, not chloramine, which is the oxidant implicated in polybutylene pipe failure in homes built from roughly 1978 through the mid-1990s, and which ordinary activated carbon removes more easily than chloramine. If you have seen the Environmental Working Group's multipliers for this water, read them with all three columns. EWG's guidelines are its own numbers, far below federal limits. Every system here is in compliance with federal law. St. George City Water System: measured level, federal limit, EWG guideline Contaminant Measured (EWG) Federal MCL EWG guideline Arsenic 9.58 ppb 10 ppb 0.004 ppb Total trihalomethanes 35.4 ppb 80 ppb 0.15 ppb Chromium (hexavalent) 0.279 ppb None 0.02 ppb Maintenance at this hardness Tankless: flush and descale every six months, not annually. Rinnai's manual says hard-water areas "may require a more frequent flushing schedule," and Rinnai units carry a service indicator with selectable intervals of 0.5, 1 or 2 years. In St. George it belongs at 0.5. Most installers leave it at the default. Check yours. Tank: flush at least once a year; popping and rumbling is scale on the bottom trapping steam. Inspect the anode at three years. Softener: the city asks residents to keep the setting low because softener salt raises TDS in the reclaimed water used for irrigation. A time-clock softener regenerates whether you used water or not; a demand-initiated one regenerates on measured volume. Set it to the measured hardness at your tap. What we’d do at your house We test hardness and TDS at your tap before recommending anything, because 118 to 936 is not one number. If we install a tankless unit, the softener is part of the installation, and we will tell you what happens to the heat exchanger warranty if you skip it. Softener sizing at this hardness is arithmetic, and we show you ours. We set the descale interval on the unit to six months and put the date on the tag.
