hoa_sienna_hills.title: Sienna Hills HOA rules · Washington City, Utah
hoa_sienna_hills.meta: Sienna Hills' landscape and wall limits, its 30-day design review window, and the twelve neighborhood associations underneath the master.
heads: The work Sienna Hills has to approve
hoa_sienna_hills.text: id="main"> HOA rules by community · Washington City Sienna Hills Sienna Hills is a master association with twelve neighborhood associations under it, each with its own manager and its own monthly dues. The master piece is small — $15 a month, folded into what your neighborhood already charges. Most of the day-to-day answers come from the neighborhood, not the master. The landscape and wall rules below come from the community's design documents as read in this research. Where a document name, section number or revision date was not captured, we have not invented one, and we say so at the bottom. Where a rule sits against a newer Utah statute, both are stated and the reader should confirm with the association or an attorney. Managed by Community Association Management (CAM), the Southern Utah arm of HOALiving, for ten of the twelve neighborhood associations; ERA Brokers Consolidated and Paul Properties for the others . Confirm the current manager with your association before you rely on it. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Design review The DRC window, and what the statute does and does not add to it. The Sienna Hills Design Review Committee runs a 30-day window on both the preliminary and the final submittal. 1 Utah has no statutory deemed-approval provision and no statutory review deadline, so whether that 30-day window operates as a deadline or as silence-equals-approval depends on the wording of Sienna Hills' own documents. 2 Utah Code § 57-8a-109(4) requires that a written denial specify each governing document provision the association relied on and the specific aspect of the plan that does not conform to it. 2 Utah Code § 57-8a-109(2) provides that an association may not charge a plan fee that exceeds the actual cost of reviewing and approving the lot plans. 2 Landscape rules Lawn proportions, rock, walls, and how they meet the Washington City ordinance and the county rebate. Sienna Hills recommends lawn at no more than 15% of the front yard and no more than 30% of the rear yard. 3 The community's landscape rules ask homeowners to minimize colored rock and pea gravel. 3 White is not allowed on paint or on roofing at Sienna Hills. 3 Perimeter walls are limited to six feet and retaining walls to four feet. 3 Washington City's residential lawn ordinance is nearly identical to St. George's cap of 8% of lot size to a maximum of 1,500 square feet, and it applies to rehabilitated landscaping, not only to new work. 3 Utah Code § 57-8a-231(3)(b) provides that, except where reasonably necessary for erosion control, an association may not require a lot owner to install or keep in place lawn or turf in an area less than eight feet wide. 2 4 more facts , with sources The Washington County Water Conservancy District's Water Efficiency Standards, October 2023, §2 state that where the standards conflict with a municipal ordinance or the requirements of a common interest community, the regulation providing the greatest water conservation benefit applies. 4 The county rebate pays $3 per square foot on the first 1,000 square feet and $2 per square foot after that, for projects completed before June 1, 2027, and requires living grass at the pre-conversion inspection. 4 The district accepts rock, bark, ungrouted stepping stones and permeable artificial turf as mulch, and requires the converted area to be free of bare soil and impermeable barriers. 4 A rebated conversion carries a conservation easement that continues in perpetuity, is recorded with the Washington County Recorder, and restricts only the converted portion of the property. 4 Working on your house Patio covers, landscape lighting, and who you are allowed to hire. Patio covers at Sienna Hills must match the roof surface, and enclosing a patio cover is prohibited. 3 Landscape lighting must be low voltage and approved by the DRC. 3 Utah Code § 57-8a-218(22)(c)(iii) and § 57-8a-212 bar restricting a lot owner from hiring a contractor solely because the contractor is not on the association's preferred vendor list, or lacks a license that is not required by law. 1 Construction work hours in Washington County come from association documents rather than city code; no municipal code reviewed in this research contained them. 3 Structure and management One master, twelve neighborhoods, three management companies. The master association is the Sienna Hills Community Association, 1593 Grapevine Crossing Rd, Washington UT 84780, 435-272-3621. 2 Master dues are $15 per month, included within each neighborhood's own dues. 2 There are twelve neighborhood associations: Copperleaf, Sienna Heights, Garden Homes, The Villas, The Casitas, Arroyo, Ladera, Paseos phases 1 to 3, Paseos phase 4, Desert Ravine, Escondido and Sendera. 2 Community Association Management manages ten of the twelve neighborhoods and can be reached at 435-627-1776; CAM is the Southern Utah arm of HOALiving. 2 Copperleaf and Ladera are managed by ERA Brokers Consolidated at 435-628-3950, and The Casitas by Paul Properties at 435-674-3444. 2 Published neighborhood dues range from $30 a month at Arroyo to $226 a month at Escondido, so which neighborhood you are in changes the bill substantially. 2 What the statute adds Provisions that bear on the rules above. Under Utah Code § 57-8a-217, a board must deliver notice to lot owners at least 15 days before the meeting at which it adopts, amends or cancels a rule or design criterion, provide an open forum, and deliver the approved change within 15 days after. 2 Utah Code § 57-8a-217(4) provides that a rule or design criterion is disapproved if, within 60 days, at least 51% of all allocated voting interests vote to disapprove it at a special meeting called for that purpose. 2 Utah Code § 57-8a-208 requires a written warning before any fine, stating the violation and the provision violated, with not less than 48 hours to cure a continuing violation, and gives the owner 30 days to request an informal hearing. 2 Late fees are capped at the greater of 10% of the assessment or $50, with interest up to 1.5% per month, and a fee schedule must be adopted by rule and distributed to every owner before any such fee is imposed. 2 Under Utah Code § 57-8a-227(4)(a), an association must comply with a written records request within 10 business days, and § 57-8a-227(5)(b) gives the owner $25 per day beginning the eleventh business day if it does not. 2 If the association has an active website, § 57-8a-227(2)(a)(ii) requires the governing documents, the most recent approved minutes and the most recent budget and financial statement to be posted there free of charge. 2 What we could not read These are the parts of Sienna Hills ’s documents we could not get to a verified copy of. We would rather say so than guess. Your association can give you the current versions, and Utah Code § 57-8a-227 says what they have to hand over on request. hoa_stone_cliff.title: Stone Cliff HOA rules · St. George, Utah
hoa_stone_cliff.meta: Stone Cliff's governing documents are not public. Here is what is verified, and how Utah law lets an owner get the rest.
heads: The work Stone Cliff has to approve
hoa_stone_cliff.text: id="main"> HOA rules by community · St. George Stone Cliff This page is thinner than the others in this set, and it is worth saying why. Stone Cliff's CC&Rs, rules, architectural guidelines, dues, gate-access rules and construction hours were not obtainable from public sources. The association's public documents portal is a JavaScript application that machine retrieval cannot read. What is verified is the shape of the community: established in 1996, gated, more than 450 homes and home sites with development still in its final phases, governed by the Stone Cliff Owners Association board and managed by PMP. The useful half of this page is therefore procedural. Utah Code § 57-8a-227 gives an owner a records right with a hard deadline and a daily penalty behind it, and it says the statute governs where the governing documents conflict with it. There are four practical routes to a copy of the declaration, and the state HOA registry is not one of them — the registry holds contacts, not documents. Managed by PMP Management . Confirm the current manager with your association before you rely on it. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Structure and management What is actually confirmed about the association, and where its documents live. Stone Cliff was established in 1996, is gated, and comprises more than 450 homes and home sites, with the community still in its final development phases. 1 Stone Cliff is governed by the Stone Cliff Owners Association board and managed by PMP. 1 PMP Management's St. George office is at 1449 N 1400 W, and its owner portal runs on Vantaca at connect.pmpmanage.com with community sites on pmpwebsites.com. 1 Stone Cliff's public documents portal is a JavaScript application and is reachable only through a browser. 1 Getting your own documents Utah law gives an owner a records right with a ten-business-day deadline and a daily penalty behind it. Under Utah Code § 57-8a-227, an association must comply with a written records request within 10 business days after the day it receives the request. 1 An association owes the owner $25 per day for each day a request for governing documents, minutes, or the budget and financial statement goes unfulfilled, beginning the eleventh business day after the request. 1 Copy charges may not exceed the actual third-party cost or 10 cents per page and $20 per hour of staff time, and an association may not charge the owner anything for electronic transmission of the documents. 1 If an association has an active website, the governing documents, the most recent approved minutes, and the most recent budget and financial statement must be posted there free of charge. 1 Where the governing documents conflict with the statute, the statute governs. 1 Recorded declarations, amendments, plats and notices of reinvestment fee covenant are held by the Washington County Recorder at 111 East Tabernacle, St. George, UT 84770, (435) 301-7680. 1 2 more facts , with sources The state HOA registry does not hold governing documents; it holds contacts only. 1 PMP delivers resale and escrow document packages through HomeWiseDocs. 1 Design review Stone Cliff's own review process is not published. What is fixed is what a denial letter has to contain and what the fee may be. Under Utah Code § 57-8a-109(4), a written denial must name each governing document provision the association relied on and the specific aspect of the plan that does not conform to it. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-109(2) provides that an association may not charge a plan fee exceeding the actual cost of reviewing and approving the lot plans. 1 Utah has no statutory deemed-approval provision and no statutory review deadline, so a review clock exists only where a community's own document creates one. 1 Under Utah Code § 57-8a-217, a board must give lot owners at least 15 days' notice and an open forum before adopting or amending a rule or design criterion, and any challenge to a procedural failure must be commenced within 18 months. 1 Working on your house Fines, access, interior work and contractor choice are all constrained by statute even where the community's own rules are unavailable. Before any fine, Utah Code § 57-8a-208 requires a written warning naming the violation and the provision violated, and for a continuing violation a cure period of not less than 48 hours; an owner may request an informal hearing within 30 days and appeal by civil action within 180 days. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-212(4)(n) bars a declaration from imposing a restriction on the interior of a dwelling except as reasonably necessary for the safety of adjacent lots. 2 Utah Code § 57-8a-212 and § 57-8a-218(22)(c)(iii) each bar an association from restricting a lot owner from hiring a contractor solely because the contractor is not on the association's preferred vendor list. 2 Under the Fair Housing Act an association cannot deny grab bars, ramps, walk-in showers or widened doorways where there is a disability nexus, and it may not require a specific contractor, extra insurance, higher deposits, or medical records; the resident pays. 3 Under Utah Code § 57-8a-224 an association is responsible for maintenance, repair and replacement of common areas and a lot owner for the lot, except as otherwise provided in the declaration or the insurance provisions. 1 An association entering a lot for planned common-area repair must give written notice hand-delivered at least 24 hours ahead; for an emergency repair, notice reasonable under the circumstances. 1 1 more fact , with sources Utah Code § 57-8a-701 provides that no governing document other than a declaration may prohibit solar, so a rule or design guideline alone cannot ban it, and size or location restrictions must not cut efficiency or raise cost by more than 5%. 3 Landscape rules Stone Cliff's landscape standards were not obtainable. The city and statutory floors below apply regardless. St. George caps residential lawn at 8% of lot size to a maximum of 1,500 square feet and prohibits lawn in park strips and in any landscape area under 8 feet wide. 3 An HOA in St. George or Washington City cannot lawfully require more lawn than the city permits. 3 Utah Code § 57-8a-231(3)(b) provides that except where reasonably necessary for erosion control, an association may not require a lot owner to install or keep in place lawn or turf in an area less than eight feet wide. 1 The Washington County Water Conservancy District pays $3 per square foot on the first 1,000 square feet of lawn converted and $2 per square foot after that, for projects completed before June 1, 2027. 4 What the statute adds Two more provisions worth knowing in a gated community, one of which turns on a fact nobody has published. hoa_sunriver.title: SunRiver St. George HOA rules · Utah
hoa_sunriver.meta: What is publicly documented about SunRiver's dues, yard maintenance boundary and manager, and what Utah statute adds on top.
heads: The work SunRiver St. George has to approve
hoa_sunriver.text: id="main"> HOA rules by community · St. George SunRiver St. George SunRiver St. George is a 55+ community on the southwest side of St. George, managed by PMP Management. The unusual thing about it, for anyone hiring work done, is that the association maintains the front yards. That changes who makes the call when something in the yard fails. SunRiver does not publish its governing documents openly, and the association's own site blocks automated retrieval of the governing-documents and landscaping pages. Nothing on this page was taken from those pages. What follows is from the association's public FAQ, from the manager's own listing, and from Utah statute. Where the answer is only in the documents, we say who to ask for them. Managed by PMP Management . Confirm the current manager with your association before you rely on it. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Structure and management Who the association is, who runs it, and what the dues cover. The association is the SunRiver St. George Community Association. 1 SunRiver is managed by PMP Management at 1449 N 1400 W, St. George, reachable at care@pmpmanage.com and (435) 287-3061. 1 SunRiver is age-restricted to 55 and over, with homes built between 1998 and 2019 ranging from 1,008 to 3,184 square feet across more than 20 floor plans. 1 SunRiver's published add-ons are $70 per month for the gated Reflections section, $54 per month for optional rear-yard maintenance, and $10 per month for the walking-mower option. 1 Landscape rules Who maintains which yard, and how that interacts with the water-wise statute and the county rebate. SunRiver's dues cover maintenance of all the front yards in the community, plus common areas, the community center, pool, sports courts and amenity maintenance. 1 Rear-yard maintenance in SunRiver is not included in base dues; it is an optional add-on at $54 per month. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-218(15)(a) requires an association to adopt rules supporting water-wise landscaping only for areas where the lot owners, not the association, do the landscape maintenance. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-231(2) bars an association from enforcing a governing document that prohibits, or has the effect of prohibiting, a lot owner of a detached dwelling from incorporating water-wise landscaping. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-231(3)(b) provides that, except where reasonably necessary for erosion control, an association may not require a lot owner to install or keep in place lawn or turf in an area less than eight feet wide. 1 St. George City caps residential lawn at 8% of lot size with a maximum of 1,500 square feet, and prohibits lawn in park strips, in any area under eight feet wide, and on slopes over 15%. 2 5 more facts , with sources The Washington County Water Conservancy District's Water Efficiency Standards, October 2023, §2 state that where the standards conflict with a municipal ordinance or the requirements of a common interest community, the regulation providing the greatest water conservation benefit applies. 3 The district's rebate pays $3 per square foot on the first 1,000 square feet and $2 per square foot after that, for projects completed before June 1, 2027. 3 The rebate requires living grass at the pre-conversion inspection, and the district states that demolishing a lawn before the approval email arrives voids eligibility. 3 A rebated conversion carries a conservation easement that continues in perpetuity and restricts only the converted portion of the property, not the whole lot. 3 The water district invites homeowners whose association compels them to keep grass to email conservation@wcwcd.org, and says associations may still enforce design standards for water-efficient landscape. 3 Design review SunRiver's own review process is not published; these are the statutory rules that apply to any Utah association's review. Utah Code § 57-8a-109(2) provides that an association may not charge a plan fee that exceeds the actual cost of reviewing and approving the lot plans. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-109(4) requires that a written denial specify each governing document provision the association relied on and the specific aspect of the plan that does not conform to it. 1 Utah has no statutory deemed-approval provision and no statutory review deadline, so any “if they don't answer in X days it's approved” rule has to come from the community's own declaration or design guidelines. 1 Under Utah Code § 57-8a-217, a board must deliver notice to lot owners at least 15 days before the meeting at which it adopts, amends or cancels a rule or design criterion, provide an open forum, and deliver the approved change within 15 days after. 1 Utah Code § 57-8a-217(4) provides that a rule or design criterion is disapproved if, within 60 days, at least 51% of all allocated voting interests vote to disapprove it at a special meeting called for that purpose. 1 Working on your house Contractor choice, and how to get the documents that set the rules. Utah Code § 57-8a-218(22)(c)(iii) and § 57-8a-212 bar restricting a lot owner from hiring a contractor solely because the contractor is not on the association's preferred vendor list, or lacks a license that is not required by law. 4 Utah plumbing work does require a state license, so the license exception in that provision does not reach a licensed plumber; the effect is that an association cannot force an owner to use the association's preferred plumber for work inside the owner's own home. 1 There is no statewide requirement that an association publish its governing documents to the public; the duty runs to members, and the state HOA registry holds contacts, not documents. 1 Under Utah Code § 57-8a-227(4)(a), an association must comply with a written records request within 10 business days of receiving it. 1 If the association misses that deadline, § 57-8a-227(5)(b) provides $25 per day to the owner for each day the request for governing documents, minutes or the budget and financial statement remains unfulfilled, beginning the eleventh business day. 1 Construction work hours in Washington County come from association documents rather than city code; no municipal code reviewed in this research set contained them. 2 What we could not read These are the parts of SunRiver St. George ’s documents we could not get to a verified copy of. A homeowner reading the White Rocks limits and applying them here will be wrong on every one of those points. The most useful line in the Cinder Bluffs document is §3.7: a plan not acted on within 30 days is deemed approved. Utah has no statutory deemed-approval provision and no statutory review deadline, so that clock exists only because the declaration created it. It is worth knowing the date a complete submittal went in, and worth having proof of when. hoa_ledges_white_rocks.text: id="main"> HOA rules by community · St. George The Ledges: White Rocks The Ledges is not one set of rules. White Rocks and Cinder Bluffs are separate documents with different limits, and a homeowner who reads the wrong one gets the wrong answer. In White Rocks, irrigated area is capped at 5,000 square feet, trees are capped at 20 feet for view protection, exterior paint must be 38% reflectance or less with a 4-foot test patch, roofs are tile only, chain link, wood, plastic and composite fences are all prohibited, and retaining walls stop at 4 feet. In Cinder Bluffs the tree limit is 25 feet, there is no irrigated-area cap at all, and construction starts an hour later. Two of those numbers are close enough to be mistaken for each other, which is exactly why they get separate pages. The enforcement side of White Rocks is where a contractor's paperwork matters. Fines run $500 per day after 15 days' notice. Contractors carry $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate commercial general liability. Work runs 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday with nothing on Sunday, and dumpsters sit 15 feet behind the curb. Every one of those is the community's own rule, not a city ordinance — the research found construction work hours in no municipal code it reviewed. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit Design review The exterior standards are written as measurable limits, which means a submittal either meets them or it does not. heads: What to ask anyone quoting this, us included
What we can show you in writing
Hydro jetting or a cable? What each one actually does
The rest of drains and sewers
services_clogged_drain.text: id="main"> Plumbing · Drains and sewers Clogged drain, one fixture One fixture is slow or stopped. We clear that line through an existing cleanout and tell you whether the problem is the fixture or the main. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms The same front yard after the sewer was replaced. Southern California. What the work is A single slow fixture is usually a local blockage: hair and soap in a lavatory arm, grease in a kitchen line, a toy in a toilet. We cable that branch through the nearest access, run water long enough to be sure it is actually clear, and put everything back. The part that matters is the diagnosis, not the cable. If one fixture is slow, it is a branch problem. If the lowest fixture in the house gurgles when you run another one, or a shower backs up when the washing machine drains, that is the main line and a different job. We will tell you which one you have before we quote it, and we would rather send you to the cheaper answer. We do not add a chemical drain opener to anything. Caustic openers sit in the trap when they fail to clear it, and the next person to open that joint gets it on their hands. What is included Cabling one line through an existing cleanout or the fixture opening Running the line long enough afterwards to prove it drains Resetting the toilet or trap we pulled, with a new wax ring or washers Telling you plainly whether this is a branch problem or a main line problem What is not Cutting a new cleanout, if there is no access. That is quoted separately and you approve it first The main sewer line. If the whole house is backing up, that is a different job Chemical drain openers. We do not use them and we would rather you did not either Repairing a drain line that turns out to be broken rather than blocked What is different here Two things show up in older St. George houses more than anywhere else. Cast iron drains that have started to scale internally will re-clog on a schedule no matter how well you cable them; the cable opens a channel through the buildup rather than restoring the pipe. And on hard water a kitchen line collects a harder deposit than grease alone. If you have had the same line cleared more than twice in a year, ask for a camera rather than a third cabling. What the work is Roots do not grow through sound pipe. They come in at a joint that has opened, a crack, or a failed connection, because that is where the water is. Cutting them out restores flow and does nothing about the opening. So we do both halves. We cut or jet the mass out, and then we look at where they entered and tell you what that is: a joint that will keep letting them in, or damage that has to be repaired. You can manage a rooted line for years by cutting on a schedule, and that is a legitimate choice if the alternative is a replacement you cannot fund yet. When the lawn goes and the watering drops, established roots go looking, and a leaking sewer joint is the wettest thing in the yard. What the work is A tankless heater draws far more gas at peak than a tank does, so the existing line is often too small. Undersized gas is the single most common fault we find on a tankless that someone else installed, and it shows up as a unit that cannot hold temperature when two fixtures run. The rest of a correct install is venting to the manufacturer's spec, condensate routed to a legal termination on a condensing unit, and a pair of isolation valves so the heat exchanger can be flushed without cutting pipe. services_tankless_descaling.text: id="main"> Plumbing · Water heaters Tankless descaling Descaling the heat exchanger. On this water it is not optional, and a unit installed without isolation valves costs more every time. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms An exterior tankless with isolation valves, so it can be descaled without cutting anything. Southern California. What the work is Descaling circulates a solution through the heat exchanger to dissolve the mineral that has plated onto it. On a unit with isolation valves it is a straightforward service. On one without, it means cutting into the pipework, which is why those valves are worth insisting on at install. Scale does two things: it costs efficiency, and it runs the clock. Read our Plain Terms Strapped at the upper and lower third, expansion tank on the cold line. Southern California. What the work is When a check valve or a pressure reducing valve sits on the water service, the plumbing becomes a closed system. Heated water expands and has nowhere to go, so pressure spikes every time the heater fires. An expansion tank gives it somewhere to go. The part that gets done wrong is the charge. The tank's air side has to be set to the actual static pressure on your service before the water is turned on. Set it to the factory number and the tank is a decoration. So we measure your pressure, set the tank to it, and tell you the number in writing. What is included The tank, correctly sized for the heater Tee, support and mounting so the tank is not hanging on the pipe Air charge set to your measured static pressure The static pressure reported to you in writing What is not A pressure reducing valve, if your incoming pressure turns out to be too high. That is a separate item and we will show you the reading Replacing a failed relief valve If your relief valve drips and then stops That is the classic sign of thermal expansion with nowhere to go: the valve relieves the spike, then reseats. People replace the valve, and it starts again. The guide below explains the sequence and what actually fixes it. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included What is my measured static pressure? What did you set the tank's air charge to? Is the tank supported, or hanging on the pipe? What we can show you in writing Every line traces to a document we read in full. The number after a sentence points to the research below. Water expands about 2 percent by volume going from 60 to 140 degrees, and it does not compress. A check valve, a backflow preventer or a pressure-reducing valve at the service entrance closes the system, and pressure climbs to the T&P setpoint of 150 psi inside a single heating cycle. 1 St. George requires backflow assemblies on outside watering systems and pressure-reducing valves are common here, so a lot of local houses are closed systems. If the T&P valve drips for a while and then stops, that is thermal expansion, not a failed valve. 1 The precharge is set to the measured static pressure of the house before the tank goes into service. A factory 40-psi precharge left on an 80-psi system means the bladder is bottomed out and the tank does nothing from the first day. 1 Press the Schrader valve on the tank. What the work is A recirculation pump moves hot water around a loop, or back down the cold line on a comfort system, so the water at the far fixture is already hot when you open the faucet. On a long single-story house, which is most of the housing stock here, the wait at the far bath can be substantial. There are two ways to do it and they suit different houses. A dedicated return loop is better and needs a return line, which usually means it has to be planned in. A crossover valve at the far fixture uses the existing cold line and can be retrofitted, at the cost of warm water at the cold tap for a moment. Either one should be on a timer or a demand control. A pump running around the clock costs energy and moves hard water through the heater continuously. What is included The pump and the control, installed and set A timer or demand control rather than continuous running Crossover valve at the far fixture on a comfort system Setting the schedule with you and writing it down What is not Running a dedicated return line, which is a separate and larger job Electrical beyond a nearby existing receptacle Insulating the hot water lines, quoted separately and usually worth it What we will tell you first On very hard water, a recirculation system moves more water through the heater and through the loop than a house without one. That is a real trade: convenience against scale. If you are putting one on a tankless unit, treat the water and check that the unit is rated for recirculation, because not all of them are. Read our Plain Terms A new main water service. Southern California. What the work is High static pressure is quietly expensive. It shortens the life of every flexible connector, every fill valve and every cartridge in the house, and it is the reason behind a lot of failures that get blamed on the fixture. The first thing is the measurement. We gauge the static pressure at a hose bibb and tell you the number. If it is high, a pressure reducing valve on the service brings it into range. Fitting one turns the house into a closed system, so a thermal expansion tank has to go on at the same time. Anyone who fits a reducing valve and does not deal with expansion has created a new problem. Read our Plain Terms What the work is Most bathroom fans that people think are broken are working; they are just ducted into an attic, into a soffit, or through fifteen feet of crushed flexible duct with four bends. The fan is not the problem. The duct is. We replace the unit, run rigid or smooth duct on the shortest sensible route, and terminate at a proper exterior cap. Then we check it actually moves air, at the grille, rather than assuming. The electrical connection beyond a like-for-like swap is our licensed electrical partner's work, and we will tell you which one yours is before you book. What is included The fan, fitted and connected where the supply is like-for-like Rigid or smooth duct on the shortest sensible run An exterior termination cap, not a soffit or an attic Confirming airflow at the grille before we leave What is not New circuits, switches, timers or humidistats wired to a new supply, which is our licensed electrical partner's work Roof penetration and flashing where a roofer should do it. We will tell you if that is the case Repairing damage from years of venting into an attic Venting into the attic is not venting It is common, and it is the reason for stained ceilings and damp insulation. A fan has to terminate outside the building envelope. We will show you where yours currently goes before we quote the fix. The rating on the box is not the airflow in your bathroom A fan's rated airflow is measured on a bench against a defined resistance, and the code rate is measured the same way, at a quarter inch of water column. Put that same fan on fifteen feet of crushed flex with four bends and what it actually moves is lower, sometimes a lot lower. So we measure at the grille rather than reading the box. It is also why the duct, and not the fan, is usually the part that gets replaced. What the code actually requires Utah has adopted the 2021 IRC. It requires bathroom exhaust to go directly outdoors and specifically prohibits discharging it into an attic, a crawl space or any other space inside the building. The minimum rate is 50 cfm for a fan that runs intermittently, or 20 cfm for one that runs continuously. If yours terminates in the attic, that is not a preference of ours. It does not meet the code now in force. We have not checked St. George or Washington County amendments on top of the state code, and we will tell you that rather than imply we have. Read our Plain Terms What the work is The lip at a doorway, a shower entry or a level change between rooms is a small thing that stops a walker completely. A ramped threshold takes it out. The two questions are slope and edges. Too steep and it does not help; unsecured edges and it becomes the thing you trip on. It has to be fixed down, and the transition has to work in both directions. What is included Measuring the rise and setting the slope to suit it The threshold, cut to the opening and fixed down Finishing both edges so nothing catches Checking it with the actual walker or chair before we leave What is not Exterior ramps and anything structural, which is a different job Altering a door or its frame Flooring repair either side Bring the equipment to the fitting A threshold that works on paper and catches a particular walker's front wheels is a common outcome. We check with the thing that actually has to cross it before we call the job done. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included What slope, and does it suit my equipment? Is it fixed down, and how? Have you tested it with my walker? What we can show you in writing Every line traces to a document we read in full. The number after a sentence points to the research below. The published ramp slope is 1:12 — an inch of rise wants a foot of run. A half-inch threshold wants six inches of ramp; a two-inch threshold wants two feet. That is longer than most people picture, and it is why a ramp sometimes will not fit where a door swings. 1 In existing buildings the standard allows steeper runs for short rises — up to 1:10 for a rise of 6 inches, up to 1:8 for 3 inches — and then stops: steeper than 1:8 is prohibited outright. A wedge cut to clear a two-inch threshold in four inches of run is steeper than anything published. 1 Below a quarter inch, a change in level needs nothing at all. Between a quarter and a half inch it wants a bevel no steeper than 1:2. Only above half an inch does it want a ramp. It is the single most useful change you can make to a bathroom if staying in the house is the goal. It works or fails on the floor build-up. Water has to run to the drain from every point, the waterproofing has to be continuous and turn up the walls, and the shower floor has to sit low enough relative to the room that the fall works without a lip. In a slab-on-grade house that usually means either recessing the drain area or building the rest of the floor up. It is not a job to take on with a linear drain and hope. What the work is Most winter calls here are an igniter, a flame sensor, a pressure switch reading a blocked flue or condensate line, or a limit switch tripping because airflow is restricted. The last one is worth saying plainly: a furnace that keeps shutting off is often not a broken furnace, it is a choked filter or a collapsed duct, and replacing the part does not fix it. Anything touching combustion gets checked before we leave, whatever we came for. The parts that fail are a short list and most of them are inexpensive: a hot surface igniter, a flame sensor that has gone dirty enough to stop proving flame, a pressure switch that is doing its job because a flue or a condensate line is blocked, or a limit switch tripping on restricted airflow. The last two are the ones worth understanding, because the part is not the fault. A pressure switch that will not close is usually telling you something is obstructed. A limit switch that keeps tripping is telling you the furnace cannot move enough air through itself, and the cause is nearly always a filter, a closed-off return, or ductwork that has come apart. Replacing the switch in either case buys you a few weeks. So the first thing we do on a no-heat call is not order a part. It is find out what the part was reacting to. A system that is low has a leak, and topping it up is a repair with a known expiry date. It is also the most common way a homeowner here pays for the same fault three years running. We look for the leak with an electronic detector, and with nitrogen and soap where the detector cannot reach. Then you get told where it is and what it costs to fix, including the case where the leak is in the evaporator coil or the line set and the honest answer is that the repair is not worth it. There is a second reason to find it rather than top it up, beyond the money. A system running low on charge runs the compressor hot and floods it with oil-poor refrigerant, and compressors are the one component whose failure usually ends the system. Repeated top-ups are not a cheaper path; they are a slower and more expensive one. Where leaks are found, in rough order: the evaporator coil, the line set connections at either end, the service valves and their caps, and the condenser coil itself. Which one it is decides everything. A fitting is an afternoon. An evaporator coil on a system out of warranty is a conversation about replacement, and we will have that conversation honestly rather than quoting the coil and letting you find out. Bigger is not better, and it is the mistake that gets made most. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the work is A load calculation works out how much heat your house actually gains and loses: its orientation, its glass, its insulation, its air leakage, its ceiling heights, room by room. It is the difference between sizing a system for your house and sizing it for its square footage. Oversizing feels like the safe choice and is not. A system too large for the load cools the air quickly, satisfies the thermostat, and shuts off before it has removed any humidity. You get a house that is cold and clammy, equipment that short cycles, and a compressor that wears out early. You can have the calculation whether or not you buy the system from us, and you can take it to anyone else. What goes into it: the orientation of the house, the area and type of every window, the insulation in the walls and the ceiling, the infiltration rate, the ceiling heights, the shading, and the number of people. The output is a heat gain and a heat loss figure for every room and for the house as a whole. The room-by-room part is what makes it worth having. A whole-house figure sizes the equipment; the room figures tell you which rooms the ducts are failing to serve, and that is usually the actual complaint that started the conversation. What is included A measured survey of the house, not a rule of thumb The room-by-room result in writing, and yours to keep What it means for the equipment size, in a sentence Window areas and orientation measured, not estimated from a floor plan What is not Sizing from the label on the old unit, which is how the old one got its size Sizing from square footage alone Why the number matters more here St. George recorded 98 days at or above 100°F in 2024, the most on record, and the all-time high is 117°F. A system sized for a mild place is not sized for this one. Design load is worked out against the temperature the house actually sees, and here that is a long way from the national default. It is also why a rule of thumb carried in from somewhere else lands wrong in both directions. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included Was a Manual J done, and can I have a copy? What size did it come out at, and what size are you quoting? If those differ, why? Is this room-by-room, or whole-house only? What did you assume about my insulation, and did you check? services_duct_sealing.text: id="main"> Heating and air · Ducts, controls and air Duct sealing and repair The cooling you already paid for, delivered to the room instead of the attic. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the work is Ducts in an unconditioned attic leak into the hottest space in the house. Every cubic foot that escapes is cooling you generated, paid for, and then threw away, and it also pulls hot attic air back in through the return side. We find the leaks, seal the joints and boots with mastic rather than cloth tape, and repair or replace runs that are crushed, disconnected or too small to carry what the system is trying to push through them. This is often the fix for the room that will not cool, and it costs a fraction of the bigger system that gets recommended instead. How we find them: pressurise the duct system and look for where it will not hold, then confirm by hand at the joints and boots. The usual offenders are boots at the register, where the duct meets the ceiling, and the plenum connections at the equipment. The other half of the job is balance. Sealing a leaky system changes the pressure everywhere in it, so registers that were roughly right can end up over- or under-served. We measure the rooms afterwards and adjust, because a sealed system that now overcools the front bedroom has moved the problem rather than fixed it. What is included The leaks found and shown to you before they are sealed Mastic on joints, boots and plenums Crushed or disconnected runs repaired or replaced The registers checked for what they actually deliver afterwards Room registers measured after sealing, and dampers adjusted What is not Cloth duct tape, which fails in an attic and is why some of these joints are open in the first place Full duct replacement, which is a separate quote after we have looked What to ask anyone quoting this, us included Where were the leaks, and can you show me? What are you sealing them with? Will you measure the room afterwards? Will you measure the rooms after you seal? How did you find the leaks? Read our Plain Terms What the work is Most thermostat problems are wiring, not the thermostat: a missing common wire, a control that expects a stage the equipment does not have, or a heat pump wired as though it were a furnace. A smart thermostat on the wrong wiring is a smart thermostat that does not work. We set the equipment type, the stages and the changeover, then leave it working and show you how to use it. If your equipment has two stages, you should know that, because a single-stage control on two-stage equipment means you paid for half a machine you never run. Heat pumps are where this goes wrong most. A heat pump needs a control that understands reversing valve orientation and when to bring on auxiliary heat, and a standard thermostat wired to one will either run the backup heat constantly or not at all. Both are expensive in different ways. We set it up and then we show you it working, including the schedule if you want one. A control nobody understands gets overridden to hold at one temperature, which throws away the only thing it was bought for. services_air_filtration.text: id="main"> Heating and air · Ducts, controls and air Air filtration and air handling Filtration sized so it cleans the air without starving the blower. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms The filter that came out, beside the one that went in. St. George, Utah. What the work is A denser filter in a housing built for a thinner one restricts airflow, and restricted airflow is the cause of a long list of expensive symptoms: a furnace tripping its limit, a coil freezing, a compressor working against itself. The filter that promises the most is not automatically the right one. The fix is filter area, not filter density. A deeper media cabinet gives you better filtration and less restriction at the same time, and it is the change worth making if anyone in the house has a reason to care about what is in the air. The number to know is total external static pressure, measured across the system. Most residential equipment is rated to about half an inch of water column and a great deal of it in the field is running well above that, mostly because of filters and undersized returns. Above the rating the blower moves less air, the coil runs colder, and the equipment works harder for less. So we measure before and after. If a filter you want cannot be carried by the system as it stands, the answer is usually more filter area rather than a thinner filter — a deeper cabinet, or a second return — and we will quote that rather than tell you to buy something worse. What is included The static pressure measured before and after, so the effect is a number rather than an opinion A filter housing sized to the system's airflow What to buy next time, written down, so nobody has to guess in an aisle Total external static pressure measured across the system, before and after What is not A filter rating the equipment cannot carry Claims about health outcomes. We move air; we are not going to tell you what it will do for anyone's asthma What to ask anyone quoting this, us included What is the static pressure now, and what should it be? Will this filter restrict my airflow? What size and rating do I buy next time? What is my static pressure, and what is the equipment rated for? Is the fix a different filter or more return? What we can show you in writing Every line traces to a document we read in full. The number after a sentence points to the research below. MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It reports a filter's ability to capture particles between 0.3 and 10 microns, on a test method developed by ASHRAE. 1 EPA recommends a filter of at least MERV 13, or as high a rating as the system fan and filter slot will take, and says most furnaces and HVAC systems can accommodate a MERV 13 filter without equipment problems provided it is replaced frequently. 1 A high MERV number does not automatically mean a high pressure drop. Filters with deeper pleats, or more of them, tend to have lower pressure drop — four-inch-deep pleats carry twice the surface area of two-inch pleats. Read our Plain Terms What the work is An evaporative cooler cools by evaporating water, which means everything dissolved in that water stays behind on the pads and in the tray. On hard water they scale, stiffen and stop absorbing, and the cooler quietly stops cooling long before it stops running. Service is the pads, the pump, the float valve and the bleed-off. The bleed-off is the part people disable to save water, and it is the part that decides whether the pads last a season or a month. It is worth being straight about what these do and do not do. An evaporative cooler adds moisture to the air as it cools it, so it works well when the air is dry and much less well during the monsoon, when the humidity climbs. That is not a fault in the machine; it is the physics, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling. They also need a window or a vent open to work, because they push air through the house rather than recirculating it. A cooler in a closed house does very little, which is the single most common complaint we hear about one. What is included Pads replaced, tray drained and cleaned Pump, float valve and distribution checked Bleed-off set and explained, rather than removed Winter shutdown and drain-down if that is what you are calling about What is not Converting to refrigerated air, which is a system replacement and quoted as one Roof structural work The water is the reason these fail early The City of St. George's Water Distribution Division instructs residents to set a water softener to 18 grains per gallon, with a maximum of 22. That is about 308 to 376 milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate, which the USGS classes as very hard. An evaporative cooler concentrates that. The water leaves and the minerals do not, so the pads and the tray take everything the incoming water carried. It is the reason the bleed-off matters here more than it does in most places, and the reason a cooler that was fine last summer can be useless by August. Almost everything that goes wrong goes wrong in the first one, and almost nobody quotes it in detail. Concrete finishes with a weak, fines-rich film on top of it called laitance. It is part of how a slab is poured, not a defect. A coating rolled onto that film is bonded to the film, and when the film lets go the floor looks like it failed. It is the common finish, it is what is in most of the photographs on this site, and the reason it works is that it hides everything a plain color shows. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms The control joints are still readable through the finish. They are part of the slab, not a defect in the floor. What the work is The base coat goes down pigmented. While it is still wet, vinyl chips are thrown into it by hand — into it, not onto it, which is why there is no second attempt at the timing. Once cured, the loose chips are scraped back and the surface is sealed under a clear coat. It is called a full broadcast when chips are thrown until the base will not take any more. services_basement_floor_coating.text: id="main"> Concrete coatings · Inside the house Basement floor coating A finished floor rather than a subfloor waiting for one. Below grade the moisture test is not a formality, and we will not quote a finish before we have the reading. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms The coating carried up the wall as a base, so there is no open joint at the floor line for water to sit in. What the work is A basement slab is in permanent contact with the ground. Water vapor moves from the ground through the slab toward the room, and a coating is a comparatively impermeable film laid on top of that. Where the vapor drive is high enough, the pressure builds under the film and the film blisters or lets go. That is not a reason to avoid coating a basement. It is the reason to test one. There are published methods, they have numbers, and the results decide whether a moisture-tolerant primer is part of your job or not. Whether a vapor retarder was installed under the slab was settled on the day the house was poured and cannot be changed now. An older house here may have none. That does not rule out a coated floor; it rules out guessing. Done properly, a coated basement is a good floor. It is hard-wearing, it cleans, it does not hold damp the way carpet does, and carrying the coating a few inches up the wall as a continuous base means there is no open joint at the floor line for water to sit in. What is included A moisture test to a published method, with the reading written down for you Grinding the slab, edges cut in by hand, with dust extraction Crack repair as its own quoted step A moisture-tolerant primer where the reading calls for one, named on the quote A coved wall base where you want one, quoted as its own line What is not Quoting a finish before the slab has been tested. We will not Fixing the source of water coming in. That is drainage or waterproofing work, and a floor coating is not a substitute for it Coating over efflorescence or a damp patch without establishing where it is coming from How the slab actually gets tested There are three published methods and they do not measure the same thing. ASTM F2170 places probes in holes drilled to 40 per cent of the slab depth and reads the internal relative humidity of the concrete — it tells you what the slab will do over time. It has been displacing the older method since 2002. ASTM F1869, the calcium chloride test, seals a dish of salt under a dome and calculates a moisture vapor emission rate from its weight gain after three days; it reflects the surface, not the interior, and since 2010 the standard has disallowed it on lightweight concrete entirely. ASTM D4263, the plastic sheet method, is the quick one: it is used, in the standard's own words, "to indicate the presence of capillary moisture in concrete", and it reveals surface conditions only. The guide that governs slabs receiving moisture-sensitive flooring is ACI 302.2R. The relationship it turns on is simple: the vapor retarder under the slab has to be less permeable than the covering going over it, or a moisture-related failure is on the table. You do not need to know any of that. You need to know that it is published, that it has numbers, and that you can ask which test was run and what it read — of us and of anyone else. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included Which moisture test are you running, and can I have the reading in writing? Does this house have a vapor retarder under the slab, and how would you know? services_concrete_slab_assessment.text: id="main"> Concrete coatings · The slab underneath Concrete slab assessment The slab tested to the published methods, the surface profile agreed in writing, and the readings handed to you whether or not you hire us. This is the part nobody quotes, and it is the part that decides whether a floor lasts. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms A slab part-way through grinding. The swirls are the passes; the extractor beside it is what keeps the dust out of the air. What the work is An assessment is a visit that produces a document rather than a sales call. We look at the slab, test it, and write down what we found: the moisture readings and the method used to get them, the condition of the cracks and joints, what is already on the floor and whether it will come off, and what surface profile the finish you want will need. You keep that. If you take it to another contractor, it works there too, and that is fine — it is a description of your slab, not a proposal. What it does is stop you comparing quotes that are not comparing the same job. It is worth doing on its own in three situations: a coating has already failed once and nobody has said why; the slab is below grade or in an older house with no known vapor retarder; or you are getting quotes that differ by more than they should and you want to know which one is pricing the real work. We will tell you if the answer is that your slab should not be coated. Some should not. What is included Moisture testing to a published method, with the method named and the readings recorded An inspection of the cracks, joints and any existing coating The surface profile the intended finish requires, written down as a number on the published scale A written summary you keep, whoever does the work Credited against the job if you go ahead with us What is not Structural assessment. If the slab is moving, that is an engineer's question and we will tell you to ask one Soil testing. Sulfate and bearing questions belong to a geotechnical lab A recommendation we cannot support from what we measured The methods, named ASTM F2170 reads the internal relative humidity of the slab from probes set at 40 per cent of its depth. ASTM F1869 gives a moisture vapor emission rate from the weight gain of calcium chloride under a sealed dome over three days, reflects the surface rather than the interior, and has been disallowed on lightweight concrete since 2010. ASTM D4263 is the plastic sheet method, used in the standard's own words "to indicate the presence of capillary moisture in concrete", and it shows surface conditions only. For the profile, the International Concrete Repair Institute's Guideline 310.2R-2013 defines a scale of concrete surface profiles from CSP 1, essentially unchanged concrete with loose debris removed, up through CSP 9 and beyond at exposed aggregate. Physical replica chips exist so a prepared slab can be accepted or rejected against the number, and most coating manufacturers now specify against that scale on their own data sheets. The guideline's own advice is to specify a range rather than a single number, because more than one profile will usually work. What the ground under a Washington County slab does The Utah Geological Survey's Special Study 127 maps nine adverse construction conditions across the St. George and Hurricane area, and several of them bear on a slab: gypsiferous soil and rock, collapsible soil, caliche, expansive soil, and shallow ground water. Washington County publishes them as GIS hazard layers you can look at yourself. The one that matters most to concrete is sulfate. Under the American Concrete Institute exposure classes, a soil sulfate test determines the required mix: class S1 at 0.10 to 0.20 per cent water-soluble sulfate in soil, S2 at 0.20 to 2.00 per cent where sulfate-resistant cement is required, S3 above that. St. George culinary water itself reaches 451 parts per million sulfate, inside class S1 for water contact. We do not test soil and we will not tell you your slab is failing from sulfate attack. What we will do is tell you your address sits in a mapped zone, show you where to look, and be honest that the condition of the concrete is a question that comes before the question of what to put on it. It is most of the labor on any coating job and all of the difference between one that holds and one that lets go. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms The corner behind the door track. It is the hardest place to finish and the first place to look. What the work is Concrete finishes with a weak, fines-rich layer on top called laitance. It is a normal product of how a slab is poured and floated, not a defect. It is also not something a coating can bond through. A finish applied over laitance is bonded to the laitance, and the day the laitance releases, the floor looks like the coating failed. Mechanical preparation is the answer, and the requirement is published. In Sika's words, concrete substrates "must be mechanically prepared to remove cement laitance, existing coatings, curing compounds, and achieve a profile that is clean, dry, and free from dirt, grease, oil". Surface grinders with diamond pads, in the same guide's words, "are used to create a surface profile, remove high spots on a concrete surface and remove coatings". Shot blasting is described there as "the industry standard for surface preparation of concrete". What that leaves behind is a texture with a number. The International Concrete Repair Institute publishes the scale, physical chips exist to check against, and the coating manufacturer states on its own data sheet which profile its product needs. So the honest question to any contractor is not whether they grind but what profile they ground to and how they verified it. Extraction runs at the machine. Concrete dust is respirable silica and it does not belong in a house or in anyone's lungs. What the work is A failed coating is evidence. How it is failing narrows the cause considerably: a film lifting cleanly in sheets with a powdery gray underside points at laitance and inadequate preparation. Blisters, and a bond that is sound everywhere except where the blisters are, point at moisture moving up through the slab. Lifting in the tire tracks and nowhere else is a different story again. So the first part of this job is not removal. It is looking at what is there and saying what we think happened. If the cause is moisture, then grinding it off and applying the same system again produces the same result, and you should not pay for that twice. Removal itself is grinding, and it is slower and dustier than grinding bare concrete. A thick or well-bonded coating can cost more to take off than the new finish costs to put on, and where that is the case we will tell you before you commit. Sometimes the honest answer is that we would not recoat this slab. We would rather say that than take the job. services_concrete_cleaning_sealing.text: id="main"> Concrete coatings · The slab underneath Concrete cleaning and sealing Washing and sealing bare or stained concrete. It is the smallest thing on this page and the one most likely to be the right answer, and it is recurring work rather than a one-time job. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms A stained and sealed entry courtyard, rather than a coated one. It is a different finish and a different job. What the work is Not every slab needs coating. A sound driveway, patio or entry that is simply dirty often needs washing and sealing and nothing else, and that costs a fraction of a coated finish. A rotary surface cleaner is what does the work on flatwork. It cleans evenly where a pressure wand leaves stripes, and the stripes are permanent in the sense that they are visible until the whole slab weathers back together. Sealing after washing does two things: it slows the absorption of oil and staining into the concrete, and it darkens and evens the color. Be clear that it darkens. A sealed slab is not the color of a dry unsealed one, and people are sometimes surprised. This is recurring. Sealer wears, particularly where tires turn and where the sun is directly on it, and it wants doing again. We will tell you roughly when rather than letting you assume it is permanent. What is included Washing with a rotary surface cleaner on flatwork, and by hand at the edges A plain account of which stains will lift and which will not Sealer applied to a dry slab Telling you that it darkens the concrete, before we do it Telling you roughly when it will want doing again What is not Removing staining that has penetrated the concrete. Washing takes what is on the surface Sealing a slab that is still wet. It has to dry first and that sets the schedule Working through wind or rain. Wet sealer holds whatever lands in it Asphalt. This is concrete work Why this is recurring here and not elsewhere Two local conditions shorten the interval. The first is sun: 98 days at or above 100°F in 2024, the most on record, with an all-time high of 117°F. The second is grit. The Utah Geological Survey maps wind-blown sand as one of nine adverse construction conditions for this area — most counties do not map blowing sand at all — and the Utah Department of Environmental Quality notes that from spring through fall, high winds combined with dry surface conditions produce dust storms that "can lead to extremely high levels of particulate matter". Sun degrades a sealer from above and wind-driven grit abrades it from the side. That is why sealing here is a maintenance item on a cycle rather than a thing you do once, and anyone who tells you otherwise has not watched a slab here for three summers. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included Will this darken my concrete, and by how much? Which of these stains are coming out? When will this want doing again? Read our Plain Terms Before: the wall as it was. St. George, Utah. What the work is Interior painting is mostly preparation and masking, and the finished room is decided long before the first coat. Nail pops and settlement cracks get cut out and patched, not painted over. Caulk that has split at the trim line is cut out and replaced, because new paint over a split caulk joint splits again in the same place within a season. We wash where washing is needed. Kitchens carry a film of cooking oil that no primer is designed to stick to, and bathrooms carry soap and hairspray. Paint applied over either one fails by peeling in sheets, and it does it a year later, which is long enough that nobody connects the failure to the cause. Then the order of work: ceilings, walls, trim, in that order, because each stage can be cut into the one before it. Everything that is not being painted is masked or moved, floors are covered, and the room is put back the same day it is finished. We paint one room as willingly as a house. A single room is a small job and we price it as one, without the surcharge that gets attached to small work to discourage it. What is included Nail pops, cracks and dents patched, sanded and spot-primed Split caulk lines cut out and re-caulked Greasy or soaped surfaces washed before primer Floors and fixtures covered, switch plates off and back on Ceilings, then walls, then trim The leftover paint labeled with the room it belongs to, and left with you What is not Painting over a wall that is wet, or over a stain whose cause is still active. We find out where the water is coming from first Painting over wallpaper that is lifting. It has to come off, and that is a separate quote Furniture we are not qualified to move: pianos, gun safes, anything on a wall mount What is different here Houses in Washington County are dry, and dry air is not neutral for painting. Water-based paint sets faster than the label assumes, which shortens the window you have to keep a wet edge and makes lap marks easier to leave on a long wall. It is a reason to work in smaller sections and to cut and roll together, rather than a reason to thin the paint. The second thing is dust. Blowing dust settles on freshly coated surfaces through the windows you opened for ventilation, so on a windy day we close the house and ventilate differently. A gritty finish is not a paint defect, it is a scheduling decision somebody made badly. It also warns that any surface preparation short of total removal of the old coating may compromise how long the system lasts. 1 Federal law treats homes built before 1978 differently. Under the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, work that disturbs more than 6 square feet of painted surface in a room inside, or 20 square feet outside, must follow the rule's work practices — and sanding or scraping paint counts as disturbance. Window replacement counts at any size. 1 The rule requires two separate credentials, and they are both checkable by anyone. The company doing the work must be an EPA-certified firm, and a certified renovator, an individual who has passed an accredited course, must be assigned to each job. The preparation is the difference between two years and ten. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the work is Cabinets are the hardest painting in a house, because they are the only surfaces people touch with wet hands, lean on, and hit with cupboard doors every day. Everything that makes a cabinet finish last happens before color goes on. Doors and drawer fronts come off and get labeled so every one goes back to the opening it came from. Hinges and hardware come off rather than getting masked: a sprayed edge around a hinge tells everyone the job was rushed. Then degreasing, because the area beside a range carries cooking oil in the finish, and then deglossing so the primer has something mechanical to hold. We spray rather than brush. A brushed cabinet holds brush marks in exactly the places light rakes across them, and spraying is the only way to get a film that looks like it came from a factory. It is porous, it holds moisture longer than it looks like it does, and when it is new it is chemically aggressive to ordinary coatings until it has cured. Cracks come first. Hairline crazing is cosmetic and a thicker coating can bridge it. A crack that runs in a straight line, or that is wide enough to catch a fingernail, is structural movement and coating over it hides a problem rather than fixing one. We show you which is which before quoting, and we say when the honest answer is a stucco repair by someone who does that work. Efflorescence, the white powdery bloom that appears on masonry, means water is moving through the wall and depositing salts as it evaporates. Coating over it traps the problem and the new finish lifts. It has to be removed and the water source understood first. Then the choice of finish. A thicker elastomeric-type coating bridges hairline cracking and is a common answer on stucco, but it is not automatically the right one: it is less permeable than standard exterior paint, and on a wall that is getting water from somewhere it can hold moisture in. Which one belongs on your house depends on what the wall is doing, and that is a decision we explain rather than one we default to. services_drywall_repair.text: id="main"> Painting · Walls and ceilings Drywall repair and patching Holes, cracks, water damage, and the patch somebody else left standing proud of the wall. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the work is A drywall repair is judged in raking light, which is the light that comes across a wall from a window or a lamp rather than straight at it. A patch that is invisible head-on and obvious from the doorway is a failed repair, and it fails for one of two reasons: the compound was built up instead of feathered out, or the texture was not matched. Small holes get a backer and compound. Anything larger gets a cut-in piece of board fastened to solid framing or to backing we add, because a patch floating on tape moves with the wall and cracks along its edges. Then compound in stages, sanded between, feathered far wider than most people expect. Cracks are diagnosed before they are filled. A crack running from the corner of a door or window is usually settlement, and it will come back if it is filled and nothing else changes. A crack along a joint line is usually a tape failure and stays fixed once it is properly re-taped. Water damage is not repaired until the water is dealt with. Stained board that is still soft has to come out, and the source has to be found. We would rather send you to the roof or to the supply line first than sell you a repair that browns through again in a month. What is included Backing added so patches sit on something solid Compound built in stages and feathered wide, sanded between coats Texture matched to the surrounding wall or ceiling Primed before paint, because bare compound and painted wall absorb differently The repair checked in raking light before we call it done What is not Repairing water-damaged board while the leak is still live Mold remediation, which is a licensed specialty and not something we will improvise Structural crack repair. We will say when a crack is a foundation question rather than a wall one Why the same crack keeps coming back here Washington County sits on ground the Utah Geological Survey calls the most troublesome construction condition it maps: expansive soil and rock, clay that swells when it gets wet and shrinks when it dries. The survey illustrates the hazard with cracks in a Santa Clara house foundation, and the documented damage from the blue clay under this area includes tilted and cracked walls. A house sitting on that does not hold still. So a crack that runs from the corner of a door or a window, and that you have filled before, is usually reporting soil movement rather than a bad patch. Collapsible soil settles when it gets wet, and the water is almost always a leaking irrigation line, a downspout discharging at the foundation, or a failed sewer lateral. Read our Plain Terms What the work is Texture is the reason most drywall repairs look like repairs. The patch is flat and the wall around it is not, so the eye finds it instantly under any light that comes across the surface. Matching is part identification and part practice. Knockdown, orange peel, splatter, skip trowel and hand-applied textures each come from a different tool and a different consistency of compound, and the same name covers a range of coarseness. We test on a board first, hold it against the wall, adjust, and only then shoot the repair. There is an honest limit to this. A texture that was hand-applied by one person twenty years ago has that person's rhythm in it, and an exact match across a large area is not always achievable. When that is the case the better answer is often to retexture a whole wall to a corner, so the eye has no boundary to find, and we will tell you when that is what it takes. Then it gets primed and painted, because new texture absorbs differently from old and a repair that is perfectly matched in texture can still show as a dull patch through the finish coat. What is included The existing texture identified and test-matched on a board first The repair textured to match, feathered into the surrounding surface Primer over new texture before the finish coat An honest answer about whether a wall-to-corner retexture is the better result What is not Matching a texture into a wall we did not repair and cannot see the back of Full-house retexturing, which is a different scope and quoted separately What is on the walls here, and why Of Washington County's 88,415 housing units, 7,613 were built before 1980 and 91% went up in 1980 or later. That is an unusually young housing stock, and it decides what you are matching: the textures that came with those decades are machine-applied knockdown and orange peel, not hand-worked plaster. That is good news for matching. A sprayed and knocked-down texture is repeatable by someone who has done it enough times, and the variation is in the coarseness of the mix and how long it is left before it is knocked down, both of which we test on a board first. The older parts of St. George, Washington City and Hurricane are where it gets harder, and where hand-applied work turns up. There the honest answer is sometimes to retexture a whole wall to the corner rather than chase an exact match across a patch. services_popcorn_removal.text: id="main"> Painting · Walls and ceilings Popcorn ceiling removal Acoustic ceiling texture scraped, the ceiling retextured or smoothed, and repainted. On a house of a certain age it gets tested first. Call (435) 850-0053 Ask for a visit One flat fee to find out what is wrong. You are told it on the phone before anyone is dispatched, and it comes off the job if you hire us. Read our Plain Terms What the work is Popcorn removal is a wet-scrape job. The texture is misted so it releases instead of powdering, scraped off in sections, and then the ceiling underneath is repaired: scraping reveals every seam, every fastener and every place the original crew relied on the texture to hide their finishing. That repair stage is most of the work and it is the stage that gets skipped. A scraped ceiling that goes straight to paint shows its seams forever, and a ceiling is the one surface in a house that is lit from every angle. Age matters here, and not for cosmetic reasons. Acoustic ceiling texture in older houses can contain asbestos, and federal rules govern how surfaces in pre-1978 housing are disturbed for lead as well. On a house old enough for either to be in play, the correct order is testing first and scraping second. We will not guess, and we will not scrape a ceiling that has not been cleared. The practical side: the room is emptied or everything in it is sealed, floors are covered wall to wall, and the scraping stage is genuinely messy even when it is done carefully. It is a room-at-a-time job and we plan it with you around where you sleep. What is included Testing before scraping on houses old enough to require it Floors and any remaining contents fully covered and sealed Wet scraping, then seam and fastener repair across the whole ceiling New texture or a smooth finish, primed and painted What is not Asbestos abatement. If a test comes back positive, the work goes to a licensed abatement contractor and we say so plainly Scraping a ceiling that has already been painted over multiple times without telling you first that it may not release cleanly Ceilings with active water staining, until the source is fixed What is different here Washington County's housing stock skews new by national standards, and most of the subdivisions that fill the county went up long after acoustic ceilings went out of fashion. But the older parts of St. George, Washington City and Hurricane have plenty of houses that are old enough to need testing first, and that is a question about the address rather than about the county. If your house predates the late seventies, treat testing as part of the job rather than an upsell. Anyone who offers to scrape it the same afternoon without asking the age of the house is telling you something about how they work. What to ask anyone quoting this, us included How old is my house, and does that mean this has to be tested first? Who does the testing, and do I get the result? What happens to the ceiling after it is scraped, and who repairs the seams? Smooth or retextured, and what does each one cost? How do you contain the mess?
